Dylan Saccoccio Mythological Imperialism Dylan traces the name Jason back through Etruscan Hason and Celtic Esus to a bronze mirror inscribed HEASUN, arguing the story reached Greece rather than starting there. Etruscan city states held their own treasuries at Delphi, the Colchian dragon from this same myth still rides the Alfa Romeo crest, and the tombs and inscriptions across ancient Italy are non-Greek down to the paintings. The claim isn't that the Greeks invented nothing, it's that they inherited a Golden Fleece story from an older Italian priesthood and passed it off as their own. The Manuscript Gap The oldest complete Argonautica comes from Apollonius of Rhodes in the third century BC, a thousand years after the voyage supposedly happened, and the so-called Orphic Argonautica, once circulated as far older, is a fifteenth-century Renaissance forgery exposed by its own late Greek vocabulary. Homer and Hesiod mention Jason centuries earlier as though their audience already knew the story, but no surviving text tells it in full until long after those passing references. A physical fragment at Delphi, dated to around 480 BC, is the oldest artifact that might show the myth in Greece, and even that identification rests on guesswork. Astrotheology of the Golden Fleece The oldest surviving description of Jason's destination places it where the rays of the sun rest in a golden storeroom, Medea escapes in a chariot drawn by her grandfather Helios, and the fleece itself hangs in a grove sacred to Ares, the same root behind Aries, the ram, and the Lamb of God. Jason's upbringing by the foster parent Chiron echoes Moses, Dionysus, and Christ, and the Argo constellation is missing its stern, the exact detail the myth explains by having it sheared off at the Clashing Rocks. Yesun and the Priesthood's Favorite Title In the Greek of Matthew 1:21, the name rendered "Jesus" is closer to Yesun, sharing a root with Kyrios and Kiros, the same title behind the historical King Cyrus and the Curetes, the priests who guarded the infant Zeus. Dylan and Chance argue this isn't wordplay for its own sake, it's the same divine-son title recycled onto a different figure in a different tradition. Myth as a Deed to Someone Else's Land Alexander's own historians told the Armenians they were long-lost Greeks descended from the Argonaut Armenus, Strabo records a temple to Jason built by Alexander's top general, and Pindar's Pythian Four uses Medea's prophecy to hand a living king a mythological deed to a Libyan colony. Every version follows the same shape: claim ancestral kinship with a place first, and the conquest that follows reads as a homecoming instead of a hostile taking. Once you see the template, Chance and Dylan argue, you start seeing it everywhere in history.

Chance Garton The Water Tower That Survived The sharpest objection here is architectural. If the 1871 fire was a bombing run meant to erase old world buildings, why does so much grand stone still stand? William W. Boyington's Water Tower, finished in 1869 out of Joliet limestone, came through in full glory while its neighbors fell, and Oscar Wilde disliked it enough to call it a castellated monstrosity with pepper boxes stuck all over it in 1882. Old St. Patrick's from 1856, the Henry B. Clarke House from 1836, and Holy Family all survived. The Sherman House was rebuilt bigger, and the fire took only about a third of the city. A City Framed In Pine Chicago invented the building method that fed the fire. George Washington Snow framed a warehouse without hand cut joints in 1832, and a couple of years later the carpenter Augustine Taylor nailed St. Mary's Church together from light 2x4s for about $400, a technique mocked as balloon construction until it became known instead as Chicago construction. Its wall cavities ran from foundation to roof with no fire stops. Add roughly 60,000 buildings that were about 90 percent wood, 561 miles of raised plank sidewalk, 57 miles of tar coated wood block street, and one inch of rain from July to October. Nobody Left To Fight It The fire department was already broken before the first alarm sounded. In the six days before October 8, Chicago's roughly 185 to 219 firemen answered 27 alarms and worked 24 fires, then spent 14 to 17 hours on the Saturday night Red Flash fire that leveled four blocks of lumber yards and mills and cost a million dollars. Hook and Ladder Company 1 lost all of its apparatus, two steam engines were disabled, and Engine Company 6 reached the O'Leary barn after 22 hours of work and one hour of rest. Watchman Matthias Schaefer then misjudged the location by a mile, and the telegraph operator refused to correct the box. Rubble Without Bombs The Tartaria case leans on how much the ruins resemble Dresden after Allied incendiary bombing, and Chance grants the resemblance before explaining it. Nineteenth century mortar most likely lost its integrity somewhere around 600 to 800 degrees, while a fuel rich structural fire easily reaches 1,200, 1,400, even 2,000, so unbound brick simply collapsed into chaotic piles. Local Lemont limestone heated past 1,500 degrees becomes quicklime and crumbles to powder. The blurry roof edges offered as proof of hidden airships are halation, a known glass plate effect. Even the Tribune's fireproof 1869 headquarters burned, undone by paper, archives, and linseed oil ink. Who Cashed In Fastest The city's own 11th annual Board of Public Works report from July 1872 tallies about $200 million lost across 1,687 acres, names no cause, and the cause has stayed undetermined ever since. What followed is documented. Three days after the fire, Mayor Roswell Mason handed authority to Lieutenant General Philip Sheridan under effective martial law that guarded bank rubble instead of feeding anyone. Two days later he routed every relief dollar, five to ten million of it, to the private Chicago Relief and Aid Society, which closed its books with $600,000 unspent. Within 30 days Joseph Medill won the mayoralty by 46 points.

Dylan Saccoccio The Eyewitness Tartaria Never Had Every old world reset story runs into the same hole: if settlers walked into finished cities, somebody's ancestor would have said so, in a journal, a diary, a passed down story. A YouTuber named Logan, of the channel Luminary Lighthouse, thought he finally had that account when a viewer named Jack Crowley commented that his ancestor, commissioned a high mason in New York, guided seventy five people to a fully built town in Kansas in 1840, all granite, with a capital type building in the middle, and a hidden journal to prove it. That journal is never produced, never even mentioned on air. What Council Grove Actually Records Council Grove takes its name from an 1825 treaty made under John Quincy Adams, in which Osage chiefs guaranteed passage along the Santa Fe Trail for an eight hundred dollar payoff. Commissioner George Champlain Sibley wrote on August 5, 1825 that he suggested the name and had it carved into an oak, a tree whose bark closed over the letters before photography existed. Seth Hays, grandson of Daniel Boone, put up the first cabin in 1847. Old photographs at kansasmemory.gov show wood framed shops, a railroad depot in 1869, and brick only after the 1886 fire. No granite, no capitol. Two Crowleys, One Broken Line The records are not close. A Morris County cemetery survey lists JJ Crowley with the 47th New York Infantry; New York's own regimental roster shows Crowley, John, aged twenty three, mustered in as a private on February 27, 1865, which puts his birth near 1842, two years after the town he supposedly founded. Allen Crowley, 1822 to 1891, reached the area in the 1850s and appears in a 1921 local history only as one of the old settlers, holding no county office. A public family tree names JJ's father as James Crowley, so Allen was never his father, and the two lines look unrelated. The Cropped Encyclopedia Page Rather than check any of this, Logan screen shared a page from the 1912 Kansas Encyclopedia of State History with the right margin cut off, then read it aloud as calling Allen Crowley the pioneer of the Neosho Valley, dropping the words that made him one of the pioneers. In a private message he conceded the dates were all wrong and offered Allen as a substitute ancestor, yet never corrected it on stream, and the video swings back to JJ. The Dutch priest and humanist printed his Greek New Testament in 1516, then again in 1519, 1522 and 1527, and that text became the Textus Receptus standing behind the King James of 1611. Chance sets this beside the wider humanist era, when Poggio Bracciolini hunted manuscripts of antiquity for a pope offering a bag of gold, and beside Erasmus's own letters to Luigi Marliano and Justus Jonas about concealing truth and keeping mysteries reserved for initiates. Christopher McIntosh The Hermetic Baptism and a Roundabout Road to Paganism McIntosh opens with what he now calls his hermetic baptism. At two or three years old, in the main quadrangle of Christ Church, Oxford, where his father lectured, he leaned too far over the fountain pool to watch the goldfish and fell in beneath the statue of Mercury, or Hermes, and his father hauled him out. He was never baptized as an infant, since both parents came from a nonconformist background, and when the usual age arrived he declined. He argues that this linear habit has migrated from religion into secular life, telling architects and artists never to look back, privileging the present over the past and eroding local cultural memory until only a global monoculture is left. His first book, written in his early twenties, was a history of astrology. Many Gods, One Source, and the Polytheistic Mind Garton cites Augustine's City of God, where Augustine grants that the pagan gods exist but argues they are all facets of Jove, and asks whether the one and the many are two ways of seeing the same thing. McIntosh offers the Indian parallel of one supreme god with many deities beneath him, yet resists the monotheistic road because it ends in a uniform liturgy imposed everywhere. He praises James Hillman's Re-Visioning Psychology for arguing that polytheism reads the psyche better, since human beings are many people under one roof, and says he regards the gods as egregores raised by generations of shared worship. Rune Circles, the Norns, and Gardens as Sacred Ground McIntosh's practice is rooted in place. He has laid a circle of flat rune stones in his garden dedicated to the Norns, where shifting sunlight, a fallen leaf or a passing insect turns the circle into an oracle, and he practices stav, a Norwegian system of runic postures, daily. Skuld, the future Norn, is shown half veiled, which he reads as wyrd, a pattern that influences a life without wholly determining it. He credits the Scottish poet Ian Hamilton Finlay, whose Pentland Hills garden held image poems and an Apollo temple, with teaching him that tradition is a set of lessons, not a chain.

Craig Koniver Walking Away From The Prescription Pad Koniver opened his Charleston, South Carolina practice in 2006 and describes stepping out of what he calls the pharmaceutical model, where the visit is spent managing a patient's medicines rather than the patient. He rejects the functional medicine label too, arguing it simply swaps pharmaceuticals for nutraceuticals and leaves people on thirty to fifty supplements a day while still treating this for that. He calls his own approach performance medicine, helping people perform at any age rather than chasing an abstract longevity target, and he tells Chance Garton that peptides, hormones and nutrients are a bridge, never the destination. Cortisol, The Sun, And The Anabolic Night On the architecture of the day, Koniver argues we are wired to be catabolic while the sun is up, driven by cortisol, and anabolic at night, when testosterone, growth hormone and melatonin take over the work of repair. He points to the stretch from 10 p.m. to 2 a.m. as the period of heaviest growth hormone output, says his clinic uses saliva cortisol testing across a twenty four hour period, and contends that cortisol also acts as a buffer against inflammation. Chance Garton hears the word itself as core and sol, heart and sun, a poetic reading rather than an etymology. Eight Hours Is Made Up, Dreaming Is Not Koniver is openly skeptical that anyone truly understands sleep, calling the eight hour standard elusive and made up, and noting that people in primitive times woke repeatedly to tend a fire and napped through the day. He suspects dream time may matter more than repair time. Chance Garton answers with his own account: his daughter, six months old at the time of recording, announced herself in a dream before his wife knew she was pregnant. Both land on the same complaint, that we are qualitative organisms living in a quantitative world of wearables, lab values and invented reference ranges. Symptoms As Messages, Not Enemies Both men treat symptoms as information rather than adversaries. Koniver says pain and illness are there for us, not to us, and goes as far as calling a cancer diagnosis the greatest gift someone could be given because of the correction it invites. He lays out five questions he works through with people, what am I, what do I do, how do I do it, who am I, and why, plus three biological temperaments he names self worth, self love and self safety. He links the self love pattern to worn out mitochondria and argues negative self banter takes a real toll. Informed Consent And A Doctor's Own Emergency Late in the hour Koniver describes the mitochondrial tools his practice is known for, NAD plus and methylene blue, framing them as the early tangible wins that give people confidence to think bigger. Chance Garton raises the criticism methylene blue has drawn online, and Koniver replies that he has found few negatives in his own clinical experience. Both then turn to informed consent, which Koniver argues no longer exists in medicine because patients are told only part of the story. He closes with his August 2020 hospitalization, which he frames publicly as the moment he felt closest to God, and with his refusal to franchise, wanting better rather than more.

Chance Garton Mind First, Matter Second Within minutes the two find common ground: reality begins in thought and only later hardens into matter. Sonja Testerman describes people as bundles of frequency that thicken into density, arguing that everything traces back to what she calls God sourced thought. Chance Garton flips the usual framing, insisting the body sits inside the mind rather than the mind inside the body, and offers that as the deepest explanation for why frequency based healing works at all. Testerman adds that physicality is roughly ten percent of reality, an afterthought pushed through from the unseen, with each frame of it built as we go. A Friendly Disagreement About Chakras Testerman presents the chakra system as a lockdown grid, claiming the top centers are coming off first so the whole brain can come online, and she ties this to an ongoing physical ascension in which organs relocate and glands enlarge. Garton pushes back gently. In his biofield tuning practice the energy centers are not a cage but an intellectual scaffolding for understanding how energy behaves, even if for many people they do function as limiters. He argues for languaging all of it in terms of empowerment rather than victimhood, so that newcomers on a Kundalini path are not handed fresh paranoia. Inside a Biofield Tuning Session Garton walks through the mechanics: an energy field roughly six feet in radius that he treats as mind and memory, read like the rings of a tree, where distance from the body maps to age. Working by phone, with crystals and candles standing in for the client's body on a table, he sweeps a tuning fork and listens for dissonance, noting its height, left or right, front or back. He describes tracing one client's pattern of frustration back to a C section birth, and another whose lifelong picky eating dissolved after a session touching father conditioning, followed by weight loss and new food cravings. Symptoms, Parasites and a Business Model The conversation turns sharply against mainstream medicine. Testerman argues there is no such thing as flu, that symptoms are the body detoxing and should be embraced, and that doctors a century and a half ago focused mainly on parasite control until, she claims, powerful banking families removed it and cancer appeared. She lists garlic, oregano oil, clove and cinnamon as everyday parasite fighters. Garton raises pleomorphism, the notion that bacteria shift form according to what the body needs cleaned up, and notes that germ means seed while biotic means life. These are contested claims well outside accepted medical science, presented as the speakers' own view. Sky as Playbook, Sky as Reflection Both reject standard cosmology, though they part ways on what the sky actually is. Testerman says the star map has not shifted in eight thousand years and points to sextant navigation and trigonometry as proof of a flat, domed reality, then recounts a remote viewing session in which Venus appeared as a self replicating crystal geode beaming to the North Star, together forming a nine dimensional projector broadcasting a playbook of events. Garton prefers reflection to projection, describing one life expressing itself as a melody with infinite instruments, and suggests deep alignment with imagination lets you play the score rather than be entrained by it.

Brandon Sterling From News Arrows to the Smart Money World Sterling traces his interest back to watching the up and down arrows on the news as a child, and to the 2008 crisis, which hit his father's work in the trades. The film The Big Short, about Michael Burry, showed him that traders could make money on markets going down as well as up. He says he began taking it seriously in 2019 after noticing hundreds of CEOs resign that fall, which he read as the sign of a coming black swan, then learned from mentors who had worked at pension funds, investment banks and hedge funds before trading his own capital. Saturn, Mercury and the Alchemy of Time Garton builds the episode's central image from a medieval alchemical engraving of Cronos, or Saturn, cutting Mercury off at the knees, and from Tracey Twyman's book Money Grows on the Tree of Knowledge, which argues that money only appears to be created ex nihilo and is really drawn from something intangible, time and human labor measured over time. Sterling supplies the modern figure on his slide: at a US average wage near thirty dollars an hour it now takes roughly 187 hours of work to buy one share of the S&P 500, against ten to twenty hours fifty years ago. Money Velocity and the Speeding Up of Life Sterling's slides argue that a thirty year mortgage has buyers paying for more than two houses once interest is counted, and that a 401k or IRA leaves a person long only and exposed to events like the 2020 crash. Garton reads Twyman on fractional reserve lending and money velocity, where a recession is a lack of velocity rather than simply a lack of money, and where inflating the supply while wages stay pegged to time means working longer for the same value as youth drains away. Garton calls the constant recession talk part of the spell. Pump and Dumps and the Trader as Sacrifice Sterling calls himself probably the world's biggest hater of crypto, describing Bitcoin as pure speculation with nothing backing it and the wave of celebrity coins as pump and dumps in the mold of Beanie Babies. He argues day trading works the same way, with online gurus telling followers to copy their trades and using them as liquidity to get out, and citing a Berkeley study he says ninety percent of day traders lose ninety percent of their money within ninety days. Garton reads Twyman on mortgage as death pledge and bond as bondage, calling the churn a sacrificial machine. Temple Coins, Put Options and Chosen Sacrifice Garton traces hedging back to Juno Moneta, the Roman goddess of memory and warning whose temple housed the mint, arguing that every coin was a receipt for a sacrifice and a hedge against divine wrath, and that where the ancients offered goats, wheat and incense, the modern trader offers a put option. Sterling defines a hedge as a trade made to reduce the risk of an adverse price move, answers Garton's ethics question by calling trading amoral because money and the corporate charter are artificial, and says he uses panicked headlines as liquidity to exit his positions.
extra.steve-falconer-scamtarctica: Beyond the Ice Wall (Music Video) Chance's Introduction Steve Challenges The Final Experiment Scamtarctica Exposed: Steve Falconer's Breakdown Zetetic Science & Observational Proofs Base Misdirection & Disputed South Pole Locations Antarctica as Inverted Tower of Babel Copyright, Strawman Law & Cosmological Commerce Sun Angles, Daylength Anomalies & Gleason's Geometry Latitude Claims, Time Zones & Compass Distortions Scamtarctica Part Three: Bases on the Gleason Map Circumnavigation Claims, Compasses, and Expedition Science Plus+ Extension Teaser Truthfully, I've never seen anything but a one-way conversion from globe to flat. Chance Garton I've gone through now and researched all of the old Antarctic expeditions from the late 1500s to the mid 1900s. Nobody has ever mentioned a 24-hour sun. Steve Falconer The nations are uniting, but not to find enlightenment and raise up to the center to seek God and truth, but they're actually at the periphery to obscure the truth. Chance Garton That's what we're doing, we're going out pretending to be our all caps name on a fake spinning ball in a fake universe that doesn't exist on a fake calendar that doesn't exist. Chance Garton I found no, not a one, not even on the same base. Like three different websites, sometimes four, on the same base, they can't agree. Steve Falconer This is again why you can't call it the final experiment, when you have people going down to do experiments. Steve Falconer It's crazy, it's literally endless, because the lie is really flimsy and a million different observations will prove to you that that's not a ball you're standing on. Steve Falconer The Final Experiment Under the Microscope Chance Garton opens with the wave of headlines announcing that flat-earthers had reverted to the globe, and Steve Falconer argues the Antarctic trip was never an experiment at all: no control, no certainty about where the group actually stood, and no proof the light they filmed was the sun. He notes that Austin, the other flat-earth traveler, did not change his position and is almost never mentioned in the coverage. Falconer says he has since read Antarctic expedition journals from the late 1500s to the mid 1900s and found no mention of a 24-hour sun, only night, dusk and next morning. One Fact Cannot Cancel Another Chance reads a passage from the old Zetetic Astronomy book that Falconer had used in his first film, arguing that one fact can never contradict another and that both must be true. Falconer builds his answer around it, contending that a light in the sky over Antarctica cannot erase the lock and canal engineering he cites through New York State, Rochester and the Suez Canal, where he argues a roughly 630 foot cascade of curvature would be required and is absent. He also points to English law books that he says instruct engineers to assume a flat datum line and a plumb line. Why Falconer Thinks the Model Is Guarded Asked whether Antarctica functions as an inverted tower of Babel, with nations gathering at the periphery to obscure rather than seek the truth, Falconer contends the stakes are physics, religion and money at once. He argues everything is a toroidal field and that light is a perturbation in the ether, so a sealed perimeter would take Newtonian particle physics down with it. He contends that the Vatican's Unam Sanctam bull and the Gregorian calendar underwrite a copyright over name, date and place, comparing the all caps straw man to performing as Harry Potter and owing the author. He points listeners to Stephen Young's Fool's Wisdom. Day Lengths, Latitude Rings and Sun Trackers In the middle stretch Falconer describes auditing sunrise, sunset and day length figures for Antarctic stations across Wikipedia, Google Earth, Stellarium and time and date sites. He says three or four sources can disagree about the very same base, differing on when its 24-hour sun begins by anywhere from two days to about twenty-five, with one outlier he threw out after tracing it to two stations with similar names. He argues that matching latitudes north and south should share day lengths and do not. Chance adds that clock time and time zones impose uniformity while dividing people from one another. Mapping the Bases and the Old Expeditions For the final stretch Falconer previews part three of Scamtarctica, made with a mapmaker named Rob and his returning Spacebusters partner Ross, plotting stations and expedition tracks onto Alex Gleason's flat map. He raises the SANAE IV knife story, where a crew was reported stranded for 190 days although Troll Station and other bases sit within a couple hundred miles on the globe, and argues those gaps widen along an ice wall perimeter. He questions the South Pole base location against Scott's journal coordinates, notes that the round-Antarctica yacht race stops at Cape Town, India and Australia, and blames phone magnets for the trip's compass trouble.
extra.james-frosch-family-fungi-2025: Music Food & Medicine Are the First Solutions Meet James Frosch of Family Fungi Compost, Chocolate Cake Soil & Mycelium Mushroom Farming as Spiritual Practice The Circle of Life is Real Work Gardening as Emotional Healing From Illness to Sovereignty Beginner Mushrooms: Oyster, Reishi & Wine Cap Fungi as Ecosystem Builders Weeds Are Messages From the Earth The Garden is Your Teacher Gratitude & Closing Reflections I'm just getting the waste stream from this lumber mill. James Frosch People look at food like putting gas in a car and it doesn't matter what the food is. As long as the tank is full, I'm fueled. Chance Garton Oysters are the first one because they're the easiest, they're the most available and they can take some neglect and still keep going. James Frosch Spent Mushroom Blocks Become Garden Soil Frosch describes Family Fungi as a mushroom farm whose most valuable output is not the mushrooms but the spent mycelium blocks left after one or two flushes, which stop being commercially viable once they take up shelf space. He drives 25 to 30 minutes to a local sawmill, takes the hardwood waste stream from lumber headed into people's houses, grows it out, then returns it to the ground. In South Louisiana, with its very high water table and heavy clay, he says the blocks need about eight months to break down into something he compares to rich Dutch chocolate cake, and stacked in thirties they keep fruiting in the garden. Quantity Farming Versus Qualitative Nourishment Garton argues that people treat food like putting gas in a car, judging only whether the tank is full, while Frosch calls boxed products food stuff: made from food, but no longer food. Frosch says he takes issue with organic labeling loopholes, observes that hurricane shelves empty first of pop tarts and beer, and estimates his family produces roughly 20 percent of its calories from about a quarter acre of intensive perennial and mixed annual planting on their four acres. Garton frames industrialization as a genuine answer to an old problem, feeding everyone, that has now produced a new one worth tackling. Where A Beginner Should Start With Fungi Asked what a novice should cultivate, Frosch names oyster mushrooms first: easy at home from a grow kit or from spawn on hardwood sawdust, expandable into fresh wood chips or freshly cut logs, widely available and forgiving of neglect. He puts reishi second, grown on a countertop, harvested fresh and dehydrated for tea, or extracted in neutral spirits such as vodka or brandy, with the 190 proof organic alcohol his farm uses as one option and a charcoal filter recommended for vodka. Third is king stropharia, the wine cap or garden giant, which he says will only fruit with soil organisms and a casing layer. Soil As A Living Sub Aquatic System Frosch separates saprotrophic fungi that break down hardwood from mycorrhizal fungi that partner with tree roots, calling the latter the unsung heroes of the food chain for extending root systems enormously and mining minerals with acids like oxalic acid that plants cannot produce. He cites a line he heard from Matt Powers and John Kempf that soil is a sub aquatic system, roughly 20,000 gallons of water per acre in the first foot. He also reports that oyster mushrooms can remediate nematodes, which cause the root knot that once cost him a whole sweet potato harvest. Weeds, Books And Permission To Start Frosch's land was a strawberry plantation 60 to 70 years ago and pine forest savanna before that, and he says it was strip mined for minerals, so he now reads weeds like thistle as indicators of deficiency, uses no herbicides, and mulches or does a chop and drop instead. For study he points to the Louisiana Herb Journal, Matt Powers on regenerative soil, John Kempf on bio fertilizers, and Masanobu Fukuoka's One Straw Revolution and The Natural Way of Farming. He describes the great mother tea his wife Elise first blended for herself, warns against expert-itis, and says a few pots on a balcony is enough to begin.
extra.inner-whirled-14: Welcome & Inner Whirled 14: The Hidden Meaning of "Amen" The Word Amon, Omen, and the Ammonian Radicals Why Wisdom Was Always Hidden in Plain Sight Charles Blount and the Two Levels of Sacred Knowledge Why the Lord Is Not the Same as God Jehovah, Yova, and the Verb "to Fall" Adonai, Adonis, and the Mysterious Name in the Psalms The Adonis Mythology and Its Christian Echoes The Tetractys and the Four-Letter Sacred Name Bull Horns, the Evil Eye, and the Phoenician Problem Faber, the Zend-Avesta, and the Etruscan Genesis Psalm 90, Adonai, and the Danger of Translation Atlantis, Invented History, and Judicial Astrology Forcing the Status Quo to Admit It Doesn't Know You ever wonder why Christians say amen at the end of their prayer? Chance Garton If you can read Etruscan, you can read Amen. It just looks like O-M-N, and that is literally closer to omen. Dylan Saccoccio Simply telling a student the answers, especially through writing, was more harmful than helpful, but leaving breadcrumbs to be deciphered would bring the student into true wisdom and knowledge. Chance Garton Why would God, the creator of this world, who can destroy and remake it, worry about priests and false prophets? Dylan Saccoccio If Dylan's research points to the truth about that, then the whole Genesis story does seem to be an Etruscan story. Chance Garton I think everybody getting to that base level of conceding we don't know will be more valuable for us as a whole than everybody fighting over what they think is true. Dylan Saccoccio Why "Amen" May Be the Name of a Hidden God The episode opens on a question Chance Garton says he put to his own father: why do Christians say amen at the end of a prayer? Dylan Saccoccio argues the word is not a Hebrew formula of assent but the name Ammon, written in Etruscan and Phoenician as the bare consonants O-M-N, with the vowel filled in later. He contends it sits closer to the Latin omen than to anything Semitic, and that the so-called kingdom of Ammon near modern Israel is a misattribution for a system he traces to the Italian peninsula. Esotericism and the Useful Lies of the Ancients Chance lays out a long case that ancient priests and philosophers hid their real doctrines on purpose, for defense against charges of heresy or atheism, and for social stability. He cites the noble lie of Plato's Republic and the Athenian doctrine of autochthony, the claim that ancestors sprang from the soil with the tools of their caste already in hand, as a story that justified conquest and kept the lower castes in place. He collects mottoes from Ovid, from Epicurus, and from Bishop Synesius of Cyrene, who advised loving wisdom at home and embracing fables abroad, alongside Proverbs 25:2. Charles Blount, Robert Taylor, and the Lord Who Is Not God Chance reads at length from Charles Blount's 1680 Great Is Diana of the Ephesians, on how princes governed an unruly creature through hope and fear, raising in the conscience what Blount calls a whip of torture, the fear of future punishment. Dylan then turns to Robert Taylor's Astronomico-Theological Lectures, written in prison, and to Taylor's warning never to confound the Lord with God. Taylor treats them as particular and general terms, reading Judges 11:24 and Jephthah's bargain with the children of Ammon as evidence that each nation claimed its own tutelary planet rather than a universal deity. Yova, Adonai and the Sun That Hides in Winter The thumbnail quote is Psalm 89:46, which Dylan renders not as Lord but as Jove or Yova, how long will you hide. He derives the name from hava, to fall or to become, the same letters read elsewhere as Eve and as life, separated only by context. From Adonai the hosts move to Adonis, following Taylor's claim that Adon is the same as Baal, the Lord common to Jupiter, Bacchus, Apollo and Osiris. Chance walks through the Adonis myth, Myrrha turned into the myrrh tree, the buried seed, the fostering by Persephone, and a death and resurrection. Horns, Precession, and the Etruscan Origin Thesis Chance reads Godfrey Higgins sorting bull headed gods from ram headed ones as successive precessional ages, Taurus giving way to Aries, with the Alexander coin bearing the horns of Ammon and a bull horned Buddha from Persia. Dylan counters that the horns may track local herding instead, and offers the Italian malocchio, bull horns hung over shops to ward off evil, as the root of the rock and roll hand sign. He closes on method, arguing that translation forces liberties nobody should cling to, and that his aim is forcing the status quo to concede it does not know.

The Pleasure Path and the Marshmallow Plant Eileen McKusick describes what she calls the pleasure path, a day built out of treats: sitting worshipfully with a morning hot beverage, hugging people and telling them you love them, sucking the marrow out of the ordinary. She says she has no interest in ascending to 5D and would rather make 3D better, and that making your coffee really good is literally enlightenment. Chance Garton reframes this as enlightened hedonism that is about gratitude rather than gratification. Kyle Denton answers with marshmallow, the plant, describing its emollient mucilaginous root, its sweet and salty flavor and its five petaled flower as a picture of softening dryness. Chance Garton The Wheel and Its Center Chance Garton and Mario Garza build the episode around Rene Guenon's The Reign of Quantity and the Signs of the Times, a book Garza says many readers consider Guenon's magnum opus and which Garton read in full before the stream. Garza uses a wheel as the master image, with the hub standing for the primordial tradition, principal unity and the sacred center, and the rim standing for multiplicity, earth and materialism. Garza relays Guenon's claim that a cycle quickens toward its end like a wheel rolling downhill, while Garton adds Guenon's stranger figure of the circle bending into a cube until motion halts and the age begins again. Vocation Against the Machine Both men linger on Guenon's chapters on the artisan, where each person fulfilled the function implicit in his own nature and, Garza says, every occupation carried a priesthood or guild behind it. Garton reads Guenon's line that the machine is in a sense the opposite of the tool, since the tool prolongs the man while the machine reduces him to its servant, and that if the tool engenders the craft, the machine kills it. Garza contrasts a traditional household, where nothing was anonymously made, with an office full of objects of unknown origin, and Garton frames his own show as vocational expression won by a leap of faith. When Number Becomes Reality Garton carries the argument into science, noting that modern chemistry appropriated the word element to mean a census of materials distinguished by counted particles, so hydrogen and helium differ by one proton rather than by essence. He revisits Zeno's paradox of Achilles and the tortoise as an early protest against atomism, points out that quantum is itself just a reference to quantity, and argues that much of astrophysics amounts to numbers fed into computer simulations. He quotes Guenon's formulation that quantity is never that which is measured but that by which things are measured, then ties the same inversion to the hard problem of consciousness. Coinage Gold and Bitcoin Garza raises Guenon's chapter on the degeneration of coinage, describing coins as sacred totems whose worth lay in their iconography before value collapsed into purchasing power, and citing an uncollected Guenon article arguing that gold was so sacred that owning it made no sense. Garton adds a philological weave linking coin, cohen, king and Cain, and reads Tubal-cain as Vulcan through the interchange of vav and bet. He recalls that old gold was tested by biting it, sets that against Bitcoin's digital coin logo and talk of universal basic income, and reads Mr. Beast's contestant counts and prize totals as the reign of quantity on screen. Cain Abel and Subjective Time Garza summarizes Guenon's Cain and Abel chapter as a contest between sedentary and nomadic peoples, with settled cultures favoring the plastic arts of agriculture, architecture and image while nomads favor music and poetry, arts that unfold over time. He links the pattern to Romulus and Remus and to a documentary about a Mongolian herder blocked by borders and taxes from following the swans. Garton separates the compressive clock time of uniform working weeks from the expansive subjective time of music festivals, and recounts moments when time paused for him entirely. He also reads Guenon's warning that animals counted too often die in greater numbers.
extra.camille-sauve-sorcerers-of-stone: Stone Sites the Textbooks Cannot Explain Alfredo Gamara's Three Ages of Stone Hananpacha, the Strange Layer Underneath Everything Huacas, Seke Lines and Charged Rock Portals, Chanting and People Who Vanish Tesla, Darwin and the Expanding Earth Graham Hancock and 300 Flood Legends Lionel Wafer and the Dorian Tribe Screen Share: Fingerprints Pressed Into Rock The Boulder That Crushed 3,000 Men Russian Geologists Say Geopolymer, Not Quarry Why 94 Years of Inca Fails This is the most mysterious and magical of all the types of constructions that one can find here in Peru. Camille Sauvé Three Ages of Stone Stacked on Top of Each Other Camille Sauvé builds much of her book Sorcerers of Stone on the work of a Cuscanian researcher named Alfredo Gamara, who identified three distinct construction styles in Peru and called them Hananpacha, Uranpacha and Ukupacha. Her central visual argument is over building: an older style sits underneath the megalithic work, and the far more recent Inca, Kilke and Ware masonry sits on top of and around both, often fitted into the grooves and recesses of the oldest layer. Sauvé argues that later cultures recognized this earlier work as sacred and deliberately built into it rather than replacing it. The Hananpacha Layer Nobody Talks About Sauvé says the megalithic walls get all the attention while the stranger, older Hananpacha work goes largely unstudied. These are gray metamorphosed limestone forms that read as art projects rather than buildings: stepped chicanas, carved basins, surreal shapes with no windows, doorways or ceilings and no obvious use as shelter. She reports finding the same forms far outside Peru, in Japan, Bulgaria, Germany, beneath the Egyptian pyramids, and in the foundation stone under the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, where both Jewish and Muslim tradition place the creation of the earth. That global spread, she contends, points toward a single worldwide civilization. Seke Lines, Charged Rock and Doorways to Elsewhere Sauvé describes 42 seke lines radiating out from the Coricancha sun temple in Cusco, with the huacas, or sacred sites, placed directly along them. She suggests these lines follow fracture zones and underground water passages, creating discontinuity zones where telluric currents flow and where quartz rich rock can hold electromagnetic charge. Andean pacos and shamans still come to these places to pray to the Apus and Pachamama and, she believes, to enter altered states. She recounts Jim Wills reportedly opening a portal at Aramu Muru near Lake Titicaca by chanting three tones, and local legends of people vanishing while singing at these doorways. Expanding Earth, Pangaea and the Global Flood Record Garton and Sauvé chase the possibility that the earth itself has grown. Sauvé notes that Nikola Tesla, Newton and Darwin all entertained expansion, with Darwin reading stepped coastal layers in Patagonia as evidence and Tesla describing a condensation of etheric material swelling every celestial body. She cites Ben Noel of the Ben Franklin Theoretical Research Institute of Australia proposing 200 million years, while stressing that none of this is concrete truth. Alongside it she stacks roughly 300 worldwide flood legends, the Aymara language's reported kinship with Japanese, and a proto Sumerian inscribed bowl unearthed near Tiwanaku. Geopolymers Versus the Quarry and Copper Chisel Story The strongest thread is Sauvé's case that these stones were poured, not carved. She points to scoop marks about four inches wide, pressed in fingerprint like impressions in the living rock, and vitrification that would require roughly 1400 Celsius. She recounts Russian geologists invited by Peru's Ministry of Culture in 2012 who tested about 30 samples, found a microcrystalline structure with the fossils pulverized out, and concluded geopolymer, an answer the Ministry disliked. Garton reads Garcilaso de la Vega's account of 20,000 men hauling one boulder that fell and crushed more than 3,000, and calls the quarrying story comical.

Chance Garton Nature Is Alive Matthew Wood traces his whole path back to a Quaker childhood, tenth generation, and a first day school teacher named Francis Hole, a soil science professor from Madison who took the children up Rib Mountain near Wausau, Wisconsin and radiated one conviction: nature is alive. Wood says he knew instantly it was true, and draws from it a shamanic rule he has kept since, that you must honor a revelation from the spirit or you will not be gifted that way again. Visiting Hole decades later, he was told he had chosen his profession well, because people crave to know nature is alive and cannot find the way there. What the Word Medicine Actually Means Pressed by Chance Garton for a definition broader than the allopathic one, Wood explains that for American Indian people medicine cannot be practiced without an inspiration, a vision or a dream, and that elder councils at the green corn dance would weigh the dreams of young people for what they meant and how they served the community. Medicine, he says, can be a plant, a dream, a song or a story, anything that heals or changes for the benefit of a person or society. He tracks the word into English through Grinnell, Brad Steiger, and Sun Bear and Wabun. Kyle Denton reframes it as a verb. The Green Language, Phossus and Logos Garton, whose stated interest is philology, mythology and symbolism, floats the idea that leaves and the shapes of plants may have been the very first form of writing. Wood answers that animals belong in there too, noting the Phoenician alphabet carried ox and snake alongside doorway and field, and calls plants and animals the primal shamanic alphabet. He credits the term green tongue to the esoteric writer David Ova's son, and says his late friend Robert Schmidt drew out the split between phossus, exact description, and logos, the syllogism Aristotle credits to Plato. Wood names Heraclitus the Dark and Jesus as the only ruthlessly phossic speakers he has found. Plant Journeying and Trusting Intuition Wood dates the flowering of plant journeying to the last thirty years or so, pointing back to Rudolf Steiner's advice that if you cannot find a teacher on the outer plane you should tune into plants, to Steiner's herbalist friend Leo Kugowski riding the commuter train into Vienna, and to Dr. Bach in the 1930s, whose society later refused any addition to his canon. Denton describes the mystery tea he learned from Jim MacDonald and Linda Conroy, where students smell an unnamed plant and report impressions before he names it and reads Wood's Earthwise Herbal back to them. The Animal Self and Deserving to Know Reading from Shamanic Herbal, Garton calls Wood's line his favorite definition of a shaman he has heard: anyone of any culture who experiences their animal self as a being as complete and important as their human self, which is why the universal symbol is the half animal, half human ideogram. Garton also relays Wood's two kinds of wisdom, one from living a good hearted life and one from learning nature's underlying patterns. Wood contrasts Native teaching, where an answer arrives as an analogous story you must deserve to decode, with no child left behind. Denton reads echinacea's spines as Pisces, pickiness and wanting one's own space.

Young, a theoretical physicist by training, says the symbolism went over his head at first, but the physics of alchemy made immediate sense, since fire, water and earth can be sensed, measured and built with. He introduces hylomorphism, hylo for matter and morphe for form, as Aristotle's alternative to atoms and molecules. Don't take my word for it, don't take his word for it, go out there and read them yourself Jack Kelley Where the Story Actually Starts Kelley traces every Atlantis claim back to two books by Plato, the Timaeus and the Critias, written in Athens by a man who lived roughly 428 to 348 BC. Both are dialogues, staged conversations in which Socrates trades speeches with Timaeus, Critias and a fourth man, Hermocrates, who almost never gets mentioned. Critias says he heard the tale as a boy from his grandfather, who had it from his father, who had it from Solon around 600 BC. Kelley flags the oddest detail: about twenty modern pages into the Critias the text simply stops mid sentence, with no note and no explanation. The Methodology of Mythology The documentary follows George Sarantitis, a Greek engineer and Platonic scholar whose paper on the methodology of mythology asks what Plato's myths were for. Kelley summarizes the position this way: the myths are not all true, since Zeus was not literally doing things on a Thursday, and not all false either, because real history and real observations about human nature sit inside them. If a story is neither, the responsibility shifts onto the reader to work out which parts are which. That, Kelley argues, is why Plato buried exact geometry and geography in the tale, above a door reading let no one ignorant of geometry enter here. Pelagos Is Not the Ocean The core linguistic claim is that Plato never calls the water around Atlantis Okeanos, the open ocean, a word he uses freely in other books. Job, Yove and the Name of Apollo Dylan traces the name Job back through the Targums to a Hebrew form he transliterates as aiub or aiuv, noting that the beit serves as both b and v and that the vowel points arrived late, so reconstructing a dead language is, in his words, all guesswork and all opinion based. He reads the poem as astrological allegory, with Jehovah and the devil as two halves of one character, the devil and the angel on each shoulder, and warns that teaching it as literal history leaves children believing that being too good makes you a target. Ventriloquist Oracles and the Degrees of the Priesthood Dylan cites a lexicon admitting that the root meaning of aub can only be remotely conjectured and that its distinction from idoni is unknown. He suggests the Pythian oracles and serpent cults worked partly by ventriloquism, a priest throwing his voice through a statue, and reads Moses as a title for an initiate who forbids the Israelites from consulting ob and idoni. He sets out a degree ladder of Christians as good fellows, Jews as men of God, Israelites as men of Chronos, then Hebrews, obri, those who passed over, tying idoni to the Greek gnostes and to Adonai and Adonis. extra.dave-maybe-auricular-medicine: Golden spirals on the sides of your head A family brings auricular medicine to Canada Otzi's ear tattoos and Dr. Nogier's map The ear as a diagnostic window Do ear piercings change anything? Red lines and the ear's tiny rivers Taking the pulse to find the VAS Why Chance's ears pop during sessions A guided tour of the ear map The back of the ear, and vitamin points Hearing loss, tinnitus and the vagus nerve Steiner, a 9-11 birthday, hidden associations If we're walking around with a couple of golden spirals on the sides of our head, it seems like that might be a clue that the ear does more than just listen. Chance Garton This idea that you could use such a small part of the body as a map of the entire system fascinated me. Chance Garton A Family Business Born From One German Doctor's Seminar Maybee traces his path back about 23 years, to when his mother was dragged to a conference by her partner, a medical doctor, and found a workshop on auricular taught by the German physician Dr. Beatrice Strittmatter. An adult educator by trade, she decided she had to bring the training to Canada, became a practitioner herself and eventually started a school. Maybee, in his early 20s and by his own account directionless, had already self studied anatomy and physiology, went to the seminars because they were free, began assisting, then teaching, and has since taken over the Canadian Institute of Auricular Medicine with his business partner Duvon. From Otzi's Ear Tattoos To Nogier's Map Of A Baby Asked how far back the practice reaches, Maybee says he is not sure anyone has the true answer, but points to very early human remains, including the iceman Chance names as Otzi, carrying tattooed points on the ear that appear to have been used over and over again. He argues it was never a full medicine until Dr. Paul Nogier began looking at the ear as a whole map of the body in the early 1950s, developed it across roughly 20 years, and published in 1972 a chart resembling a baby in fetal position. In that sense, Maybee says, auricular is quite new, and possibly a rediscovery. Golden Spirals And The Body's Other Microsystems Chance opens the show with the observation that the ear may be the most obvious expression of the Fibonacci sequence on the body, a pair of golden spirals sitting on the sides of the head. Maybee agrees, saying the ear is in his mind already designed like a map, a landscape topography set up to orient you, and hazards a guess that far more microsystems exist than we have noticed, naming scalp acupuncture, the abdomen, the hands, the soles of the feet and iridology. He adds that on the chart the hand occupies nearly a fifth of the ear, reflecting nerve density rather than size. Listening To The Ear Through Somebody's Pulse Maybee's favourite form of assessment is pulse guided. Holding the person's pulse and feeling its amplitude, he describes passing a pen, or a substance such as a flower essence, over the ear without contact, and reports that the amplitude grows over an active point. He calls this the VAS, the vascular autonomic signal, and explains it as a very subtle fight or flight response in which the blood vessels all constrict at once, with no delay. He says he registers the same shift in his own pulse, has confirmed students' findings remotely over Zoom, and reads Chance's ear popping during biofield tuning as a related nervous system cue. Old Traumas As Blockages To Healing Whether the picture is tinnitus, chronic pain or migraines, Maybee says he always goes looking for old traumas, what he calls blockages to healing, arguing that anything chronic usually has something underneath maintaining it, sometimes attached to a particular age or body part. He describes vitamin indicator points on the chart, including B12, folic acid and B5, and claims a trauma still live in the nervous system can tether itself to a nutrient. Chance's outro extends the idea with a Rudolf Steiner passage about a train passenger whose memory surfaces unnoticed, and a tuning client whose eleventh birthday fell on September 11, 2001.
extra.inner-whirled-6: Why The Devil Needs Talking About Picking Up Robert Taylor's Lectures Blaming Everything On Fallen Angels Victimhood As The Cancer Of Society Original Sin And Dust To Dust The Creator And Destroyer Split Apart Why Paul's Letter Makes No Sense Taylor On The Beggarly Gospel Eusebius And The Egyptian Therapeutae This Is Not A Satanism Pitch Horns As Rays Of The Sun Who Is Really Behind Scripture It's a crime really so we decided to continue with that work and allow some of the themes that he brings forward to inspire us to add on our own weaves to the topic Chance Garton It's no different than the Gnostic pop culture simulation theory demiurge fake world prison planet bullshit that is been pervasive and perennial Probably for hundreds or thousands of years, but it's actually what the entire priest jive revolves around in terms of a control system Chance Garton Convincing people that they are intrinsically broken the original sin idea that there's a tempter that causes them to do the bad things That they don't have choice in the matter Chance Garton This is like the cancer of our society is this victim hood and it's instilled in us And I see this all the time today where I can just state an abject fact About something I prefer What my standards are what my code of honor is and other people will choose to be offended by it Dylan Socoscio why would Paul write a letter to the Romans to preach the good news the gospel? to Italians in Greek That's like Appealing to the British and writing them a letter in Arabic totally a futile Nonsensical thing Dylan Socoscio So, you know invoke or worship that and that's not our pitch here. We are remaining neutral and we keep in mind that everything scriptural is allegory for nature and the cycles of nature that are created by the light of this world the Sun Chance Garton That yes, this is 100% not a pitch for any of these Abrahamic systems I don't care if it's Satanism. I don't care if it's Christianity Islam Judaism, this is not my culture and I'm not pitching you to have anything to do with it not interested in it Dylan Socoscio perhaps the reason the devil quoted scripture or can quote scripture the best in your fantasy world is because that's who's behind the scripture in the first place and That becomes more apparent The more you look into the meanings of everything the more you transliterate the more you see the corruption Dylan Socoscio The Devil As The Ultimate Boogeyman Chance opens by pushing back on the wave of literalist Christianity moving through the truther scene, where Noah is a real man, the thousand year millennial reign has come and gone, and every problem gets blamed on Satan, Belial, Beelzebub, the Nephilim and the spirits of fallen angels. He argues this is the same product as the Gnostic prison planet, demiurge and simulation theory pitch. Every control system needs an ultimate boogeyman, because blame is what keeps people spending what he calls victim currency instead of taking responsibility for their own lives. Original Sin And The Broken Self The pair treat original sin as the load bearing lie of the whole structure. Chance describes it as convincing people they are intrinsically broken, that a tempter causes them to do bad things and that they have no real choice in the matter. Most people never say that out loud, but it is what the devil concept quietly installs in a culture. Dylan calls modern victimhood the cancer of society, noting how people now choose to be offended by a plain statement of preference, standards or a code of honor, and how coddling somebody in hard times helps nobody. Language As Forensic Evidence Of Forgery Dylan makes the case that scripture betrays itself through its own words. He asks why Paul would write to Romans in Greek to preach good news to Italians, comparing it to appealing to the British in Arabic. He points to terms like agion and agios carrying a martyrdom context alien to the Roman mind, arguing these passages cannot have been written when they are claimed to have been. Language is forensic, he says, because even a forgery leaves its fingerprints, and this is what exposes the third and fourth century takeover that severed the stories from nature. Robert Taylor And The Beggarly Gospel They continue their reading of Reverend Robert Taylor, a man they say was swept into the dustbin of history. The quoted passage calls the gospel peculiarly adapted for the poor, a beggarly gospel whose order of the day was to bring in the maimed, the halt and the blind and compel them to come in without ever asking their consent. Taylor calls it the morality necessary to keep the lower orders in subjection, and charges that those who thrive on it are too cowardly to defend it in open controversy against the infidels who challenge them. Neutral Ground Between Creator And Destroyer Both hosts insist this is not a Satanism pitch. Chance says they remain neutral, holding that everything scriptural is allegory for nature and the cycles created by the sun, so the symbolic identity of God and the devil is not an invitation to worship horns and a pitchfork. He traces the creator and destroyer schism to the Zoroastrian era and the split between Ahriman and his counterpart, and reads the devil's horns as the Hebrew qaran, radiance and light, the same rays and cornucopia symbolism found on old sculptures of Moses. Dylan adds that none of these Abrahamic systems are his culture.

Birth Knowledge as a Birthright Chance Garton opens by explaining that this episode is being kept free to the public because he agrees this material ought to be common knowledge, passed folklore style from parent to child rather than sitting behind an expensive paywall. Elise picks the thread up with a story about a woman she spoke to weeks earlier who had never heard the term free birth, and argues that an option you have never heard of cannot be an option for you. Her position is not that one route is correct: she says plainly that no way in her mind is wrong, and that comfort is what decides it. The Forty Four Week Pregnancy She Described For her third, Elise says she calculated a due date of March 20 and then watched March 20, March 30, April Fools and April 10 all pass, reaching just over 44 weeks. She describes staying home because she did not want to hear what anyone had to say about it, then standing in the middle of a field for what she calls a come to Jesus moment, where the message she got back was, can you honor the mystery that I am. She woke with cramps around four in the morning, Avalon made her a pallet upstairs, and her daughter Sovie arrived while James was outside unlocking the gate. Rehearsal, Rebozo and Real Communication Mid episode Elise brings out props and her friend Avalon, using a balloon her son drew on as a stand in belly, and demonstrates rebozo work, compressions and a yoga ball for the lower back. Postpartum Ecstasy and the Maiden to Mother Turn Late in the conversation Elise says the postpartum window gets discussed almost only as depression, and she wants the ecstatic side of it named as well. extra.dental-shaman: Why Holistic Health Forgets the Mouth Forty Years From Guy's Hospital to Shamanism Never Jump Into Bed With a Dentist Trapped Emotions and Ancestral Trauma in Teeth What Teeth Actually Represent The Inner Smile Beats the Outer Smile Saliva, the Oral Gold Humming, Chanting and the Vagus Nerve Clove, Eugenol and the Spice Trade The Man Who Wanted to Die Clean Vets, Dogs and the Primal Chew A Lakota Sweat Lodge and a Pocket Stone Today we've got an extremely unique guest who knows that like all other forms of wellness, a sound mouth is an inside job. Chance Garton One of my big messages is never jump into bed with a stranger or a dentist, never jump into bed with a dentist. Marc Mortiboys We're layering on more stuff like cooties and 9-11 and it's like the rings of a tree where you can see the years where there was a forest fire. Chance Garton That's kind of what I feel is a very primal, number one kind of aspect about teeth is it's kind of like showing your boundaries and showing your virility and your ability to be self-empowered. Chance Garton Forty Years From Guy's Hospital to the Sweat Lodge Mortiboys traces a path from mainstream training at Guy's Hospital in London in the early 1980s, where he says he was already an outlier for hanging around the Stonehenge free festivals and playing Hawkwind, through travels in Australia and the Far East that included living with Aboriginal communities and the Mentawai tribe on Siberut off Sumatra. Back in the UK he moved through hypnotherapy, regression, neuro linguistics and a Tony Robbins course, kept a gong in his clinic for 32 years, sold his practice five years ago, and got word on the day of taping that a 12 acre Isle of Wight property was his. Fear, White Coats and Courting a Dentist Roughly 95 percent of dentistry, Mortiboys says, happens while the patient is wide awake and asked to surrender to a stranger, which is why he cites a UK figure of over 50 percent of people simply not going, with cost as the smoke screen. His advice on the relationship, not the treatment, is blunt: never jump into bed with a dentist, get an examination and a follow up first, and trust your intuition about their hands and intentions. He also blames the room itself, naming white coatitis, arguing sterile white reads as anti life, and describing his own turquoise walls, aromatherapy and patient painted ceiling art. Teeth as Boundaries, Virility and the Inner Smile Prompted by a neighbour's Alsatian barking through the recording, Mortiboys builds his symbolic reading of teeth: an animal shows canines to mark a boundary, so teeth stand for self empowerment and virility, and hiding them signals shame. He points to travellers he has met with brown or missing teeth whose inner smile, as he puts it, is so strong the outer one follows, and to betel nut chewers in India with bright red teeth. He is wary of cosmetic work, calling enamel removal for veneers enamel amputation, and notes agents telling singers aged 16 to 20 to get their teeth fixed fast. Saliva as Oral Gold and the Vagus Nerve The centre of Mortiboys' framework is saliva, which he calls oral gold and describes as a protective elixir that dries up in fight or flight and turns acidic under anxiety, poor breathing and reflux. He describes the waking pH check with litmus paper as the clue clinicians look at, and frames tooth decay as demineralisation, an osteoporosis of the teeth, since enamel is a crystal that dissolves in acid. Decay and gum disease are bifactorial in his view, an outside job and an inside job, and he links the shamanic staples of chanting, humming and drumming to published vagus nerve research. Parasites, Hulda Clark and a Patient's Last Wish Mortiboys contends that some gum cases which never respond to hygienist care are parasitic rather than bacterial, citing amoebic organisms feeding in gum tissue, and he references the late Hulda Clark, her Mexico clinic and books like Cure for All Diseases, including her hard line that dead or damaged teeth should simply go. His most personal story is a terminally ill man who asked to have old root canal and mercury work removed so he could die clean, came in with his two daughters, and was remembered in a phone call after he passed. He closes on vets pulling dogs' teeth for one to two thousand pounds.
extra.dawn-lester: Germs, Fear, and the Science Trademark How the 800 Page Book Came Together Reiki, Reality Courses, and Open Minded Research A Shamanic Healing Crisis in the West Why Labels Turn a Process Into a Thing Out of Homeostasis, Not Diseased A Racing Heart and the Ancestral River The Normal Range Nobody Actually Fits Astrology in the Biofield Leaving Unnecessary Fear Behind The 1911 Lecture That Questioned Germ Theory Two Invisible Boogeymen, Germs and Climate You shouldn't have to put the word real in front of science, but I think more and more of us are realising that it's become scientism. Dawn Lester You guys are probably the poster children for why there were articles coming out during cooties that said why it's not safe to do your own research. Chance Garton And to be able to take the control back is very empowering. It does require responsibility as well. Dawn Lester That's the whole problem with reductionism in general is trying to boil everything down to almost programming code of if this, then that. The invisible boogeyman is spreading the germ. Do you see the similarity here? Chance Garton An 800-Page Book That Landed in December 2019 Lester describes how What Really Makes You Ill? Why Everything You Thought You Knew About Disease Is Wrong grew out of a course she and co-author David Parker were running on the nature of reality, until the health section kept expanding into an almost 800 page tome with pages of references. They briefly considered splitting it into two smaller volumes, then kept it whole so readers could reach the second part on vested interests. Neither author has a medical background, which Lester frames as an advantage: no biases to overcome. Publication landed weeks before 2020, timing she calls divine guidance. Reiki, a Reality Course, and a Mid-Nineties Wake-Up Call Lester traces her path from a childhood spent at the window wondering about eternity, through years of reading she now reads as escapism, to a mid-1990s diagnosis she carefully calls the C word. She says she was frustrated and unhappy at the time, never fully committed to the system's authority, and knew the answer had something to do with mindset. Changes followed: leaving a marriage, a local center, a reiki class that immediately drew her in, and David's course, parts of which felt like something she already knew. Garton hears the shape of a shamanic healing crisis, a hero's journey with information brought back for the tribe. The Case Lester Makes Against the Disease Model Lester argues that labels turn processes into things, that a symptom in one part need not mean anything is wrong with that part, and that the body drifts around homeostasis rather than sitting inside a narrow band. She calls the lab's normal range arbitrary, notes that blood pressure readings run high because people are nervous, and points to Bruce Lipton's work for the claim that genes do not control biology. She mentions German New Medicine and the asbestos and mesothelioma link without treating either as a total answer. Garton's outro reports her Substack citations: Leverson's 1911 London lecture, Bailey's 1928 London Medical World article, Stefan Lanka, and Virus Mania. The Ancestral River and a Client Half a World Away Garton walks through a recent biofield tuning with a New Zealand client whose digestive blockages triggered a racing heart. He was pulled instead to the crown chakra and the zone he calls the ancestral river, where he read a paternal grandmother raising small children in poverty and fear. The client confirmed a grandmother in London through World War Two, husband away, bombs overhead. Because stuck energy sits further from the body the older it is, roughly ten inches out, maternal on the left and paternal on the right, he floats a theory that the 2020 to 2022 charge transited that river. Lester calls it worth investigating. Fear, Word Magic, and Where to Find Dawn The through line Lester names for two years of writing at dawnlester.substack.com, titled Dawn's Writings, is helping people come away from fear that is unnecessary, since frightened people stop thinking. Both speakers turn to language: Garton notes that screen once meant separating the worthless from the valuable, from the Latin cerno, and that a victim is literally a living being sacrificed to a deity, with the state as the modern deity. Lester's answer to division is conversation without any need to convince. Garton's outro draws a parallel he sees between germ fear and climate fear, two invisible boogeymen. Lester was headed to Music and Sky as a speaker.

Doctrine Of Signatures And Plant Lore A large share of the episode is Kyle's interpretive method rather than any protocol. How Richard Schwartz Stumbled Into IFS Falconer credits Richard Schwartz, whom everyone calls Dick, with discovering rather than inventing IFS about forty years ago. Schwartz was a tenured family therapy professor testing whether reorganizing families would resolve their children's eating disorders, and as Falconer retells it, the children did not realize they had been cured and kept doing the behaviors. So Schwartz started asking what was going on inside them instead. The turning point Falconer describes came when Schwartz tried to team up with one client's other parts to argue a protective part out of its job, watched that backfire badly, and instead began a respectful conversation with the protector. Protectors, Exiles, Managers and Firefighters The model Falconer lays out has two basic kinds of parts. Protectors work to stop or prevent emotional pain, and exiles, usually much younger, are the ones carrying it. Protectors divide again into managers, which are proactive and socially acceptable, such as the workaholic, the perfectionist and the inner critic, and firefighters, which arrive once the manager's strategy stops working and which, he says, do not care about collateral damage. Order matters in his account: practitioners go to the protectors first for permission before witnessing and unburdening the exiles. Experience varies, with roughly eighty percent seeing images, Schwartz hearing voices instead, and others reporting Eugene Gendlin's felt sense. Legacy Burdens and the Startled Rats Past a person's own history, Falconer says, come legacy burdens, material that is not from the individual's lifetime at all. He points to Rachel Yehuda, who he says has published more than 500 peer reviewed papers on neurochemical changes in the children and grandchildren of Holocaust survivors, and to an experiment run by Dias in Atlanta with a Harvard collaborator named Ressler. Male rats were conditioned with a shock until an almond like smell alone triggered a startle response, their sperm was used to impregnate females that had never met them, and the pups startled at the same smell. Falconer calls the epigenetics behind this hard science. Unattached Burdens and the Case That Changed Him Deeper still, Falconer argues, sit what IFS calls unattached burdens, presences he says belong neither to the person nor to their ancestors, and which he is willing to describe using the older cross cultural language of spirit possession. He recounts a training session where a woman's savage inner critic offered none of the good intention a genuine part would, and answered plainly when asked whether it was part of her. Being Called Crazy for Fifty Years The thread running through Ray's account with Chance Garton is rejection. As a boy hiding in basements and closets for hours, he saw energy in walls and talked with beings he thought everyone could see, and was told never to say it again. Paramedics who heard him ask about the voice and the light decided he was not all right. His mother said it never happened. The Father in Law on the Movie Screen After his future wife bought him a distance clearing for his birthday, Ray started seeing a heavy, bearded, dark haired man on what he calls the movie screen in his third eye, repeating that he had made a mistake and that Ray could help her. His wife, a doctor of psychology and neuropsychology, recognized the description as her dead father and showed a later photo that matched. Ray explains to Chance that the dead only want a message delivered, so refusing plainly makes them leave, while setting an open window like tomorrow afternoon in the living room invites them in. A second mentor, the artist who drew his wife's father, chose eleven applicants from hundreds and became the father figure Ray never had. Thermodynamics, Dark Energy and the Buddha Ray likes attaching physics to spiritual claims. He leans on the first law of thermodynamics, that energy cannot be created or destroyed, to argue that consciousness emitted by the brain has to go somewhere at death. extra.christopher-mcintosh-tetrad: Why Magic Gets a Bad Name How This Novel Came to Be The Crowley Disciple Who Inspired Gilbert North Science Religion Art and Magic The Magic Hidden Inside Mathematics Concerts and Plays as Secret Rituals Why Black Magic Is Like Black Electricity Do Hidden Forces Steer Political Movements Do You Believe in the Devil Look at Reality and Find the Miraculous Keeping a Magical Diary Saying Yes to the Universe Is magic something that we lose in puberty, only attainable through some Doctor Strange pilgrimage to a far-off Kamar-Taj? Chance Garton And so I create in a way a kind of egregore, an egregore being a thought form, a collective thought form on the invisible plane created by a group of people thinking the same thoughts and focusing on the same symbols and ideas. McIntosh sketches four phases of his own life, from Christian upbringing to rationalist skepticism to astrology, Rosicrucianism and a doctoral thesis on an eighteenth century neo-Rosicrucian order. The mentor figure Gilbert North is loosely based on Gerald Yorke, once Aleister Crowley's chief disciple, who amassed the Crowley archive he later donated to a London library. The narrator, journalist Paul Cairns, is loosely based on McIntosh as a young man. Four Ways of Operating in the World The heart of the conversation is Lionel Snell, who writes as Ramsey Dukes, and his first book SSOTBME, which McIntosh says he personally prompted him to write. Snell maps four modalities, science, religion, art and magic, onto Carl Jung's four functions. Science is observation plus reason, religion reason plus intuition, art intuition plus feeling, and magic feeling plus observation. McIntosh argues that much of what we call science or art is really magic that nobody wants to name. He illustrates the as if principle with Snell's maths lesson on the square root of minus one. Rituals We Perform Without Noticing McIntosh reframes ordinary cultural life as ritual. Watching Hamlet is a magical act because the audience suspends disbelief and immerses itself as though the play were real. An orchestral concert is another, with the tension of tuning, the silence, the conductor raising a baton that functions as a magic wand. Garton extends this with John Cage's piece 4'33", where the same silent performance feels different each time because of coughs and the psychic energy of the room. Both agree that fiction writing creates egregores, collective thought forms that outlive their authors. Black Electricity and the Question of Evil Garton reads the novel's line that black magic is a term used by simpletons, and that talking about black magic is like talking about black electricity. McIntosh calls the saints of evil speech narrative theatrics, but agrees magic is a neutral force that rebounds on anyone who uses it for harm. He describes Eliphas Levi's astral light, borrowed later by the Theosophists, as the field where egregores live, some of them genuinely unpleasant. He points to Stephen Flowers and The Occult Roots of Bolshevism, plus the Ernest Butler and Dolores Ashcroft-Nowicki entity transfer story from Herbie Brennan's Whisperers. Loki, the Cosmic Joke and Staying in the Wow Asked whether he believes in the devil as an individual, McIntosh says no, then turns to Loki and the line from Goethe's Faust where Mephistopheles calls himself part of the power that wills the bad and causes the good. Loki is the grain of sand that makes the pearl, and the jester whose mockery deflates authority, which is why dictatorships hate humor. McIntosh tells the owl synchronicity story from his living room. The book's real message, delivered by North in a London park, is to look at reality and find the miraculous.

The Evidence Gober Puts In Front Of Skeptics Asked what he finds most compelling, Gober gives three items. First, the CIA documents declassified from the remote viewing program the US government began in the 1970s, which he says state that remote viewing is a real phenomenon, that the implications are revolutionary and the evidence too impressive to dismiss as coincidence; he notes another document declassified days before this April 2024 conversation. A Country That Forgot Its Own Grail Teaching English at the University of Bremen, McIntosh asked a class what the Holy Grail was, and only one young man ventured that it had something to do with rejuvenation and the quest for eternal life. He calls that a pity, since Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival is one of the great medieval epics and Wagner returned to the Grail in Parsifal and Lohengrin. He notes the archaeologist Marija Gimbutas argued such figures evidence an early matriarchal culture in Europe. Chance raises the golden conical hats; McIntosh suggests the cone may serve a purpose similar to a bishop's mitre. Spirituality Brought Down Through the Hands The thread McIntosh calls distinctly German is the marriage of the spiritual with the material. Hildegard of Bingen was an abbess, physician, herbalist, composer and painter whose remedies, he says, were imparted to her in visions, and who repeatedly got into trouble with the church yet argued her way out. Paracelsus wrote as much theology as medicine, Jacob Boehme wrote in alchemical metaphor, and the poet Novalis worked as a mining engineer. Rudolf Steiner, who placed himself in the Rosicrucian line, insisted spirituality be brought into the physical world, yielding homeopathic remedies, biodynamic agriculture, Waldorf schools and eurythmy. Abraxas, Loki and the Union of Opposites Chance argues the deepest thread in Occult Germany is the union of opposites, contending that the church's split of an authorized god of light from a devil produced a sterilizing, anti life force. He cites Hermann Hesse's novel Demian, where Abraxas is both god and devil, and Jung's Seven Sermons to the Dead, where Abraxas is effectiveness itself, a power that non power cannot cancel out. McIntosh agrees that element is suppressed in the Christian scheme and offers Loki, the Nordic trickster who is still part of the universe, the grain of sand in the oyster.
