Chance Garton The People Before the Greeks Chance opens by defining the Pelasgi through Encyclopedia Britannica as the people who occupied Greece before the twelfth century BC, the era of the Bronze Age collapse and its baffling, intricate metalwork. Homer, Herodotus and Thucydides name them in Thrace, Argos, Crete and Chalcidice, and later Greek usage applied the label to every aboriginal Aegean population. Britannica adds that surviving fifth century villages preserved a common non-Greek language, a claim Dylan flatly calls disputable, alongside the admitted uncertainty that any ancient people ever called themselves by this name at all. Sailors, Storks and Grasping Straws Chance walks through competing origins for the name. Bishop Cumberland, writing in 1794, derived it from the Greek pelagos, the sea, reading it as a word for strangers and adventurers who came by ship to settle more comfortably. Marcellus of Lesbos tied it to storks that depart and return, an etymology Aristophanes mocked in a comedy of men dressed as birds. Godfrey Higgins doubted the sailors used the name themselves. William Betham instead read Celtic roots in the Iguvine tables, where night, light, day and people combine to mean navigators who could sail by darkness as well as daylight. Chance links that syllable to Homer's verb pello, to become or come into existence, and to the British deity Belenus. Dylan shows Etruscan Aplu written right to left, ties it to Apulia in the heel of Italy, and stresses that B, P and V trade places, that Castur and Puk are exclusive to Etruria, and that C worked as G before 230 BC. Camps That Followed the Sun Rather than treat sky watching as a curiosity, Lundwall argues that oral peoples organized survival around it. He describes the Lakota, hunter gatherers who broke winter camp for spring camp and then summer camp not simply to chase herds but to follow the sun through their constellations, each camp representing a constellation so the ground carried a sky map while the sky carried a land map. How Knowledge Survived Without Writing For ninety nine percent of human history there was no writing, so anything worth keeping had to be passed down in memorable form. Lundwall describes oral cultures telling the same knowledge in as many mediums as possible: oral narrative as myth, somatic narrative as dance, ritual timed to a rising sun, a heliacal star rising, or a phase of the moon. Analogy, Orion and the Rain Making Head Oral peoples think analogically, Lundwall argues, and the Pyramid of Unas texts show it. The same logic, he contends, is why Maya and American Southwest cultures tied heads and scalps to rain ceremonies: a head arrives when a woman's water breaks, holds every divine function, and produces tears. His example is Caribbean vodou, where a village founder's spirit, recalled alongside the Loa, is gradually absorbed into the deity until the historical person is forgotten. He reads the biblical flood as the creation story retold beat for beat, and argues the flood that Utnapishtim recites in the Epic of Gilgamesh is not a clumsy insertion but a resurrection sequence, matching chapter 175 of the Papyrus of Ani.

extra.john-mchugh-rock-art: Is history a circle or a line The archaeologist who lives in two worlds Why Utah might really mean Judah The pueblos everyone abandoned by 1300 Did rock faces teach us the constellations How desert varnish reveals the age What it took to kill a mammoth The wobble that ended the ice age Ghost figures and doorways in the rock Are the snakes really flash floods Are kachinas angels by another name Are these symbols innate or culturally shared The butterfly that landed on our faces From looking extensively into alternate opinions on the good old days, it's my opinion that chronological cover-ups and lies agreed upon that comprise most authorized textbook teachings on antiquity seem mostly concerned with pinning society's evolutionary processes on the great men and their wars that fill most of our school days' notebooks on the subject. One half is the linguistic archaeoastronomy of The Celestial Code of Scripture, his book decoding the astral cipher behind miracle stories in the Bible and the Quran. The other half is entirely pre-literate: Southwest Native American rock art in the Four Corners region of Utah, Arizona, Colorado and New Mexico. He is a licensed archaeologist with the Utah Rock Art Research Association and the Utah Cultural Astronomy Project, and he leads a youth archaeology club called the Shovel Bums that documents undiscovered petroglyphs for the Bureau of Land Management. How you actually date a petroglyph Much of the episode is a practical lesson in reading time off a rock face. Stratigraphy is the excavator's tool, but rock art needs different rules. McHugh explains patina, also called desert varnish, the dark mineral coating that leaches back over a carving: the closer a petroglyph is to the surrounding rock color, the older it is, and the brighter it is, the younger. Superimposition marks where one image was pecked over another. At Newspaper Rock the oldest work sits at the bottom, and any Native American shown on a horse has to postdate 1500 AD. Mammoth hunters and the end of the ice age Walking backward through the Puebloan, Basketmaker, Archaic and Paleoindian periods, McHugh describes people arriving perhaps 25,000 years before present by land bridge or by rafting the coast, then hunting Columbian mammoth, bison antiquus and bison latifrons with hafted Clovis and Folsom fluted points thrown by atlatl. He argues the ice age ended around 6000 BC through the Milankovitch cycle of obliquity, eccentricity, precession and albedo. Chance Garton reads the spiritual consequence: in a world that dangerous, shamans who conferred with spirits about where and when to hunt were survival infrastructure, not decoration. Barrier Canyon ghosts and the snake that brings rain The strangest material is the Barrier Canyon style, ghostly armless and legless figures that follow clay figurines appearing around 5000 BC. McHugh relays the theory that eyeless figures mark a portal, with spirits passing into and out of the rock. Native elders say a figure without arms and legs is a deity, which reminds Chance Garton of the seraphim and of energy bodies stripped of flesh. Rakes mean rain, and snakes mean flash floods, which is why the Hopi snake dance controls serpents to control water. He also notes hunter gatherer panels show no shields, scalps or warfare until agriculture and land ownership arrive. Kachinas, the eternal return, and the open question McHugh says what strikes him most is that kachinas are not merely like Christian angels, they function identically as intermediaries between deities and mankind, going home in July and returning at winter solstice in the cycle Mircea Eliade called the eternal return. Sun priests tracked the sunrise along the horizon, and the solstice rituals turned the sun so no one froze or burned. McHugh declines the ancient aliens framing, preferring shamanic explanation. Chance Garton closes still undecided whether these shared symbols are innate Jungian archetypes, cultural diffusion, or both, and he shares a butterfly story about the pregnancy he and his wife lost.

Hakan Hisim What Psychedelics Did and Did Not Do Hakan traces his turn toward visionary art to one stretch of time when he found the work of Alex Grey and had his first DMT experiences, which pushed him from oils and acrylics into digital tools so he could show people what that realm looked like. Yet he says plainly that psychedelics did not make him a better person. They pulled him out of a bleak spell of devout atheism, but years of solo experimentation, Erowid trip reports and festival hedonism became an excuse to get high. He then quit everything cold turkey for four years of tutorials and effects work, and in 2012 his Serpentine Apotheosis went viral. Creativity as a Spiritual Path Chance pushes back on the evangelism that sells psychedelics as a cure-all and argues that creativity is the most authentic spiritual path, because translating imagination into form eventually demands that you drop an addiction, clear your head and grow healthier in mind, body and spirit. Hakan agrees and extends the idea to fatherhood, with two children and a third on the way, as the so below version of creation and a passage through the alchemical crucible. That is why he calls himself an alchemist: everyone transmutes matter and information, and being aware of it is the realization. Alien Scripts From Childhood Dreams Long before any psychedelic, Hakan spent roughly ages ten to fifteen filling journals with alphabets he did not understand, scribbled each morning from his dreams and folded into Dungeons & Dragons games with friends. When he later tried DMT he recognized the same writing, and found other visionary artists recording similar script. In 2013 his Tetragrammaton piece seeded the Universal Transmissions series, a brave swerve away from the style that was selling. A decade on, he says, the Codex Kickstarter raised nearly double its goal with no advertising, releasing a 150 page first volume of a planned 450 page trilogy meant to feel familiar yet alien. Language in Geometry and the Body Hakan's own explorations convince him that alphabets are cymatic imprints of real vibrations, and that modern scripts are watered down versions of older ones built on toroidal geometry. Chance connects this to the Oera Linda alphabet, whose letters can all be drawn from a six spoked wheel, and Hakan adds the Hebrew letters fitting together into the Star of David. Chance then reframes technology in its older sense as a specialized language, casting the chakras as a language you speak to your body through, something he learned doing biofield tuning. Hakan, raised around New Age chakra books, says the centers only became real to him through breathwork and meditation. Making a Living From Your Art Asked how to turn art into a livelihood, Hakan says early work is fragile, so lean on feedback from people who love you and ignore strangers. He advises against expensive art school, where he learned more from an older student than from any professor, and recalls a teacher warning that only two of thirty classmates would become artists, which is exactly what happened. Mostly, he says, just do the work: after drifting into cinema and animation back in Turkey, he ground past ten thousand hours before a concept art forum post opened doors. Chance names frustration as the trap, tying it to the sacral chakra, whose positive pole is satisfaction.
extra.vibe-rant-107: Libra season and the Egyptian underworld The Book of the Dead as a star map Is the bull's leg Ursa Major or Boötes? Corona Borealis as the Bear's Den and bident Cygnus, the Northern Cross and the Alpha Omega Andrew Collins, Cygnus and the dark rift The cross as a symbol of crossing over Black gods, the Nile and black soil The dark half of the zodiac as roots Thoth, the moon and Mercury Lunar calendars, the Exodus and the Farmers' Almanac Nut, Geb and the dome of the firmament Shamash, the cubit and Jason's solar ratios Measuring time with your outstretched hand Gabe on the missing half of Know Thyself Thoth's measurements and solar angles in artifacts Were there stellar, lunar and solar ages? The Star, Moon and Sun tarot cards Jason's reading of Atlantis in the pole stars The adze tool and the opening of the mouth When we talk about the journey to the underworld, the Book of the Dead, it's also a metaphor of the journey of the Sun through the seasons or through the constellations. Jason Quitt I just find it fascinating that the word Bear Den, it's an English word, but it still conveys the message that transcends language. Mario Garza When you really get into these stories and you pull them apart, you realize they're all talking about basically the same thing just with different cast and characters. Jason Quitt All of the mythological system, on one layer, is about the time of year and what qualities of nature are expressed in that time of year. Mario Garza Book of the Dead as a Star Map Jason Quitt opens with a Book of the Dead vignette in which Isis, holding a grain of wheat, guides the deceased singer out of Virgo toward the scales of Libra, while Boötes seems to offer the bull's leg to Osiris as Orion. He reads the underworld journey as the sun, and the soul, passing through the constellations and being judged at Libra, the cross and doorway of the fall equinox. The panel places a gateway of souls at Cygnus and the Milky Way's dark rift, and Jason frames Cancer and Capricorn as the two gates set by the Earth's 23.5 degree tilt. Hades, the Bear and the Northern Sky Mario Garza asks whether the bull's leg in Egyptian art is Ursa Major, and Jason argues the goddess Taweret is Ursa Major, since the Big Dipper's handle points to Arcturus in Boötes, the leg held by a chain that keeps darkness bound. Mario adds that a Setian he interviewed pairs Taweret with Draco. Gabe reads Boötes as Hades holding a bident, with Corona Borealis as the Bear's Den of Native American lore and Persephone's bitten fruit, and later suggests the Libra glyph may be that barred semicircle. Jason calls Draco, coiled around the pole, the uraeus serpent on the pharaoh's crown. Black Soil, Harvest and the Dark Half Jason lays out an Egyptian colour code of black soil for life and red desert for death, with Osiris as the fertility that returns with the waters of the Nile, and reads Sumerian and Akkadian gods holding a bucket and a pine cone as bearers of water and airborne seed. Mario sees the dark, night half of the zodiac, from Libra until Aries, as its root system, the ancestral season of Halloween and the Day of the Dead when roots strengthen underground. The panel ties the season to harvest, the altar and sacrifice, and Jason argues the sun sacrifices a sign such as Taurus by hiding it from view. Measuring the Heavens With the Body Jason presents what he calls a rediscovery: solar ratios drawn from the sun's height at the solstices and equinoxes for a given latitude, which he says appear in images of Nut, Geb and Shu from his book Astral Genesis, in the ring and rod Shamash holds, and in artifacts he describes as up to 12,000 years old. He argues Peruvian pieces fit only Peru's ratios, and that a hand held at arm's length measures 15 degrees, one hour of sky. Chance recalls Chinese dynasties tuning a flute to the ruler's royal cubit, and Mario notes that moon words like minute, month and men share an M and N. The Moon, Mercury and the Symbolic Ages Mario asks about Thoth as a moon god and his own blurring of lunar and Mercurial symbolism, and Jason answers that the moon is the soul's first stop in the underworld while Mercury carries messages between worlds, retelling how Thoth won five extra days to make the 365 day year. Mario proposes three symbolic ages, stellar, lunar and solar, which he matches to the Star, Moon and Sun cards of the tarot. Jason describes the precession ages from Taurus to Aries to Pisces, with Aquarius, in his view, arriving within a century, and the panel weighs the Farmers' Almanac's advice on timing work by the moon.
extra.marty-leeds-pi: Welcome: Libra Season, Balance, and the God Who Geometrized Marty Leeds Returns: Missouri, the Gnostic Academy, and Community Real Gnosticism vs the Black-Pill Demiurge Trap Exposing the Priestly Fraud and Reviving the Sacred Keys The Power of Pi: Math Is the One Language That Cannot Lie The Chi Rho Decoded: Christ, Chiropractors, and 365 Hidden in Pi Encoded or Synchromystic? The Logos Speaking Through Us Surrounded by Healers: Eileen McKusick and the Spiritual Healer's Path Pi as Zero and One: Genesis, Kabbalah, and the Generative Powers Why They Taught You to Hate Math: Ma'at, 42, and the Number Line The Key Is in Your Hands: The Septenary Cipher, Seven, Pi, and Tau The Riddle to Find the Middle Why the Middle Matters: Five and the Golden Mean The Milky Way Draws a Compass Overhead Is God a Hand Made of Hands Twenty-Eight Finger Bones and Thirteen Moon Cycles In Hebrew the Mouth Is Called Pi Closing Thoughts: Awe, Order, and the Antidote to Materialism What Didn't Make the Cut: Nine and Ancient Alphabets Ponder Pi: Sound Healing, Herbs, and a Song To truly bring equity to the scales of our perception, it seems clear enough to me that the center of ourselves is the best place to be. Chance Garton I make the metaphor that eventually it's like you actually do hit a bottom and realize there is a bottom to the darkness, but there is no top to the light. Marty Leeds Math is not going to lie to you. And I always say, yes, people can lie about math, but math won't lie. Marty Leeds Whenever you create something, whenever you use the imagination, stuff comes out that other people notice in it that you never put there on purpose. Chance Garton You're not going to suck the divine meaning out of this realm in the name of Gnosticism. Not on my watch. Marty Leeds Why Marty Trusts Mathematics Marty traces his road to pi back to a simple crisis of trust: if men cannot be trusted, what can be? His answer was mathematics, which he calls universal, incorruptible and present in every science, adding that people can lie about math but math itself never does. From there he asks why the universe hands us constants like pi, tau and e at all. Pi, the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, returns the same endless irrational string for any circle of any size, and Marty describes holding it in mind for years until connections began lighting up, even noting that the word philosophy opens with phi. Seven at the Center of the Alphabet Marty lays out why he considers the septenary cipher superior to every other way of numbering English letters. Counting one to seven and back down to one sums to 49, which he points out is how a child could square seven, so squaring is built into the pattern itself. Seven, sacred across creation stories and scriptures, falls on G and T, and the word seven totals 22, giving 22 over 7, the classic approximation of pi. T, he adds, echoes tau, which is two pis. Chance layers in philology, reading G to T as got, a Germanic form of God, and as a gate sitting at the middle. Received or Invented? Words and the Logos Chance spots the first letters of Christ hiding in pi's ratio of circumference to radius, a C to an R, echoing the chi rho, and Marty adds that chi reads 365 in English gematria and roots the word chiropractor, which he links to the 33 bones of the spine. Chance asks how much of this was encoded on purpose and how much is synchromystic, suggesting the logos speaks through our imagination. Marty's answer is that nobody designed it; people received it, the way he writes music and sermons as a stenographer for the Lord. He argues truth was hidden in everyday speech so no book burning could erase it. Gnosticism Without the Black Pill Chance draws a hard line between the Gnosticism Marty teaches and the popular online version, where an evil demiurge traps everyone in a meaningless simulation, a view Chance calls the ultimate excuse for victimhood. Marty says his forthcoming tenets of the order spend pages rejecting it, and describes truth seeking as a descent with a floor: there is a bottom to the darkness but no top to the light, and those who climb back out return stronger and bolder. He also faults a priest class he likens to a moat between ordinary people and God. The realm itself, Marty insists, is dripping wet with meaning. Zero, One, and the Middle Path Chance reads the symbol of pi, a circle with a line to its center, as a one and a zero pulled apart: the masculine and feminine generative powers, with the spark between them as the savior. Marty takes zero and one as the metaphysical and the physical, hearing the same math in Genesis, where a formless void precedes light and duality. His riddle is to find the middle: five sits at the center of the number line, the golden mean names a balance between extremes, and the middle path is, he says, the way of God. He notes the Milky Way cuts the circle of stars like a diameter.

Chance Garton Allegory Over History Chance sets aside whether the Oera Linda describes real events, arguing that allegory is more valuable than history because history is always someone's best attempt or deliberate distortion. Dylan lays out why he doubts the manuscript's claimed antiquity: an alphabet of well over twenty letters, left to right writing, words that read like English, and no surviving examples outside a single codex. He compares it to reading The Lord of the Rings as history and doubts a woman could have written it in the sixth century BC. Gabe counters that not being literate may have meant standing above words, and all agree its value lies in its symbolic keys. Frya, Liberty and the Mother Goddess Adela's speech ties the goddess Frya to freedom, and the hosts follow that thread through Venus as the morning star, Lady Liberty as Columbia with her dove, and the Roman Liberalia. Dylan argues the consonants are the bones of a word, tracing Frya through its Greek spellings, and Chance links the shifting F, P and B sounds to the Phrygian cap. The manuscript's three mothers, Lyda, Finda and Frya, are read as seasonal figures, with Finda's lions pointing to Leo and Frya to spring and Venus. Chance closes on Mayahuel, the Mexican goddess of four hundred breasts, and the Malinalli to Marina to Mary wordplay. Persephone, Bootes and the Holy Ship As the sky clock turns toward autumn, the hosts read Persephone's abduction as Virgo taken down into winter. Chance, quoting Godfrey Higgins' Anacalypsis, suggests the crescent moon on goddess statues may really be a ship, the mystic Argha with both ends alike and seven sailors standing for the seven planets. He hears the same number in the manuscript's citadel laws, where seven maidens always attend the lamp. Gabe offers his own reading of Bootes as Hades, proposing that a meteor shower near its head at the top and bottom of the analemma may be a hidden key to the Eleusinian Mysteries. Etruscans, Amber and the Sea Peoples Dylan argues that mainstream history bends Europe's story toward Greece and the Orient, maintaining that the Pelasgians were Etruscans and that the Basque trace back to what he calls Spanish Phoenician. He cites Polybius admitting the northern lands were unknown in his day, and Pliny's claim that a tiny amber figure sold for more than a healthy slave. Chance shows an Etruscan amber siren, a handmaiden of Persephone, and reads the manuscript's Ghouls, the missionary priests of Sidon, as the Galli priests of Cybele, then sets its founding of Massalia beside the versions told by Aristotle and Strabo. Priestcraft and the Deified Teacher The longest reading is the manuscript's story of a teacher born in Kashmir, whom the priests called Fo, the folk called herdsman and his Frya friend called Buddha. After his death, the text says, false priests declared him a god, preached poverty and suffering as the gateway to his kingdom, and grew rich without working. Chance reads it as allegory for priestcraft, then lists the Jesus and Buddha parallels and shows Manichaean paintings of a Buddha Jesus. The same pattern returns with Woden, ensnared and crowned by the Magi, and the hosts trace hero worship into modern political fandom.

Chance Garton Methylene Blue, From Dye to Remedy Clive opens with methylene blue, which he says began as a blue dye around 1890 until microscopists found it killed the very pathogens they were trying to stain, and which he credits as an early malaria cure. He is studying Dr. Klinghardt's view that it is a big hitter against Lyme disease. Asked why the establishment uses it, Clive says emergency rooms reach for it against cyanide and carbon monoxide poisoning, notes that it cannot be patented while hydroxychloroquine, which he says derives from it, can, and urges everyone to do their own research. Where Toxins Hide and How They Leave Clive describes the body splitting toxins it cannot flush into secondary toxins, and argues MSM sulfur turns metals like mercury and lead into water-soluble sulfates, warning that a half-finished detox can leave someone feeling worse. Chance brings in the old alchemical pairing of Saturn with lead, authority and the knees, which he says has surfaced in his biofield tuning work. Clive points to dental work as a major source of toxic metals, saying dissimilar fillings in acidic saliva can form a battery, stresses hydration over mere irrigation, and argues modern stress drains magnesium, his easiest fix for sluggish bowels. Weston Price and the Case for K2 Clive makes his case for vitamin K2 by reading risk-reduction statistics and telling the story of Weston Price, the dentist who photographed native peoples on traditional diets and, as Clive tells it, never saw a cavity. Price's Factor X came from cod liver oil and butter oil from cows grazing spring meadows, which Clive says was later identified as K2 and vitamin D. He argues a cavity can heal like a cut if it is kept clean, asking whether anyone would rush to a fingernail dentist, and points to ozone dentists who, he says, simply sterilize a cavity so the tooth can regrow. Fluoride, Chlorine and the Case for Iodine Clive calls fluoride a neurotoxin, retells a story that Soviet gulags gave it to prisoners to dumb them down, and argues the aluminum industry offloads its fluoride waste through toothpaste and tap water. He groups fluoride with bromine and chlorine as toxic halogens that displace iodine, and describes a video in which chlorine indicator drops stopped reacting after he dipped his fingers or a slice of raw potato into tap water, which suggested to him the body takes in far more chlorine than he had assumed. He links low iodine to thyroid trouble and brain fog, and says vitamin C neutralizes chlorine in a bath. Bicarbonate, Niacin and a Demonized Gas Clive turns to sodium bicarbonate, recommending Dr. Mark Sircus's book on it and stressing that baking soda is not necessarily the pure form. He calls bicarbonate almost the equivalent of carbon dioxide, a gas he says has been demonized, and quizzes Chance on its share of the atmosphere, which he puts at 0.04 percent. Chance, who had assumed it was high because we all exhale it, files the answer under a world of inversion. Clive then argues acid reflux usually means too little stomach acid, and retells how Bill W., a founder of Alcoholics Anonymous, wanted niacin to become AA's 13th step, which Clive says never happened.
extra.adam-stevens-grateful-harvest: Harvest Season Welcome and Guest Intro Leaving the Stockbroker Life Behind Unseen Forces Behind the Leap of Faith Trusting God Instead of Forcing Outcomes Reading Nature's Patterns in Permaculture Function Stacking Hobbies Into Side Businesses Inside Grateful Harvest Seed Company The Soil Book That Changed Everything Adam's Vision of Fully Healed Soil Genetic Memory in Living Soil Why Adam Is on the Electroculture Fence Where to Find Grateful Harvest Seeds My favorite conspiracy theory, you might say, that everything's going to be fine, and nobody can stop you from living a healthy and vibrant life. Chance Garton I think just being willing to stick your foot out there and see what that next step feels like, whether you stumble or whether you run, that's the big thing. Adam Stevens When we're playing in the corporate Babylon world, there's all these illusions set up and constant messaging set up to make you afraid that what you need is not available in your environment. Chance Garton The patterns which God has given us, or as a lot of people would say, the patterns observed in nature, that's your template. Chance Garton I think one of the really interesting things to me about being human is I believe that we can be the greatest force for destruction or the greatest force for good. Adam Stevens From Stockbroker to Missouri Farmer Adam got into financial services young and landed a stockbroker job, expecting a hard city life chasing the dollar, until marriage and a first child in Texas raised the question of what to feed his son. A 10 by 10 community garden plot in North Austin soon doubled, a brutal Texas drought pushed the family to the Pacific Northwest, and he left the stock market for banking after seeing things he could not unsee. Raw milk, a farm internship and 32 acres followed, until a client who wholesaled organic dry goods told him to get off the fence. Two years later the family sold up for Missouri. Faith as an Action, Not Lip Service Asked whether unseen forces helped when he jumped, Adam offers what he calls a theory: God can either be listened to or can make not listening painful enough that you eventually do. He says he took a promotion he had waited three years for on the day a buyer was coming back to see his house, then was left siloed after a bank merger until he quit and relisted. His advice is to just do it, knowing plans shift, since his own Missouri plan has changed a dozen times. Chance frames staying in work that harms the soul as telling God "I don't trust you" and calls faith an action. Permaculture as a Way of Seeing Patterns Adam says permaculture changed his life in every way, one of the biggest being that he now sees patterns everywhere, from the dendritic branching of trees and rivers to a rare tomatillo whose seed pulp looked like a morel, along with behavioral and spiritual ones. He treats the patterns God has given, or those observed in nature, as a template that makes function stacking possible. His own ventures show it, since building a house on rural land opens talk of a permaculture design, a garden and seeds. He encourages people to turn hobbies into side businesses, and Chance adds that pursuing what resonates can grow into something fruitful. Building Soil From the Microbes Up Adam describes a fork between the chemical route and the natural one, and says his path led to soil, still an enigma to him. Matt Powers' book Regenerative Soil was his game changer, gathering ideas from Elaine Ingham's soil food web, John Kempf's work on complete photosynthesis and Chris Trump's preps, then laying out home methods like biochar, bioinoculants and liquid plant foods. Instead of asking why a plant is sick, he says, ask whether the microbes are healthy, since he sees deficiency climbing the food chain to us. He argues that food trucked in from far away lacks the resonance of where you live. Can Soil Hold a Memory? Chance loves the idea that soil could hold dormant genetic information, even of extinct life, and asks whether frequency could clear the Earth's emotional blockages. Adam points to horizontal gene transfer, then argues that silica, which he calls the main component of clay, silt and sand, stores energy and information the way computer chips do. He is still on the fence about electroculture, though his tomatoes and cucumbers on metal cattle panels do better. Chance suggests soil memory surfaces when needed, like memories in an energy field, and relays a story about dinosaur shrimp appearing in Arizona. Adam calls it an intelligence people may meet in old growth forests.

Chance Garton Two Modalities Under One Roof Chance Garton opens by framing the show as mixed mental arts and introduces Michaela Crandell of AuthenticPathHealing.com, a practitioner who pairs internal family systems therapy with biofield tuning. His worry is quieter, that we become so reliant on technology that when the people who understand it retire and die, or an EMP wipes the systems, nobody can rebuild what we lost. He compares it to forgetting how the ancients built strong columns, except a microprocessor cannot be reverse engineered without matching technology. He also warns about faulty rules creeping into models, likening it to what he calls the Rockefeller medicine system, which in his telling treats a symptom and leaves you months later wondering why your leg is swollen. Chance Argues That Logic Is a Light Chance Garton offers a counter case. Every doomsday has been a false alarm, so instead of Terminator 2 he frames AI spiritually. Computing runs on logic, and logic is the yang half of yin and yang, the ordering, clarifying, light bringing force. He argues we have been sold the idea that logic is dehumanizing, when logic is what lifts us out of chaos, so a system built on sound logic should produce good, and one built on broken logic will simply self destruct. Gorence pushes back that good logic is as abstract a promise as good communism. Thirteen Billion Dials and the Inverted Keys The most important shift, Gorence argues, is that we inverted our control over technology. Programmers used to write the logic and understand it. Now a trained model has something like thirteen billion little dials, more parameters than any human could hold in mind at once, and we spend our time reverse engineering what it is already doing. AI has taken the car keys. He notes it finds correlations humans would never look for, which is why big data became the currency and why Nvidia stock is shooting through the roof as everyone buys GPUs. Why the Video Jitters and Hands Got Fixed Asked why AI video feels like a string of parallel potentials rather than one fluid recording, Gorence explains stable diffusion. Each frame begins as random static from a seed, then denoises into detail, and settings like previous frame influence, clip skip and CFG control how wild the motion gets. He names Deforum for prompt blending, Runway ML Gen 2 for coherence, and Control Net with Open Pose plus the hand extension, which places a colored stick figure and finger joints so hands are no longer a problem. He also points to Across the Spider Verse.

Matt Presti A documentary aimed at dimensional delusion Chance Garton welcomes back Matt Presti to unpack his film Dispelling Dimensional Madness, a ten year project built from more than two hundred hours of research. Presti argues that belief in higher dimensions is not ancient wisdom but a recent invention traced through spiritualism, scientific romance and academic mathematics. He says the hardest part of making the film was that he could find no other detractors, only papers written by people friendly to the idea. His stated purpose is blunt, to hold people's feet back to the ground and get their heads back into the life they are actually living. Where the fourth dimension actually came from The conversation walks the history in detail. Henry More coined the term fourth dimension in his 1671 Enchiridion Metaphysicum, opposing Cartesian dualism and describing a spiritual substance he called essential spissitude, essentially Plato's realm of ideal forms. Jean le Rond d'Alembert was the first mathematician to fold time in as a fourth dimension. Presti also cites Gerrard Hickson's book Kings Dethroned, which argues time cannot be a fourth dimension because length, breadth and width are not independent of one another, while Einstein treats his dimensions as if they were. Seances, fraud and the fourth dimension craze Presti traces the popular version of higher dimensions to the spiritualist craze of 1850s to 1880s London, which he calls New Age 1.0. Johann Zollner of Leipzig University hired the medium Henry Slade, recommended by Helena Blavatsky, who wrote on a chalk slate with his foot and claimed spirits in the fourth dimension were doing it. Slade was caught, fled Europe and died broke. Sir William Crookes, inventor of the cathode ray tube, was fooled at seances by a woman dressed as a ghost called Katie King. Escapism, ascension symptoms and honesty Both men separate healthy escape, a walk in the woods or a sitcom, from what Presti calls toxic escapism, the Gnostic sense that this place is a hell hole to flee. Chance pushes back gently on the flat earth example, noting most flat earthers he knows are homesteading rather than waiting for the ice wall. They then criticize ascension cults that rebrand poor health and unprocessed trauma as five dimensional ascension symptoms. Presti invokes Carl Jung, saying wholeness comes from integrating your own noetic darkness, and Chance argues honesty is the actual key to health. Presti reads from Atomic Suicide by Walter and Lao Russell on everything being three, then extends the point through fulcrums, the door jamb, the guitar bridge, the seesaw, motion always moving on stillness at ninety degrees. Chance connects this to his biofield tuning work and to mind as the mental plane rather than a physical ether. Presti closes by naming himself a hermeticist and telling listeners their own mind is the fulcrum and the savior.

Orion, low in the west, is titled sepa or reu, shepherd or shepherds, and also suka, a deified messenger, which is angel of the Lord. Libra rising in the southeast is written dingir gish erin, and erin also renders sabu, army, producing army of heaven. Leo's poetic title labu doubles as the verb to wrap up, Lugal doubles as a fine cloth, and M44 is fatne, manger, spelling out a firstborn son swaddled and laid in a manger. Orion steps onto the celestial waters seven centuries before Jesus, and his cuneiform titles include Dingir Damu, son god, and Sukal, anointed one. The case that birth is not an emergency Much of the hour is spent challenging the idea that birth is a malfunction needing management. What she says the hospital room does to labor Elise walks through the standard sequence: triage, an IV placed just in case, monitors that limit movement, no food because a C section might be coming, and a clock that expects half a centimeter of progress every twenty to thirty minutes. He tells Chance Garton that everything he learned in music college was essentially German and Austrian church music, a rule set handed down rather than discovered. The 432 versus 440 hertz debate is his opening example, but he refuses to treat 432 as a cure. If that number alone saved people, he says, humanity would have been saved already. The deeper problem is that fixing any note as the letter A is itself a construct. Limitless pitch narrowed to twelve frets Jorge compares the note wheel to a color wheel. Everyone accepts that there are limitless colors between colors, yet pianos and fretted instruments quietly train us to accept only twelve pitches out of an infinite field. He explains equal temperament, where the octave is split into twelve equal steps so every note can serve as a tonal center, and notes that this convenience destroys the true proportions the overtone series calls for. Tuning a guitar to 432 and then playing rock music, he tells Chance, changes very little. The real practice is finding a fundamental pitch and resonating with everything inside it. Tonal centers, ragas and the loss of free meter Before Western notation, Jorge says, melody had a tonal center you danced around and came home to, the way a sitar's sympathetic strings or a bagpipe drone hold one pitch. He describes bokashi as a Japanese method rooted in the crowded Edo period that can digest even meat and bones on a kitchen counter, shows the auto composter he built with his son from a bounce house blower, and closes with his core advice: compost is the key and the starting place. DNA, E. coli and Nature's Memory Matt says his DNA sequencing of compost and natural soils turned up roughly 40 percent unclassified material and E. coli in 40 to 50 percent of each sample, leading him to argue that E. coli is a vast, mostly harmless family living inside plants and fixes nitrogen. He proposes that much of the unclassified share is durable DNA fragments that microbes absorb through horizontal gene transfer, by viruses, conjugation or taking up dead DNA, and that in waterlogged, poorly made compost they may draw on old genes to express pathogenic traits. Asked whether nature keeps a permanent genetic record, Matt points to fungal spores and the mycogenesis theory. Viruses, Messages and Nature's Filters Chance asks whether viruses are widely misdescribed, and Matt answers that it depends where you look: he says the literature includes viruses that act as messengers and signals, and cites work on fusarium wilt in tomatoes where, he says, a particular pseudomonas endophyte retasked the virus. Chance suggests pathogens arising from damaged soil may be nature's message to the person who altered it, and Matt adds that it is also a push toward equilibrium. He argues that when trees, watersheds and living stream edges are lost, people become the filtration system for toxins, which he sees as why heavily concreted cities are so hard on the people living in them. A Soil Roadmap for Backyard Gardeners Asked how a novice with a possibly sprayed yard can get to great soil, Matt starts with testing, since every site holds and repels things differently, then recommends watering in high quality compost as a slurry or a compost tea extract that he says carries remediating microbes. He shows a wettable arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi powder to mix with unchlorinated water or dust onto roots at planting, claims it can multiply phosphorus uptake and root reach dramatically, and explains endophytes, the microbes living inside healthy plants that he credits with their best smells, tastes and colors. Over time, he says, these associations link into an underground communication network. Citizen Science Versus Scientific Dogma Matt describes soil testing as a black box full of false positives and is building a database so growers can compare results, bridging the biology camp and the mineral camp and, he hopes, testing whether moon cycles matter for planting. He explains why he avoids PCR with a delay pedal analogy, arguing that too many amplification cycles can make a sample read as almost anything, and the talk turns to the idea of a cult of scientism and the backlash the speakers say Tyrone Hayes faced over his atrazine research. Matt also gives away a free, peer reviewed permaculture textbook he frames as an update to Bill Mollison's 1980s material.

Chance counters that nature, lived in alignment, already offers the abundance and beauty those circuses imitate, and symbolic literacy is offered as a form of psychic self-defense. The Sonic Panoptilectric Frequency Fence After Chance recalls a secret online voting project he heard about years ago, Emily argues the system crowdsources solutions from creative thinkers and wants people outside the box, but not too far outside it. She describes a researcher who isolates background radio frequencies in recordings, and Chance coins the sonic panoptilectric frequency fence for this listening sound field. He offers his own view, drawn from Twyman and Keynes, that endless hidden government spending could make large stalking operations plausible, while Emily says the field touches everyone and that a person's own field strength and health decide how sensitive they are to it. The Watchers and the Conscious Ether Chance argues that the panopticon was a spiritual idea long before it was a technological one, pointing to the Watchers, the devil on your shoulder and a Middle Eastern companion spirit said to report back to the demiurge, and he sees little border between secret societies, intelligence agencies and the mafia. Contrasting forest bathing with a humming refrigerator and Wi-Fi left on overnight, he calls dissonance a posture of fear, and suggests the ether is a record of everything and the Watcher itself, which is why we sense no privacy from the higher self. Emily links this to the eyes people describe seeing on mushrooms. Guardians of the Threshold and I'm Unity Emily frames the immune system as pattern recognition, arguing that how healthy you are inside decides how clearly you read patterns outside, and that a settled mind sees the watching eyes as itself or its ancestors rather than as a threat. From dancing to underground electronic music she describes boundary guards, strangers who appear just as the line between realities starts to dissolve, and says getting too far ahead of yourself calls in the guard. Chance shares a group tuning session where one buzzing participant wanted a drink to tamp the energy down, and closes with his reading of immunity as I'm unity.

Strange as a Mirror of Aleister Crowley The episode title plays on Jekyll and Hyde, and the hosts stress they are not claiming a one to one match. Healing the Hands by Surrendering the Ego Strange begins as a hyper materialistic surgeon who turns down cases for fear that failure will stain his reputation, and the crash that wrecks his hands leaves him, in Chance's reading, a divided man. Chance treats the hands as a fractal microcosm of the whole self, echoed in the trip where fingers sprout hands. On the mountain Strange overthinks until he surrenders, and the hosts unpack the Ancient One's line that you cannot beat a river into submission. Natural Time Versus Clock Time Bells, Strange's drawer of spinning watches and his smashed watch after the mugging all mark time as a controlling force, and Chance reads the bells as a nod to Baal and to the bill that comes due. When Kaecilius says time is the enemy of us all, Chance separates two things English calls time: natural time, the cycles of nature and change that let each life grow uniquely, and Kronos time, the repeating workweek rat race. The Ancient One as a Terrible Mother Chance sees the Ancient One, whose name he reads as Tao and Tau, as more complex than a kindly teacher. He reads her fans through Dylan Saccoccio's writing as tools of Venusian purification, and ties her Celtic origin to Michael Tsarion's Irish Origins of Civilization and the idea that Eastern wisdom first came from a northern homeland. Because druid is said to mean door, he hears Dormammu as the door to darkness, and he casts her as a terrible goddess who draws on the Dark Dimension to stay immortal while withholding the full truth from her students. Another panelist compares her to the goddess Cybele.
extra.howdie-mickoski-holographic-khonsu: Welcome & Howdie's Recent Work The Carrington Event: Was It Fabricated? Can Fake History Be Seeded Into Public Belief? Howdie Mickoski Each of us has a type of way that we explore ourselves and reality. Mine just happens to be writing with a pen on paper. Howdie Mickoski How can there be that which is beyond nature, if nature is all of existence? And in much the same way, how can there be a multiverse in a universe? Chance Garton It's one thing to just get somebody something. It's another thing to get somebody something that they need. Howdie Mickoski A Solar Storm Missing From the Record Howdie opens with his video on the Carrington event, the solar storm said to have struck in 1859, knocking out telegraph lines worldwide and lighting the skies like an aurora. He relays another researcher's search of old Encyclopaedia Britannica editions back to 1879 that list Carrington the astronomer but never the event, and says people who checked September 1859 newspapers found nothing. His question is why a story that barely surfaces before 2000 is being revived now, and he suggests it is being primed for future talk of power grid failure. Chance hears a self-referential loop with no foundation and wonders whether mass belief helps make such things possible. Painted Curtains and Plato's Cave When the talk turns to Plato's Cave, Howdie reaches for the history book he is writing alongside his Plato's Cave project. A Last Supper in the main gallery in Nantes sets the table as a twisted square and frames the scene with two curtains pulled aside, and on his first visit to the Sistine Chapel he ignored the ceiling to study walls painted with curtains. He reads both as the theater of Plato's Cave and the veil of Isis, where the task is to open the curtains. Painted curtains add a twist, since parting them would only meet a wall, yet Howdie guesses hours of meditative staring might dissolve them. A Second Relief Behind the First Howdie describes sitting about an hour and a half in a side room of the seldom visited Temple of Khonsu at Karnak, where guards who knew him from repeat visits left him alone. The wall shimmered like a heat mirage and a different relief appeared, a more feminine scene with different hieroglyphs, for ten or fifteen minutes before the original returned. He concluded the carvings were made holographically in layers reached through one's state of being. Chance links this to defocusing the gaze, wonders whether the artists carved an astral version in dream time, and notes that Disney's Moon Knight gives Khonsu an avatar who sees layers others miss. Tapping the Selves You Might Have Been Talk of avatars opens onto the multiverse. Howdie says he has experienced himself living other lives, with different jobs and marriages, each a small turn away from this one, and argues a simulation would run many versions to gather experience, though no version of him becomes the Dallas Cowboys quarterback. He suspects some vivid dreams are bleed from those lives. Chance asks whether we could borrow the mastery of a self who spent a lifetime painting, and Howdie runs with it, picturing fixing a car by tapping a self who knows mechanics. Chance's outro adds a reservation: reality is one, so how can a universe hold a multiverse? Cathedrals, Iron and the Stone Circle Hotspot Howdie's World's Fair research began on a 2019 trip to Florence studying cathedrals as energy structures. He describes energy drawn down through domes, towers and copper and up from sites built over older temples, meeting and circling the side aisles, with the organ steering it out through rose windows he reads as cymatic patterns and iron balconies drawing it into homes. Chance suggests iron reinforced columns held a constant magnetic field and wonders about mercury engines spinning in octagonal cavities. Howdie adds that in the fifty or sixty Norwegian stone circles he has visited, one spot always runs strongest, and nearly everyone he tests picks the same one.
extra.juan-ayala-gnosticism: Chance and Juan Ayala open their first swapcast Capital T truth versus facts and history Reptilian overlords and Pierre Sabak's dragon books Why Chance rejects pop culture Gnosticism Juan's Pentecostal roots and the Gnostic demiurge Chance on Abraxas, Jehovah and the adversary Where Chance stands on Jesus Christ and belief Archons, egregores and the layers of the body Juan on forgiveness, faith and good works Is ascension physical or all in your head Godfrey Higgins on myth written as history Chance on the lens behind his views The only simulation that we're in is one inside of our own head, and that we created for ourself, and nobody's keeping you in the simulation. You're doing it. Chance Garton I like connecting the dots. I like when one conspiracy weaves in with the next conspiracy and you see the bigger picture. Juan Ayala The bad guy in this entire story is the opposite of existence, so he doesn't exist, which means it's fiction. Chance Garton Just because something bad happened, it doesn't necessarily mean it's bad. It's just the universe itself maintaining order within itself. Juan Ayala Nouns don't exist in nature. It's always going to be somebody's version of it. Chance Garton Capital T Truth Versus Facts Chance opens by separating capital T truth from facts. In his view truth follows nature's template of wholeness, the fractal and the septenary repeating across scales, which is why he reads Plato's idea that all learning is remembering as learning about yourself. Facts, stories and history are human contrivances; he praises Juan's grip on the Jack Parsons story while calling it fact rather than truth. Juan answers with Nietzsche's perspectivism, arguing nobody interprets anything from an unbiased place and that dates and names deserve a grain of salt. Why Chance Rejects Pop Culture Gnosticism Asked by Juan about the dark Gnostic worldview, Chance draws a line between the Marty Leeds style of gnosis, where everything is God and you are its reflection, and the pop culture version of a prison planet run by an evil demiurge. He calls simulation theory the same Gnosticism repackaged in materialist form and says the only simulation we are in is the one inside our own head. When Juan asks who is really in charge, Chance offers what he calls his gnarliest conspiracy theory: nobody is. Juan's Reptilian Overlords as Metaphor Juan, raised Pentecostal, traces his signature phrase reptilian overlords to his deep dive into Gnosticism, and says he uses it in a metaphorical sense for forces at work in the world. He sketches Gnostic cosmology with Yaldabaoth as a Satan archetype ruling the lower aeons, and calls the sect that saw bodies as traps for angels a very dark view. His own leaning is emanationist: one source radiating out, with hardship, like hunting that keeps an ecosystem balanced, as the universe maintaining order. Chance recommends Pierre Sabak's books on dragon symbolism. Chance on Archons as Self Made Filters Chance argues that archons, the demiurge and egregores are real in a sense but hold no power over us. He describes layers of the body, physical, emotional and astral, and the nine chakras he works with, as filters between us and the undifferentiated pleroma. He says all boundaries are self imposed and frames archons as servitors we made and then forgot. Drawing on Abraxas from Jung's Seven Sermons to the Dead, he argues an adversary to existence cannot itself exist. Chance warns that his All Is Self axiom can tip into a god complex, and Juan adds it can excuse reckless living. Religion, Free Will and Natural Law Chance says he worships no specific deity but respects Jesus Christ symbolically, reading the name as meaning Jehovah is salvation and Jehovah as a verb for self existing life force, so following Christ means following nature's law. He links spirit with free will and argues there is a moral side to natural law. Juan recalls being told in church that works do not matter, calls the Bible a manual for being a good person, and counters that works matter because they shape how your life goes. Godfrey Higgins and Dylan Saccoccio frame Chance's case that scripture is allegory read as history.
extra.jack-parsons-sorcerers-of-scientism: Chance frames Jack Parsons and the Gnostic jailbreak Juan introduces Jack Parsons, mystic rocket pioneer Parsons, Crowley, Hubbard and the Babalon Working Chance on magic, fantasy and the fragmented self Mario on sevens, Babalon and the Silver Star Kayleigh on the astrology of key Parsons dates Naval intelligence ties and the homunculus rumors Juan on Tony Stark, Mephisto and Parsons Mario asks whether science fiction is propaganda Slick Dissident on scientism as a seance Kayleigh reads Jack Parsons' birth chart Closing thoughts and doubts about Parsons' death This whole thing seems to just be riddled with what I consider a corruption of the Gnostic ideal, that there is a jailbreaking needing to be done to this reality. Chance Garton A lot of these figures were mystics. A lot of these guys that were doing these things back then, they were doing it mystically. Juan Ayala Lilith can represent things that we don't want to even talk about or look at, and we shove into the back. Ron Hubbard in the desert. Fiction as a tool on the world mind Chance Garton argues that Parsons, Crowley, Lovecraft and Hubbard formed an alchemical inversion aimed at the world mind, getting people to act out a fantasy until parts of it come true. The panel chases that idea through popular culture: Juan's claim that Tony Stark's father is modeled on Parsons' father, with Marvel later tying Stark to Mephisto; Chance's reading of Jonathan Hickman's comic East of West, with a child named Babylon and an AI called Balloon; and a Punisher plot Chance says makes a real conspiracy look fictional. Juan adds that a script Parsons wrote with Frank Malina had its hero blow himself up years before Parsons did. Sevens, Babalon and the Silver Star Mario Garza follows the number seven through the story: Juan's account of an entity telling Parsons something would unfold if he lived seven more years, the call of the seventh aether recited in the Babalon Working, and the seven-pointed star of Crowley's Silver Star order with Babalon written in its points. Sharing Lon Milo DuQuette's tarot cards and the short film The Wormwood Star about Marjorie Cameron, Mario links that star to the Lust card, where Babalon rides the seven-headed beast. The panel also notes the respelling of Babylon as Babalon for gematria, which one guest hears as balloon, a word he ties to official UFO explanations. Reading Jack Parsons through astrology Kayleigh Berkana reads the story astrologically, starting with the Mars and Saturn conjunction she finds in the sky when the Babalon Working began, a pairing she associates with blow-ups. In Parsons' chart she points to two grand water trines, which she reads as deep psychic sensitivity, and Saturn conjunct Pluto in Cancer in his first house, which she ties to issues with authority and father figures. She calls scientism dark side Aquarius, reads his Jupiter and Uranus in Aquarius as a scientific legacy, and places Lilith in his twelfth house. Juan, who says he does not really believe in astrology, concedes the father figure reading fits. Scientism as a modern seance Chance argues that scientism is only presented as materialist in public, while the science with lasting impact is alchemical. Slick Dissident answers with seancism: science as a seance that evokes the names of long dead men of renown, like Einstein, to claim the power to predict outcomes, which he calls necromantic. Another panelist calls scientism a heliocentric program of anti-spirituality that teaches how far away Mars is but never what it means. Mario Garza goes further, calling science fiction mostly propaganda and saying the moon landing looks like science fiction to him, while Juan suggests the alchemists' elixir of eternal life is living on in people's minds.

Heartbreak and the Expansion of God Asked for her cosmology, Chaney offers a philosophy she heard the night before: perhaps we reincarnate until we learn to love God, and so ourselves. In her view every person, book, song and religion holds a puzzle piece, and living authentically with discernment, love and joy expands God, whom she pictures as lonely and waiting for companions. Loosh, Outrage and Where Energy Goes Chaney says talk of loosh means little until you observe yourself, noticing when one sentence flushes your face or raises the hair on your neck. Chance defines loosh as life force drained through self-harming emotional states and wonders whether, rather than archons, it is nature filling a void, scavengers like buzzards at roadkill.
