Gabriel links the Hermetic as above, so below to the Christian on earth as it is in heaven, calling both expressions of correspondence. Chance frames the system as a teaching tool, since the more linkages you hold the more you can recall, and he argues symbolic literacy strengthens psychic self-defense. Both stress that the map's borders stay fuzzy, like a late spring snow. How the Tarot Territories Began Gabriel traces the system to a conversation about the Moors in the Americas and the possibility of a black queen behind the name California, the golden califa. Since the Empress card belongs to Pisces, and Pisces falls on Southern California when he lays the zodiac on the map, he looked 180 degrees across the globe and found Tibet under Virgo, the Hermit's sign. North Korea, the Great Wall of China and Japan's long isolation followed, and months later he learned that the phrase hermetic kingdom is used for exactly those closed-off countries. Laying the Zodiac Clock on America Gabriel uses the 37th parallel as his equinox line, which he identifies with the Mason-Dixon line and ties to Civil War soldiers throwing away playing cards before death, to the Strait of Gibraltar, and to cannabis growers he says sourced Afghan seeds along the same latitude. The Mississippi River marks his solstice axis, and the signs run clockwise from Aries in the west. To explain cardinal, fixed and mutable signs he pictures the wheel as the hill of Golgotha, with Christ and the two thieves as three crosses, while Chance spots the ram of Aries sitting on mountainous Colorado. From the Fool to the World Card Gabriel places the Fool, card zero, outside the wheel at the Mississippi confluence near Kentucky, where he says all the waters fall, and reads Kentucky as the Portuguese caindo aqui, to fall right here; Chance adds the nearby town of Fulton as the fulcrum of the wheel. The Major Arcana then spiral outward in two layers, skipping Aquarius on the first pass as a child's innocence of the abyss. Virginia meets the Virgo Hermit, Augusta, Maine sits under Leo's Strength card, Chance pairs Texas with the Star, the Moon lands on Hawaii, and the World card crowns Canada near the Pole Star. A Framework of Truth, Loaded With Lies Gabriel's master thesis is that the map is a structural grid of fundamental truth, and he argues that those who understand it load that framework with whatever they want people to believe, feeding truth-starved audiences what he calls 50 percent truth. Chance says media and Hollywood have always worked this way, comparing it to baiting a rat with something edible alongside the poison, and he reads California's shape as mirroring Hollywood's merger of fiction and reality. Chance also stresses that neither of them claims a human mastermind drew the map, suggesting the patterns express archetype through the psyche, perhaps with unseen spiritual influence.
extra.marvel-spider-man-no-way-home: Opening themes: fixing the multivirus Gabe's view: Spider-Man mirrors Jung and Philemon MJ's Joan of Arc shirt and blurred history The toxic neon green running through the film Interrogation scene: MJ as private, Ned as public Jung, Goethe, Mount Brocken and Allen Dulles Tarot readings: Peter Parker as the Hanged Man Gabe's theory: Doctor Strange as Aleister Crowley Anagrams and green language hidden in props Doc Ock and the villains read as variants Electro, Sandman and Lizard read as illness vectors Green Goblin, Scorpio and the kiss of betrayal J. Jonah Jameson recast as a conspiracy theorist Astral scene: Peter's higher self as Philemon Aunt May's death and the self-sacrifice message Summoning Andrew Garfield's Spider-Man through a portal The Statue of Liberty and the Mandela effect Garfield's Spider-Man saves MJ as shadow integration The Parker Probe, influenza and Venom's symbiote Chance's closing weave: the multivirus as cybernetics I believe Peter Parker and Spider-Man correspond with Carl Jung and Philemon, and there are other characters in the Marvel universe that are one-to-one correspondences to real people from history. Gabe (Slick Dissident) Jung warned about society moving in the direction of a one-dimensional man where, instead of the integration of the shadow, the shadow is eliminated. Chance Garton It's not a terrible movie, it's entertaining, it's got a lot of good humor, but also just so much programming, especially for transhumanism. Chance Garton As much as we love these movies, they're incredibly entertaining, there is a lot of disclosure going on between the lines, and that is just something to think about. Gabe (Slick Dissident) It's a no-brainer with Peter Parker here, he's absolutely the Hanged Man. Doctor Strange is absolutely the Magician. Gabe (Slick Dissident) This is one of those murals that is showing you the mythology of scientism, which is a key part of this movie. Chance Garton The echidna in Greek mythology is the she viper, and I've done a whole series on how the echidna is very significant to the occult world. Gabe (Slick Dissident) His whole goal is to rescue the villains from themselves, to help them integrate their shadow, because he's Carl Jung. Gabe (Slick Dissident) Instead of doing the right thing because it's the right thing, we're doing the right thing because we're being told that it's the right thing. Chance Garton There is no healing other people. You heal yourself, and if you do that, then you get to be part of the process for other people to do that for themselves. Chance Garton The ultimate plan to all these mystery schools is to get your left brain to be in constant battle with your right brain, to make us fight within ourselves, and that is divide and conquer. Gabe (Slick Dissident) The real multivirus is the illusion of separateness created by the fracturing and fragmenting of our holistic communication web of the life force. Chance Garton Fixing the multivirus with five villains Chance frames the multiverse plot of No Way Home as a multivirus, and he reads each of the five villains Peter fights as a different route by which illness is said to spread: Doctor Octopus as injection, Electro as electromagnetic exposure under a pink, cell-tower sky that Gabe spotted, Sandman as aerosol spraying, the Lizard as animal spillover and the Green Goblin as the airborne variant who argues with his own mask. The hosts track how often the word fix recurs, from The Daily Fix to the chip, serum and harness built to cure the villains, which Chance mocks as scientism conjured in an apartment. Public and private identity The plot turns on Peter's secret identity going public, and Gabe connects it to the public and private episode he and Chance recorded the week the film came out. In the interrogation scene Chance reads MJ as the private, feminine side who will not talk without a lawyer and Ned as the public side who spills everything, while Matt Murdock warns them about the court of public opinion. The ending returns Peter to the private as the whole world forgets him, and Chance closes by arguing that surnames and public personas make people controllable, contrasting commerce with charity. Jung, Philemon and the shadow Gabe's central thesis is that Peter Parker and Spider-Man mirror Carl Jung and his spirit guide Philemon, and the astral scene with Doctor Strange is read as Peter meeting his higher self. Chance maps the three Spider-Men onto light, shadow and integration: Tom Holland fully lit, Andrew Garfield consumed by trauma and Tobey Maguire half in shadow, with Garfield catching MJ as his redemption for Gwen Stacy. Gabe says Peter's goal is to help the villains integrate their shadow, the hosts note that the villains' cures wipe the shadow out rather than integrate it, and the hosts link all this to dissociative identity as a trend across Marvel and social media. Real history woven into Marvel fiction Gabe argues that Marvel folds real historical figures into its characters, and his headline case is Doctor Strange as Aleister Crowley, built on the legend that Yeats kicked Crowley down the stairs and on Strange's slip as his cape carries him down a staircase. Chance opens the screenshots with MJ's Joan of Arc shirt as a wink at confusing myth with history, and Gabe reads the school mural as pairing rivals, Howard Stark against Hank Pym and Einstein against Tesla. Another riff traces Jung's claimed kinship with Goethe, the Mount Brocken broadcast tower and Allen Dulles, and the hosts link MCU to MK Ultra by gematria. Colors, tarot and hidden wordplay Chance and Gabe read the film as coded in color and wordplay: an unnatural neon green Chance ties to contagion imagery in the news, blue and yellow flashes they connect to Ukraine, and purple crown energy leaking through a cracking dome. Gabe casts Peter as the Hanged Man, Strange as the Magician and Oscorp as Scorpio, the sign of the betrayal behind May's death. They trace an anagram puzzle book in Peter's room, FEAST rearranged into fates, the echidna as the she viper, the Parker Probe as a nod to Doc Ock's power of the sun, and a Statue of Liberty carrying Captain America's shield, viewed through the Mandela effect.
extra.mike-winner-alfa-vedic: Chance welcomes Mike Winner of Alfa Vedic Mike's minimalist take on nutrition and detox Germ theory versus terrain in Mike's view Is karma wiped clean each lifetime? Chance's idea of redemption in the afterlife Mike on old souls and new souls arriving David Icke, Walter Russell and a mental universe Is the prison planet a story we tell? Rethinking money, value and the Qortal project Inside the Music and Sky festival Chance asks if nature responds to our consciousness How music festivals changed Chance's life I think it's important right now for us to simplify and get more minimal with our approach to our health, because really we have an inherent zero point machine of consciousness. Mike Winner Consciousness is the light that shines on the darkness and clears it, so that means you have to become aware of it and you have to feel it. Chance Garton What I call scientism, or what traditionally is known as science today, is a religion of our time, and it is based on pure materialism. Mike Winner We could reframe a difficult life situation as being a more advanced and older soul coming in to experience something that requires even more compassion to level up. Chance Garton You of course are the master of your own reality, but also we're all in this together. We all create this realm together. Mike Winner The only warfare that exists in the world is worldview warfare, because that's what allows the world to be shaped into the semblance of a prison planet. Chance Garton We are the divine creators of our reality, and it's really where we put our attention is what matters most. Mike Winner We are in a conversation with archetypes at all times, and our perspective on the archetypes and on life changes the archetypes as much as their communication to us changes us. Chance Garton We believe art and culture and entertainment needs to be grounded in sovereignty, because that's how movements form. Mike Winner This idea of us even being a savior of others plays right into victim consciousness. Mike Winner Minimalism and detox in Mike's routine Asked about his nutrition and supplementation, Mike Winner says his strategy has gone completely minimalist, arguing that consciousness matters more than anything we put in our bodies and that a toxic environment makes detox his main focus. He walks through his morning: rising early for sun gazing during yoga and qigong, a tonic of Smith River structured water with lemon, and Alfa Vedic's fulvic mineral liquid, then one meal a day, a habit he credits to Dr. Barre Lando. For Mike, simple daily ritual is how we reconnect to source instead of getting lost in complexity, and Chance later agrees detoxing may matter most. Terrain versus germ theory, in Mike's view Chance opens the germ theory question by linking the idea of a hostile, infectious universe to a pop culture Gnostic belief that nature is a prison and the body is base. Mike calls modern science scientism, a materialist religion, and retells the Alfa Cast story of Antoine Béchamp's inner terrain versus Louis Pasteur, whom he casts as a jealous politician whose single-microbe model fed what he calls Rockefeller medicine and a war on microbes. Chance wonders whether belief in an external germ, or a transmissible vibe, helps people get sick, and Mike points to Dr. Hamer's New German Medicine and the body as a biocomputer. Karma, redemption and the afterlife Chance shares an insight from the Gene Keys reading of the I Ching's 22nd hexagram, grace, suggesting karma may be wiped clean each lifetime rather than punished in the next. Mike, a volunteer firefighter who asks why bad things happen to good people, would rather believe in a karmic wheel, citing Edgar Cayce. Chance offers a middle path: an astral life review where even the worst souls face what they caused, since consciousness is the light that clears darkness, and he reframes hard lives as older souls choosing deeper compassion. Mike recalls a hitman's near-death redemption and a UCLA parapsychology club's astral projection experiments. A mental universe we shape together Mike credits David Icke's The Biggest Secret with sparking his awakening around 2000, when he read it on lunch breaks while selling shoes at Nordstrom. Drawing on Walter Russell, he describes reality as a mental construct of the universal one: each of us masters our own reality, yet we create this plastic realm together. A friend's dream of Icke and a horse stopping at a torn-down electric fence becomes his metaphor for self-imposed limits, and he calls leaving victim consciousness the key work now, citing Dean Radin's psi research. Chance, recalling his treasure-hunter father's intuition, argues the only real warfare is worldview warfare, shaping how we see our ancestors. Sovereignty through Qortal and Music and Sky Mike's passion for economics and value systems leads to Qortal, a decentralized network he says is rebuilding the internet outside fiat-based exchanges, with decentralized groups that turn into real-world meetups and a food-backed coin in development with food forest grower Jim Gale. Chance notes Mike was the first guest to break down crypto on Higher Side Chats. The Music and Sky festival, started by burners disillusioned with Burning Man and people seeking connection during the pandemic, is what Mike calls his biggest passion: family focused, centered on ice baths, workshops and a 24-hour art gallery, because he believes culture grounded in sovereignty is how movements form.
extra.hp-lovecraft-cthulu: Chance opens the Lovecraft super panel Juan Ayala on Lovecraft's life and letters Was Lovecraft possessed by a jinn Mario Garza on Lovecraft's influence on the occult Kayleigh Berkana on Lovecraft and Pluto Is it all one giant black magic LARP I Am Providence, Morpheus and the silver key Azathoth, the dreaming god, and forbidden knowledge Mario on Lovecraftian rituals and astral gateways Kayleigh Berkana reads Lovecraft's astrology charts Andrew Jackson, the bank monster and fear of collapse Chance's closing on reclaiming power from boogeymen Lovecraft is in everyone's hearts even if you don't know who he is. He has influenced modern pop culture, literature, on the levels, I say, even of William Shakespeare. Juan Ayala If you pay attention to nature and we learn these symbolic correspondences and we recognize the amazing mystical architecture of how everything is connected, then it seems like maybe we weren't abandoned. Chance Garton Regardless of how Lovecraft's work came to be, we know that he was tapped in, and so he kind of updated an older pantheon for modern sensibilities. Mario Garza The theme of Pluto in astrology is all about the dark, the deep transformation and rebirth, sure, but the darker side first, before that transformation occurs. Kayleigh Berkana What I'd like to just put in people's minds is maybe all of this is the first and largest black magic LARP of all time. Gabe (Slick Dissident) That was the one thing that Lovecraft really put into perspective: the indifference, that we're just a speck of nothingness in this vast ocean of the universe. Juan Ayala I'm in control of my imagination. I'm steering this ship, and I'm not letting anybody try to put me in a state of fear. Gabe (Slick Dissident) There's this reverence and this nod to the north and the North Star and Ursa Major that I think goes really, really under the radar. Mario Garza If we ever believe that such a boogeyman exists, there will always be a bigger one than that one, and then a bigger one than that one. Chance Garton Anybody can look at a chart, but the one thing that you'll never see in the chart is the human soul, their individual willpower and their soul. Kayleigh Berkana I like to keep it anagrams because anagrams are objective truth. You don't leave any letters out, you use all the letters, and it says something crystal clear. Gabe (Slick Dissident) We are the source, we are the imagination, we are God, the God that dreams reality into existence, all of us. Chance Garton Juan Ayala's Portrait of Lovecraft Juan Ayala sets the stage by calling Lovecraft one of history's most prolific letter writers, with estimates he puts at 75,000 to 100,000 letters, many as long as books, written by a man Juan describes as a virtual hermit who never really held a job. Juan traces the mythos to a childhood obsession with the Arabian Nights, which he says inspired the alter ego Abdul Alhazred, supposed author of the Necronomicon, and to a grandfather's library said to hold the Picatrix. He names Lovecraft's racism plainly while crediting his reach into films like The Thing and Color Out of Space, plus video, card and board games. Pluto as Lovecraft's Planet Kayleigh Berkana comes at Lovecraft through Pluto, a planet she says astrologers tie to darkness before deep transformation and rebirth. She recounts Percival Lowell's search for a Planet X beyond Neptune and Clyde Tombaugh's discovery on February 18, 1930, noting that Lovecraft, a keen student of astronomy who wrote for journals, lived until 1937, and she places the discovery in Cancer near Ursa Major and Ursa Minor. Gabe says the first recorded hint of Pluto fell on Lovecraft's nineteenth birthday, the panel notes a feature on Pluto named for Cthulhu, and Gabe frames the coming American Pluto return to its 1776 position as the scale of the spell. How Occultists Adopted the Mythos Mario Garza argues that however Lovecraft's work came to be, he was tapped in, updating an older pantheon for modern sensibilities, and that his influence runs through an underground of black magical books and groups. Mario says he found a reverence for the north, the North Star and Ursa Major that goes largely unnoticed, and that some Lovecraftian groups vet initiates by whether their psyche survives a ritual, while others treat the North Star as an astral gateway out and back. Pointing to the steady stream of rituals, spells and new versions of the Necronomicon, he says he doubts people would keep doing this if it did not work. Fiction, Fear and the Dreaming God Gabe floats the theory that the whole Lovecraft web may be the largest black magic LARP of all time, run by masters of fiction, while Chance questions the idea of entities outside reality and frames Mark Passio's notion of cosmic abandonment as a perspective gap that nature's symbolic correspondences can close. The panel turns to Azathoth, the blind idiot god whose dream is said to be our reality, and the conversation reads this as fictionalized pop gnosticism, suggesting that people who crack open expanded consciousness while carrying fear and impurity find that fear amplified back at them. Taking Back the Power From Fear The closing strand turns from horror to agency. Gabe says horror fans tend to adopt a passive posture while he steers his imagination, and he reads the image of Andrew Jackson slaying the many headed bank monster as a way of stirring inherited fears of financial collapse. Kayleigh counters that anyone can read a chart but no chart shows the human soul or its willpower, and Chance closes by arguing that believing in any boogeyman greater than our divine spark only breeds bigger ones, insisting we are the imagination that dreams reality. In a last exchange, the panel weighs Lovecraft's line that fear is the strongest emotion against love.
extra.tim-james-health-hero: Chance welcomes Tim James of Chemical Free Body Tim's art: consciousness, frequency and guitar Tim's view that nature heals, not synthetic drugs The personal story behind Tim's health mission Tim's first visit to the Hippocrates Health Institute Which organs to cleanse first, in Tim's view Are we born carrying toxic chemicals? Emotional baggage and using food as a dope Emotional releases at the Hippocrates Health Institute How Tim built Chemical Free Body Tim's critique of synthetic supplements and fillers Chance's closing thoughts on clearing our filters Our health is our wealth, and when we're following our creative and spiritual paths, which ought to be one and the same, we inevitably encounter the pressing need to purify our body temple. Chance Garton We can hear a lot of stuff and it's good theory, but until we actually do something with it and take action, that's all it really is: it's theory. Tim James It's like you have a symphony orchestra at your beck and call, your command, and yet you just call on one oboe. That would be the synthetic version. Tim James It's just crazy that they have all these side effects that people will accept because they've taken authority for truth instead of truth for authority. Chance Garton We don't live in nature, we don't live with nature, we are an expression of nature. We are nature. Tim James Changing the food, the diet, is the easy stuff, but being able to tap in and tune into the emotional stuff that's holding us back and turning it into something to empower us rather than to drag us down. Tim James The best thing that we can do to help heal the world is put ourselves first and put our own healing first. Chance Garton Vote with your dollars. That's a very powerful way to change things. The voting systems are kind of jacked right now, but you can still vote with your dollars. Tim James Nature Heals, In Tim's View Tim James argues that the body is built to self-heal when we reduce stress, clean up at the cellular level and flood it with nutrition. He points to animals and Native American healers learning from sick horses, and says pharmaceutical companies isolate one compound from a plant, which he likens to calling on a single oboe when a whole symphony orchestra is available. Chance adds that people accept long lists of side effects because they have taken authority for truth instead of truth for authority, and both agree that we are not separate from nature but an expression of it. Tim's Road to the Hippocrates Health Institute Tim grew up on a cattle and hay farm in eastern Oregon, played baseball for decades and lived on the standard American diet until, by his late thirties, his energy and clarity were gone and a health crisis on a trip to Peru showed him that his poor health affected everyone he loved. Accompanying his friend Charles to the Hippocrates Health Institute in West Palm Beach, he sat through an internal awareness class and realised it is an inside job: like a farm tractor, the body needs maintenance, yet nobody gave us an owner's manual. He went on to teach juicing and detox classes to over 5,500 people. Cleansing the Pathway of Elimination First Chance asks what order the organs should be cleansed in, since each release sends toxins down the line. Tim's answer is to clear the pathway of elimination first, then move to kidney cleansing and a liver and gallbladder flush, otherwise, he says, released waste recirculates through the liver and drags out detox symptoms. He recommends colon hydrotherapy sessions back to back, points listeners to his Health Hero Show episode with Rebecca Harder, and describes Gut Detox as a gentler option. Chance recalls his own 2017 colon cleanse using bentonite clay and questions why mucoid plaque is dismissed online. Emotional Detox and Food as a Dope Coaching some 600 people, Tim says he kept finding emotional baggage underneath eating habits, and concluded that many of us use food as a dope to push painful feelings back down. He describes Dr Clement at the Hippocrates Health Institute watching rough cowboys break down crying on the massage table once that dope was removed, his own unexpected release by the pool, and a Reiki master who sensed the change in him. Chance connects this to his tuning fork sessions, noting there are always more layers to the onion and that healing ourselves first is the best way to help heal the world. Chemical Free Body and Everyday Toxins Tim traces Chemical Free Body to reading studies on chemicals found in umbilical cord blood, which convinced him, he says, that we are all polluted and accumulate more toxins with age. He flags synthetic carpet, fresh paint, shampoo with sodium lauryl sulfate and toothpaste warning labels, and says most supplements on the market are synthetic or carry fillers like magnesium stearate and silicon dioxide. After years of growing sprouts and wheatgrass in his garage for local clients, he built a line including Gut Detox, Toxin Detox and a hyper absorbable turmeric tincture, urging listeners to vote with their dollars.
extra.marvel-shang-chi: First impressions of Shang-Chi and kung fu nostalgia An I Ching reading for the film The post-credits symbol and the Death card The Ten Rings as an ancient secret society Shang-Chi, Chinese chess and red versus black The ten rings and lunar standstill calendars Fight club escape and the golden rabbit skull Guardian lions and the Shaolin temple gate The blip read as a pandemic metaphor How Shang-Chi's parents first met in the forest Hotel California, the twins and the zodiac Background symbols after the bus fight ends Fighting the Death Dealer and conditioning themes The water map and the ciborium Electrified weapons versus living chi Nine-tailed fox spirits and possession folklore The Dweller in the Deep and Cthulhu imagery Michelle Yeoh's training scene and the air element Sinking in the lake and rising on the dragon The post-credits bar scene and final notes It was all about the journey of self-discovery for the main character Shang-Chi, as he learned to understand and integrate both the light and darkness in his heart. Chance Garton That's the five petaled flower of Venus, and if anybody looks at the kiss of Venus, it is the pattern that Venus makes as it retrogrades five times through its cycle. Gabe (Slick Dissident) As we increase the flow of our chi in our field and in our body, we uncover more aspects of the unconscious, both for good and bad. Gabe (Slick Dissident) You become one with life force energy and spirit, so you become aligned with that which is eternal and unconquerable in the first place. Chance Garton Once he sliced it in half with his sacred sword, there's no going back. The prophecy is fulfilled whether you like the way it was fulfilled or not. Gabe (Slick Dissident) The electrified weapons are against this living life force energy weaponry, I think a very important dichotomy of the artificial versus the natural. Chance Garton There's always a high road, and sometimes, with a little style, you can just leave them with their own problems. This isn't mine, this is yours. Gabe (Slick Dissident) Integrating light and darkness on the hero's journey Chance frames Shang-Chi as a journey of self-discovery in which the hero must integrate the light and darkness in his heart, while Gabe notes the film's focus on carrying multi-generational trauma and a parent's legacy. The I Ching throw at the top, hexagram three, Difficulty at the Beginning, becomes the lens for the whole reading. In the hosts' reading, Shang-Chi only defeats his father after his aunt teaches him the softer style that once conquered Wenwu, and Chance notes the final duel mirrors his parents' dance-like first fight, so the hero wins by flowing with life force rather than forcing it. The number ten behind the Ten Rings The hosts treat the Ten Rings as a lens on secret societies and the number ten. Chance ties them to the kabbalistic ten and the Pythagorean tetractys, and, drawing on Pierre Sabak, reads rings that fell from the sky as a symbol of a hidden vessel behind ruling power. Gabe links the ten rings to the Sephiroth and to a ten-ring spiral calendar from Chaco Canyon used for tracking lunar standstills, and runs gematria on the two pendants to arrive at the 18.6 year lunar cycle. He also spots the five petaled flower of Venus inside the post-credits logo and on the tarot Death card. Red, black and a game of Chinese chess Chance argues the film is built like Xiangqi, the red and black Chinese chess whose name sounds like Shang-Chi, a link credited on air to Jimmy B. Heroes wear red and villains wear black, the Ten Rings soldiers line up like chess pieces, and the hosts compare the Xiangqi rule that the king cannot leave his palace square to the villagers who cannot leave their hidden village. Color carries the arc: green for the boy, white for his mother's purity, a single yellow gold scene when his training is complete, and finally red armor over black, which Chance reads as the light side placed on top of his darkness. A zodiac and tarot path through the plot The hosts map the story onto the sky clock. Katie and Shang-Chi start as Gemini twins who keep sharing vehicles, the bus fight with Razor Fist moves them into Cancer, and his silent sister running a business plays Virgo. They continue with the father's capture of them as Libra, the water map and dungeon as Scorpio, the bamboo forest as a labyrinth, a final battle launched under Capricorn with a horn call, and Shang-Chi submerged in the lake as Pisces before he rides the dragon up in an Aries moment. Katie's archery montage is tied to the Ten of Wands. Possession, false chi and hidden signals A running thread from Chance is that the film encodes entity attachment: the dragon heart handed down to Shang-Chi, the villains' electrified weapons as artificial chi set against the villagers' living qi, and nine-tailed fox spirits drawn from Japanese possession folklore. The hosts read the repeating voice from behind the gate as mind control and the Dweller in the Deep and its soul suckers as Lovecraftian imagery. They also flag background details in their view: blip support graffiti read as pandemic messaging, masked fight club crowds, and a CVS sign and Alcatraz behind the crashed bus.
extra.lcking-electric-flat-earth: Welcome and introducing guest Lucas King Lucas's early path and creating your own reality Kinesiology and the intelligence of the body Balancing someone at a distance through a surrogate Lucas maps the four elements onto a battery Reconciling sidereal and tropical astrology Is the precession of the equinoxes real? Tower of Babel and fragmenting attention spans Planetary cycles and the sidereal day puzzle Lucas finds the number 27 in planetary cycles Chance's closing thoughts on the conversation Closing song North Star by Lucas King Information-based worldview warfare may be the oldest form of divide and conquer in the tyrant's textbook. Chance Garton Why did that occur? There's a reflection going on between your life and your inner world. Lucas King You're looking at the meridian system as like power lines through the body, and that's how I view them. Lucas King When you apply the self-similarity across scales that is true to all forms of nature and dimensions of nature, all of a sudden the world becomes way less disjointed and confusing. Chance Garton Get a grasp of just the operation of the battery and then see how it applies to multiple fields. Lucas King If you're a farmer, you need to know where you are in the season, what to plant, the weather, those sort of things, cycles. Lucas King The further we get into that level of complexity and abstraction away from the simple truth of nature, the less centered we are, the less still we are, the less rooted we are. Chance Garton We're in an environment where the stars are actually fixed, and there's a perception thing going on where we're just viewing this rotation. Lucas King Kinesiology and the Body's Intelligence Lucas traces his path from studying conservation and land management to reading Jane Roberts' Seth Speaks, which turned a victim mindset into the idea that you create your own reality, and then to kinesiology in his late twenties. He describes muscle testing as an on and off switch for asking the body questions, working through charts, meridians and sound balances, and says a surrogate can stand in for someone at a distance. Chance compares this with his own remote sound work using dowsing rods, crystals and candles, and Lucas says he views the meridians as power lines and treats the zodiac and the Chinese meridian system as the same map. Lucas's Battery Model of Nature Lucas brings the conversation back to his galvanic battery model, arguing that the four classical elements line up with a battery's parts: earth as earth, the salt waters as the electrolyte, and air and fire at the anode and cathode, where he notes oxygen and hydrogen are produced. He says he has been moving away from the model lately as research pulls him elsewhere, but still treats it as a toolkit, arguing that once you look at electrochemistry you cannot unsee it. Chance answers that consistency is the hallmark of truth, and that self-similarity across scales lets a person grasp one field without being a specialist in it. Reconciling Sidereal and Tropical Astrology Asked how to square sidereal and tropical astrology, Lucas starts from what a farmer would do: watch the sky at the same time every day, since midnight, evening and 2am views show different stars. Checking Stellarium an hour before sunrise on the equinox, he found Aquarius heralding the sun, while in the evening Aries follows it like a sheep following the shepherd, with the sun sitting between the two signs. He links the morning view to the old man, bull, lion and eagle, and the evening view to the tropical zodiac, and Chance recaps that each consistent viewing habit could produce its own astrology. Lucas Questions the Precession of the Equinoxes Lucas argues precession may not happen at all. In his model the stars are fixed to one another like a painting on a wall that can be turned but never rearranged, and he hypothesises that the electromagnetics of the system lock the sun and stars together. He calls the textbook rate of one degree every 72 years too slow for anyone to check, and adds that if a thousand years were added to the calendar, historical star positions could not be trusted. Chance suggests precession adds a layer of confusion that props up a false history of zodiac ages, comparing it to the Tower of Babel and shrinking attention spans. Sky Clock Math and the Number 27 Walking through a slide, Lucas multiplies a sidereal day of 23 hours 56 minutes, about 0.997 of a solar day, by 365.25 to get roughly 364.23 days, and argues the resulting day of drift never shows up, likening it to two runners at different speeds crossing a finish line together. He explains synodic periods, tracked against a star, and says published sidereal periods for the outer planets are derived from them. Starting from the moon's 27 day sidereal cycle, he finds multiples of 27 behind synodic periods, such as 108 times 0.27 giving 29.16 days, and Chance ties the sun's base number 50 to the Sumerian chief god.

So what happens when the cartographers haven't even seen the land themselves and they're just copying other maps? Mario Garza There's the literal story, then there's the sun god solar story, then there's the polar story, and then there's the all of this exists within you truth. Chance Garton Everything seems to be a symbol of the pole of some kind. Mario Garza All it would take is one inversion in the foundation of a belief system or a worldview, and everything that's built upon that would have an unstable ground. Chance Garton With solar psychology, because everything is external, you don't even trust your own senses anymore, which is the wildest thing. Mario Garza If we all take responsibility for our own freedom and for our own self in a heroically masculine way, male or female, then we're all good. Chance Garton Art as the Path to Individuation Mario traces Symbolic Studies back to childhood doodling, a Kubrick obsession that carried him into film school, and a later turn toward tarot, and he argues that art is the key to individuation, that being an artist is doing your shadow work, and that creativity and freedom are inseparable. He cites Crowley's line that destruction is the first act of creation, and says his own finished pieces keep teaching him things he never intended months after he made them. Chance, a former film studies minor, adds that it almost doesn't matter what you create, only that you do. Simulacra and the Map That Replaced the Land Mario read Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulation for a small book club and now uses the word model for it: the models handed to us about how the sky, science and reality work eventually flip into their opposites, so news outlets mislead and schools blunt knowledge. He points to cartography, where copies of copies made the map realer than the land it described, and notes how often modern maps crop the poles away. Chance frames the same idea through screens, saying we accept truth from black mirror scrying devices and let that overlay filter out what our own senses report. Polar Gods Made Solar Mario's central claim is that deities we now file as solar were revered as polar first, with Mercury the clearest case: the Magician lifting his wand, the phallus, the caduceus rod with its two snakes, and by extension Hermes and Thoth. He reads the spine and its 33 vertebrae as the same pole expressed in the body, and the toroid's center as the trunk of the world tree and a gateway between realms. Chance layers initiation on top of it, describing a literal story, then a solar one, then a polar one, then the truth that all of it exists within you. Earth Shape Agnosticism and the Apophatic Method Mario dates his interest to 2014, reading Eric Dubay on a flight to India, and the story he tells is of a young man in Mumbai who volunteered, unprompted, that his guru teaches a stationary Earth. He calls himself agnostic about the shape and more interested in whether the realm is geocentric. Chance answers with method rather than a model, arguing that truth is approached apophatically by ruling out what it is not, that one inversion at the base of a worldview leaves everything above it unstable, and that a source caught lying a dozen times has earned no further trust. The External Savior and Taking Responsibility Chance builds the closing argument: if the solar perspective is at root a feminine, goddess oriented one, it explains the sacrificial streak in ancient sun cults and, he suggests, reappears in the external savior at the heart of communism and of the redeemer myth, where a solar deity dies for everyone and sets the example. His counter is that if everyone sacrifices themselves nobody is left, so the heroic move is to take responsibility for your own freedom. Mario had already supplied the psychology, noting that when everything is external you stop trusting your own senses.

Kallenbach From a Golf Patent to the Zygote Kallenbach traces his search to a golf company he launched at the 2008 PGA Show and a design patent he began to feel he did not really own. Years later, he says, he found the beginning of life itself: fertilization, where building materials from each parent become a zygote, a single cell holding all 46 chromosomes inside a membrane he likens to a fence around a biological estate. He drops the word conception, which he says has meant implantation since Roe v. Wade, and argues there is no calendar in the womb, joking that no squirrel wears a watch. Why He Calls a Birthday a Cake Kallenbach argues that the baby, the umbilical cord and the extra embryonic material are one unit, and that clamping and cutting the cord leaves the rest of the baby behind. In his reading the afterbirth, not the child, is what the birth certificate describes, and since he takes placenta to mean cake, every birthday celebrates the cake rather than the baby. That material dies within days, he says, becoming a decedent estate that needs fiduciaries, while the missing 40 weeks get filled by a straw man that disappears once the truth is known. His mantra: all present and accounted for from fertilization to last breath. Reading Luke 5:31 as Wholeness Reading from the King James Version, Kallenbach builds a long argument on Luke 5:31, "They that are whole need not a physician." He argues that Jesus is both telling the whole they do not need him and claiming to be a physician, and he casts Jesus, the Lamb of God, as the amnion, the missing biology. The question being answered, in Luke 5:30, asks why Jesus eats with publicans and sinners; Kallenbach reads publicans as tax collectors, which he maps onto the Social Security number character, and sinners as debtors. Chance adds that much of the allegory concerns legal fiction versus natural law. The Bar Association as a Hyphen Kallenbach argues the cut creates two positions that do not exist in nature, the material left behind in the womb and the baby on the land, and that the Bar Association acts as the go-between, a ferryman across the River Styx reconnecting the man to his account. Picking up the image of the bar as a hyphen, he says the hyphen is the umbilical cord and a bond, and that like glue it is only needed when something is broken. Chance offers his own etymology, bar as son in Aramaic and kernel in Hebrew, tying it to Cronus, the scythe and the black robes. Pursuing Truth Rather Than Freedom Asked what a future parent should actually do about the cord and the afterbirth, Kallenbach says the easiest step is simply knowing your origin, and that in his view neither skipping the hospital nor leaving the cord on changes anything under the system as it stands. He asks whether any book in the Library of Congress can harm you and argues that no word on a document can hurt the living, who author their own lives. A tainted motive taints the outcome, he warns, and he frames the real choice as pursuing truth rather than freedom, since the truth is what makes you free.

Topher Gardner Biodynamics and anchoring intention on the land Topher traces his path to a Costa Rican organic farm that taught permaculture design courses and biodynamics, where he ran the greenhouse, handled the composting and spent two unpaid years helping terraform a 27 hectare property. He describes the biodynamic practice of packing a bull horn with insect ashes, crystal dust and intention, then pointing two horns at each other across a farm, and says it raised productivity. In his view such practices ground intention through a physical act, our bodies work like villi transceiving with the environment, and the land answers right away, an idea he now applies to perimeter protection for his clients. From the Joe cell to the Mojo cell Topher recounts installing orgone accumulators in cars, starting with the Joe cell, which he says a man called Joe built in 1980s Australia from nested metal cylinders holding water, echoing ratios Wilhelm Reich used in his cloud busters. He compares the design to bamboo and heart of palm, plants he calls bio accumulators because they are hard outside and soft inside. He reports big mileage gains on carbureted cars, then describes his friend Moshe's spherical Mojo cell, a night when two cells resonated and a quiet helicopter hovered at dawn, and efficiencies he says collapsed inside new 3G coverage. Water, implosion and rethinking temperature Topher tells of charging water in a Mojo cell, lighting its nano bubble foam and hearing an implosion rather than an explosion, which he took as Viktor Schauberger's principle at work, with a temperature gun reading the water cooler. He ties this to George Wiseman's Brown's gas, a flame he says reads thousands of degrees yet passes harmlessly over a hand. Drawing on Schauberger's idea that electricity is temperature differential, he calls electricity the ability to do work, describes water as a universal solvent that can act as a portal, and argues that microwave radiation disrupts it and that the humidity around us carries memory. Memory holes and the human biofield Chance says his sound healing work has convinced him that memory is not filed away in cells but held in the plasma of the biofield, and that punctures in that sheath form what he calls the memory hole, leaking the life force and self knowledge a person needs. He adds that our culture trains people to feed their light to others and call it goodness. Topher connects the picture to parasites, needles and ticks that puncture, and draws on 23 years as a massage therapist, saying he felt dead pockets around people and met only two in thousands whose fields felt whole. Biomimicry and nature's repeating signal Chance sees the nested cylinders of the Joe cell mirrored in tree rings, chakras and the auric field, and offers his idea of the ring of truth: a concept shaped like the rest of nature is probably onto something true. Topher answers with a lesson from a raja yogi mentor, given while they watched waves on a shore, that nature signals subtly and constantly through repetition, like a billion leaves on one tree. Build a cylinder within a cylinder, he says, and you repeat the signal back, and nature responds with abundance. He calls people little biomimicry machines who only ever copy what they see.

Clint Richardson Clint's case against the patriot redemption myth Clint says he first absorbed the patriot mythology in Los Angeles around 2003, repeated it without checking, and later retracted it, which is why he now works only from primary sources like the legal code and agency websites. He argues the founding story that the United States went bankrupt is false, since nation states default rather than declare bankruptcy, unlike municipalities such as Stockton. Legal persons versus the living man Clint explains his view that a person is a legal status rather than a human being, using the push to grant robots personhood as his example, and says a natural person in law means natural to the state, not of nature. He argues commercial speech is not protected by the Constitution, so people acting as commercial persons find their rights constantly overridden. Revisiting his book Strawman, he calls the straw man a legitimate legal concept from homo stramineus, and reads the Bible as a book of law whose repeated instruction not to respect persons, in his view, warns against corporations and titles. Nation states, Unidroit and uniform law Clint argues that after the Civil War the nation became a commercial nation state, absorbing the militias and the states' sovereignty and later ceding it through United Nations treaties, which he says is why a republic is nothing special when China and Russia are republics too. He describes Unidroit, the International Institute for the Unification of Private Law in Rome, as steering people into arbitration through end user agreements, and says the Uniform Law Commission and groups like the National Governors Association, which he says holds the copyright on Common Core, spread uniform codes state by state. Accepted for value and citizenship claims Clint says instruments like accepted for value are real but meant for corporations, and that gurus sell paperwork promising access to a secret treasury account tied to the birth certificate, stretching a smidgen of truth into a big lie. In his account, clerks whose only job is to process cannot reject such filings, so fraud gets filed and caught later, which matches Chance's story of a friend who spent the money and was fined. Clint adds that renouncing citizenship requires appearing before a consular officer, and that the non-citizen national passport was meant for places like Guam and the Virgin Islands.

Chance Garton A Live I Ching Coin Toss Allen Marcus opens the show by having all three men flip coins on camera, one line of an I Ching hexagram per round, with heads for an unbroken line and tails for a broken one. The toss lands on hexagram 35, Progress, fire over earth, which Chance says he had already drawn from his deck that morning, and two changing lines turn it into hexagram 2, the Receptive, pure yin. Chance admits he cannot explain how it works; he just wants viewers to see that magic is not something you control. Later readings follow Treading into Sincerity around the new moon. Calendars, Commerce and the New Uniform A question about why October, whose name means eight, sits tenth in the Gregorian calendar opens a thread on how timekeeping was reorganized around Roman feast days and why the day is said to begin at an unseen midnight. Gabe calls the calendar a master stroke toward global governance and a uniform commercial code, which he traces to Catalonia, and he reads Catalan demands for autonomy as a shaking of that foundation. In his view people are now expected to wear a new uniform to do commerce in person, and a mask becomes a persona. Dune, Artifice and the Creative Spark Allen notes that Frank Herbert's birthday falls on the day of the stream, and uses Dune's war on thinking machines, which leads to humans bred as mentats, to argue that reality is not a mechanistic clockwork set by Greenwich time servers. Chance counters that art sits at the root of both artificial and technology, and he says Dune's characters only get creative in order to survive or wage war, a fire with no water. He sets it against The Neverending Story, where creativity means forgetting what you knew to reach the flow. Talk later turns to Dune's long history of screen adaptations and adult actors playing the teenage Paul Atreides. Numbers, Names and Synchronicity The trio reads the day itself as a sign: an eight eight day, since October was once the eighth month, with 108 turning up in the date and on a rosary, and a Dune reference landing at 44 minutes 44 seconds. Gabe describes a life full of sevens, from his birth year to his name, and ties seven times seven to forgiveness. Jung's idea of acausal synchronicity is illustrated with ducks mocking a selfie in the background, Chance's own name is read as a chain of chance, and Chance reveals that InnerVerse, first published December 10, 2015, is a Sagittarius. Crowley, 93 and the Will of I Am One guest argues that the nine months in the womb deserve honoring alongside the birth date, and the number 93 leads to Highway 93 and the Betty and Barney Hill case, then to Aleister Crowley, whose Thelemic followers greet each other with 93. The group runs Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the law through gematria and argues that the phrase has been cut off from its source in love. In the reading offered here, the will that matters is the shared sense of I am-ness, identical in every living being across the fractal.

Chance Garton The Daimon as a Guide to Destiny Cat Rose Neligan found the daimon through astrology and a podcast about locating a personal daimon in the birth chart, a word that first called up the animal companions of Philip Pullman's His Dark Materials. Raised Catholic with a guardian angel at her bedside, she says guardian turned into guiding for her. She retells the Myth of Er from Plato's Republic, where souls choose their lives and a daimon to hold them to it, and Socrates, whose daimon warned him away but did not object to his death. In her view the daimon wants to hold us to our destiny, not merely keep us safe. Daimon, Demon and Possession Chance points to the Greek daimos, which he says means dread, as a sign of how feared these spirits were, and argues that a demon can be read as the divided self, fragmented parts of our energy that stop communicating. Cat, fresh from watching The Conjuring, says the daimon turns demonic when we deny it, pointing to great artists and writers overcome by it. Asked how to tell a guiding spirit from an earthbound hitchhiker, she suggests practice, noticing a consistent voice, and being fairly self-possessed, while Chance argues that being closed to spirit leaves a person more open to manipulation. Intention, Flow and the Body's Yes Chance treats scratches, bruises and stubbed toes as an early warning that he is forcing something out of flow, arguing that nature moves in smooth transitions until a cataclysm is the only option left. He lives by the rule that if it ain't a hell yes, it's a hell no, and reads intention as being in tension, a rubber band pulled back and released. Cat shares a skateboarding lesson about which inner voice to trust, and both prefer a yes and approach when people call the same guidance intuition, the shadow or the anima. Childhood Callings and Imaginary Friends Following an astrologer's tip to look back at childhood, Cat recalls wanting to be an artist before being told it was a tough road, and says she still paints because it keeps her daimon happy, feeling something is off when she stops for too long. She talked to Beanie Babies until she was about ten and still wants to build dens, while Chance remembers blanket forts where he read whole Harry Potter novels. Cat describes the loneliness of traveling in 2019 as a search for the other, and sees familiars, spirit guides and imaginary friends as versions of that companionship. Dragons, Watchers and Playful Spirit Cat describes meeting a small black and purple dragon in meditation and later flying on a far larger one in a tea ceremony. Chance says the word dragon comes from the Greek drakon, one who sees, and links it to the seraphim as watchers and steersmen of the body. Cat adds that the household daimon of ancient Alexandria was pictured as a snake, echoed in the snake ring she wears. Chance describes rhyming spontaneously when in flow, connects genius to the jinn, and asks whether fear of such spirits has been taught, while Cat wonders whether people tuned in to their daimon would buy as much.

Chance Garton Following the Alignments Michelle Gibson dates her own research to 2016, when she noticed North American cities falling along straight lines, extended those lines, and recognized the shape of a star tetrahedron. She says about nineteen or twenty spreadsheets now hold the places that sit on her circles and global alignments. Earlier grounding came from Drunvalo Melchizedek's work, sacred geometry and the Flower of Life during her years in Fairbanks, and from the Megalithomania conference she first attended in 2011. She started with a flat map, switched to a globe, and insists the alignments drove the conclusions rather than any prior theory. Old World Architecture Michelle Gibson argues the evidence sits in everyone's home town: courthouses, libraries, schools, theaters and museums, plus prisons and asylums she says were used through the nineteenth century to warehouse adults and children. Chance Garton offers the asylum beside his own house, a castle dropped into a city for no obvious reason, and his Springfield, said to be built on three star forts for a Civil War that found a town already standing, above a tunnel network only the rich and large corporations can enter. She credits the Shrine Mosque to the Moors rather than its official 1923 story. The Moorish Umbrella The spine of Michelle Gibson's screen share is the Ouachita Empire, which she calls an ancient matriarchal civilization of the Ouachita Moors, surviving only in place names like the Ouachita Mountains and Lake Ouachita, with Monroe, Louisiana as its imperial seat and Poverty Point a major center. She spells Moors as Muurs to tie them to Mu, also known as Lemuria, and treats Phoenician, Persian, Mughal and Tartarian as regional names under one Moorish umbrella. Laying the Mississippi Delta beside the Nile Delta, she reads the straight channels in both as the work of a canal-building civilization. Chance Garton adds the Egyptian-style temples reported in the Grand Canyon. Artificial Time Chance Garton frames the false matrix as a problem of artificial timekeeping: there is no such thing as seven in the morning, no such thing as Tuesday, and the only measure is the moon running new moon to new moon. Michelle Gibson answers that old buildings were lined up to the full moon and the equinoxes, and describes a Mayan calendar of day signs and tones meshing like cogs in a wheel. She believes the linear system was brought in to trap us in a year circuit, that the timeline and the Earth's grid were hijacked, and that dates like 3/22 and 9/11 carry ritual weight for the controllers. Worldview Healing and the Reset Chance Garton sets worldview healing as the day's agenda and asks near the end of the free hour how the research healed hers. Michelle Gibson answers that love wins and God wins, that the controllers could never have come in without our consent and had to make us think it was our idea, and that now is the time to take our power back, since everything spirals out of our personal energy. In his solo outro Chance floats the cosmic egg, a cosmology of concentric ring lands that expands outward, and wonders whether mud is new land emerging and whether the Great Reset crowd is hijacking an ancestral memory.

extra.clive-de-carle-health-club-secrets: Introducing Clive de Carle and his work Clive's path from optics to natural health Clive on Rockefeller and the medical schools Clive's view of food and the modern diet Chance on eating organic, whatever the cost Fulvic minerals and glyphosate, in Clive's view Why Clive would pick magnesium first Clive's view that doctors never study health Detoxing every day, from bowels to metals Colon cleanses with bentonite clay and psyllium Inside Clive's Secret Health Club Chance's solo wrap-up after the interview So many of the keys to health actually cost nothing. Chance Garton Rockefeller and Medicine, in Clive's View Clive de Carle argues that money, not health, shaped modern medicine. In his telling, Rockefeller, who owned oil and much of the press by the 1920s, found he could make pharmaceuticals from oil and paid schools of homeopathy, acupuncture and herbalism to drop their teaching, and he says England's 1939 Cancer Act then restricted who could treat cancer. He claims the average doctor gets about four hours of health study in five years, and recounts doctors he interviewed describing cover-ups in training and a Harvard professor admitting half the teaching was wrong. Chance calls it a medical mafia and points listeners to James Corbett's documentary Rockefeller Medicine. Clive on How Modern Food Went Wrong Clive describes a world two centuries ago where villages ate fresh, local, seasonal food and supplements were rarely needed. He dates the decline to around 1850, blaming cottonseed and other cooking oils, then processed carbohydrates and sugar, and he links unnatural fats to dementia. He argues that dwarf wheat and glyphosate spraying, rather than gluten itself, explain widespread wheat problems, and calls bread before a meal a restaurant trick to make you hungrier. Chance shares his rule that food not organic and local barely counts as food, says getting used to its cost early makes it easier, and warns that some organic labels trace back to big food companies. Fulvic Minerals and Magnesium, Clive's Staples Clive's two favorite supplements get the longest airing. He describes fulvic minerals as a water extract of soil from a small deposit in the United States he says is around 30 million years old, claims they help cells release toxins and take in trace elements and that they neutralize glyphosate, and warns against mixing them with chlorinated or fluoridated water. If he could recommend only one supplement, he says, it would be magnesium, which he links to cramps, sleep, anxiety and heart function, arguing that calcium lets muscle contract while magnesium lets it relax. He cautions that cheap magnesium oxide works poorly and that most bottles suggest too little. Everyday Detox and the Colon Cleanse Asked about cleansing, Clive says the point today is less a harsh ten day detox than detoxing every day, starting with working bowels, a healthy liver and enough water. He suggests raw vegan eating may suit someone overweight while meat, fish, dairy and eggs build up someone thin, and names vitamin C, charcoal and sulfur-rich foods such as eggs, onions and garlic as his tools against toxins and heavy metals. Chance recalls a colon cleanse with bentonite clay from his early episode Metaphysical Dumps, Clive describes a coconut water, clay and psyllium fast in Thailand, and Chance ties physical lightness to spiritual growth. The Secret Health Club and Censorship Clive explains that around 2014 UK authorities made him take down his YouTube videos, and that he and fellow UK Column contributors saw views fall from about 40,000 to 400, so he moved his material behind a members' club hosted in Iceland. The Secret Health Club, he says, holds concise videos on topics like Tesla era technology and the sounds newborn babies use, with a forum and a USB version coming. He says UK rules bar him from making almost any claims about his products. Chance, who got a YouTube strike over a guest's website containing the word healing, argues health is censored because it is the linchpin of control.

Lindsey Scharmyn Why Good People Stay Naive Opening the slides from her article Conditioned by Psychopathy, Lindsey Scharmyn argues that humans in general are good, helpful and empathetic, and that this very goodness makes us naive. Because we are mostly good, she says, we expect others to be good and assume that whatever people are doing must be good, or else they would not do it. Her example is the person who asks why anyone would make a medication that might harm millions, and stops there. In his closing reflection Chance says we project our virtue onto other people, and admits he has been gullible with people who put up a spiritual or generous face. Natural Versus Artificial Hierarchy Lindsey says we are pack animals who naturally expect leaders, so hierarchy itself is not the problem. Chance adds that people mistake artificial, malignant hierarchy for all hierarchy, contrasting a grandfather advising his clan, quietly checked by a grandmother who knows everyone, with a figurehead placed over an entire continent, where there is no empathy in the machine. In a small community, Lindsey says, leadership passes to whoever actually knows the forest, while permanent positions of leadership never make sense. In unnatural systems, she argues, we choose leaders for reasons that have nothing to do with what they actually do. Do Our Systems Breed Psychopaths? Picking up Chance's example of a First World War general who sent men into battle hours before the armistice, Lindsey argues that government as it stands is both a psychopath magnet and a breeding ground, and that schooling is designed to sever empathy and inner wisdom. She adds that the Dunning Kruger effect compounds this, since confident ignorance gets rewarded while careful thinkers hedge and are overlooked. Chance contrasts his days at a Domino's franchise with family-run restaurants and his mother's company of about 50 employees, and Lindsey calls a corporation a dead entity that cannot feel. The Euphoric Pull of Groupthink Chance argues that part of what we are here to do is individuate from the group, and that surrendering to a group mind brings a real bioenergetic rush, which he links to mass hysteria in the streets. Lindsey, who marched with 50,000 people against the war in 2003 without losing herself, recalls feeling exactly that rush at a sports game with her sister. The pair also touch on bloodlust in soldiers sacking a town, while Lindsey stresses the positive side, saying that together people attempt healing or change they would never try alone. Recognize It Without Diagnosing Lindsey stresses that the point of studying psychopathy is to recognize it and hold strong boundaries, not to pathologize or diagnose yourself or the people around you; if you can see yourself in these traits and wonder, she says, you are probably not a psychopath. Chance quotes Michael Tsarion's idea that the sage and the psychopath are millimeters apart. He believes maintaining your personal energy field keeps energy vampires from touching you, and he closes by tying our vulnerability to the psychopath to our personal boundaries and whether we build independent or dependent lives.

He now calls that phase a form of bypassing, and says his real shadow work began when he stopped blaming everyone else and took responsibility for what he was creating, before he returned to releasing music in 2019. Why spiritual bypassing keeps people stuck Both men push back on spirituality that asks nothing of you. Chance argues that non-action quietly becomes permission for the world to stay out of balance, and, drawing on Michael Tsarion's work, that any one-size-fits-all philosophy is the death knell of the individual, turning people into a drop in the ocean instead of the ocean itself. Joel says underworld cycles cannot be bypassed, reads the opening cards of the major arcana as the hero's journey through them, and warns against waiting for a savior. His answer is to start sharpening the sword, because, as he puts it, you are your own shaman. Creativity, flow and the right brain Chance describes creativity as several rungs on any universal spiritual ladder, arguing that creative plateaus track plateaus in personal development and in cleaning up the body temple. Joel ties this to bioenergy and the idea of the body as the shadow, where ignored blocks leave expression stagnant. Both see the wider culture as heavily left brained, and Chance suggests most people's intuition has been tuned toward self-criticism. Daily practice, he says, retrains the right brain from hindrance into helper, just as Joel finds lyrics arrive constantly once he is in a songwriting zone, and Joel adds that even basic tarot builds symbolic literacy. How the Taroscopes system works Joel found Michael Tsarion's Taroscopes after leaving his family's construction business, and says it was his first real contact with astrology. In his account, astrology, numerology, Kabbalah and tarot were designed to work together. He pairs the twelve signs with twelve tarot cards, and links 36 ten-degree constellations he says the Egyptians charted to the 36 numbered minor arcana cards, giving each person a significator. His is the Seven of Cups, which he reads as imagination and poetry with distraction as its shadow. He also walks through Tsarion's personal life chart, the system's handling of precession, and his own Taurus rising. Symbolic literacy and corrupted archetypes Joel reads the commandment against graven images as an early war on symbolic literacy, and Chance finds it telling that desert sky god religions reject astrology, which he calls the sky clock. Joel argues that worship began with a sky goddess named Taur, a root he connects to truth, church and tarot, and that solar cult theology grew from a male drive to dominate that, in his view, still shapes society. Chance says the problem cuts both ways: goddess cults had their own excesses, archetypes on both sides have been corrupted, and a purer conversation with them, free of Disney and Marvel versions, is part of the cure.

A second guest from the Telegram group says her morning rune pulls show the theme of the day and what she is not looking at, and that ego or fear driven questions get a different answer than the one asked. Runes as Glyphs of Nature and Wealth Rachel sees the runes as glyphs that grew out of pictographs, patterns of nature that describe growth the way Chance's I Ching hexagrams do. She lays out the Elder Futhark as three sets of eight and opens with a pair of cattle runes: Fehu, the herd you own and work with symbiotically, and Uruz, the wild ox, the free abundance of nature, like the wild kale in her yard. She links those runes to tarot pentacles and Taurus, and shows the set she made herself from bottle caps instead of wood. A Spiral Hero's Journey Up Yggdrasil Asked about a hero's journey, Rachel reads each set of eight as a stage up the world tree Yggdrasil: arrival on earth, Raidho the horse and the journey, a gift that comes with a sacrifice such as an old belief, and finally joy. The three sets move from the foundation of being, to time and cycles, to stepping into your own divinity. She calls it a spiral rather than a circle, since no fall is ever the same fall, and Chance ties it to eternal return and the paradox of freeing your will into the cosmic will. Isa, Ice and the Present Moment Rachel names Isa, the ice rune, as a favourite and draws on the Havamal, attributed to Odin, where ice sits among the things you cannot trust. In her reading ice is the now moment, with only an illusion of stability, so she treats it as a lesson in healthy non-attachment and being okay with mistakes. She places the past with Hel, Loki's daughter, the underworld of ancestors and memory, and describes the whole Norse cosmology as a balance of fire and ice. Chance adds that the present is a narrow band between the two. Odin, Peter Pan and Growing Up Chance says so many people tell him Odin or Hermes visits their dreams that he wonders whether the figure is a mature higher self. Rachel sees such gods as ancient ancestors, says the father archetype is surfacing as an era shifts, and cautions against treating Odin and Hermes as one entity, a point Chance concedes. Chance then reads Peter Pan, since pan means all, as an inverted All Father stuck in eternal childhood, and Rachel adds wolf cults of Odin and the Aries challenge of keeping an inner child alive.
extra.eileen-mckusick-self-talk-electric-healt: Intro & Eileen's Second Visit The Stillness Before the Next Wave Raised in Captivity: Reclaiming Your Wildness Your Home as a Fractal Map of Your Biofield Solar Plexus Over Pineal: The Center of Inner Radiance Alpha Brainwaves & the Lost Art of Deep Listening "I Am" Statements: Do Your Words Create Your Body? Eileen McKusick If our field is an exploded view of our body, our home is an exploded view of that, that what is going on around us is going to reflect what's going on inside. Eileen McKusick The heart can be very childlike. The brain goes off into the future and in the past, and sees things through filters and is very confused, but the gut knows.
