Chance Garton The same electricity that powers us is the same electricity that powers the sun and all the stars in the heavens. Eileen McKusick Stillness, Wildness And Cleaning The Drawers Eileen describes a stretch after a busy spring of keynotes when she chose to stop being busy, framing it with the idea that any waveform begins in stillness. She argues we are conditioned toward guilt-driven overdoing, that we have been raised in captivity for generations and lost touch with our wildness, and that health means getting back to it. Chance draws an I Ching card, "Work on what has been spoiled," and Eileen answers with her motto, "When in doubt, clean." She casts the home as an exploded view of the biofield, so clutter mirrors undigested emotion, and says clients often go home after a tuning and clear it out. Why The Gut Knows Better Than The Head Eileen says that until a couple of hundred years ago the center of consciousness was never placed in the brain, and she suspects widespread literacy pulled us up out of our bodies. She prefers keeping awareness in the solar plexus, treating the organs of digestion as a council rather than a single advisor: the heart can be childlike, the brain confused, but the gut knows. She calls the fixation on the pineal gland unnecessary. Her simplest route out of the thinking mind is listening, to birds, a brook or a single tuning fork, and she says an EEG once recorded her holding alpha for four minutes at a time. Words Are Spells And I Am Statements Asked how to call out negative self-talk tactfully, Eileen names "I am" statements as the biggest thing, since, in her view, by our word we create our life. She once said "I'm fat, I'm broke, I'm sick" herself, and now asks people to restate "I am this" as "I have been this," which she says adds fluidity and lets the future differ. She argues we cannot berate ourselves into health any more than we could raise plants or pets that way. Chance says some people call self-loathing their only motivation, and that labels like "I have anxiety" have become a kind of social currency, especially among teenagers. Untangling Hate And Choosing Appreciation Eileen breaks hate into four feelings arriving together: powerlessness, anger, hurt and fear. She calls it valid but incoherent, and harmful to wellbeing if left alone. After moving to Burlington she caught herself hating cyclists, and by asking whether she was afraid, hurt or powerless she reached acceptance. Chance calls that the proper use of thinking, aimed at getting to the bottom of something. For people who insist they cannot choose how they feel, Eileen allows that some lows are genuine, then offers her favorite word, appreciation: gratitude pulls in, while appreciation extends energy outward. Chance adds that, like a house, whatever you appreciate grows in value. The Electric Age And What Plasma Is Asked about the turning of the ages, Eileen reads the symbol for Aquarius as electric waves and predicts medicine moving from a chemical, mechanical model toward frequency, saying sound healing went from unheard of to everywhere in her 25 years in the field. She says that while researching her master's thesis in 2010 she could barely find plasma in space in mainstream publications. Chance reads the Pisces symbol as regressive. Eileen defines plasma as the flow of electric charge, from the northern lights to lightning, and gives the definition of the biofield she says made her a renegade: the current flowing through the body plus the magnetic field around it.
extra.santos-bonacci-syncretism-astrology: Welcome Santos Bonacci and astro-theology What syncretism actually means The hex of the name Every word conditions your DNA Jesus, the zodiac, and twelve disciples Chrism oil, charisma, and continence Sexual energy on the female side Lion, lamb, and the Mandela effect Tropical versus sidereal astrology When the sun was slowed down Chance wraps up the conversation Discernment on demons and sexual energy We can use names as a description, but we'll know going forward that we're not a noun, that we aren't identified. Chance Garton Every word is conditioning your DNA because your whole body is listening. Santos Bonacci The lies are dying under the weight of their own details, but a lot of people I know are still more interested in catching the next plot point. Chance Garton The fall of man caused us to forget the unity of belief and knowledge that we did once have. Santos Bonacci The story in the Bible is a story about you. Santos Bonacci We were never even taught the functionality of our bodies, and even led to use them in a way that's self-destructive. Chance Garton So if you go to tropical first, you'll have a much more correct system. Santos Bonacci 2,750 years ago, all cultures added five days to their calendars. Santos Bonacci One Religion Behind Every Mythology Santos Bonacci's core claim is that syncretism uncovers a single original religion, astrotheology, sitting underneath every tradition. He points to Jesus walking the Circuit of Galilee with twelve disciples, King Arthur's twelve, Jason's twelve voyages and the twelve labors of Hercules, arguing they encode the zodiac rather than separate histories. He rejects the church's diabolical mimicry theory, saying it was far easier to divide people by language than to plant identical savior stories in India, Egypt and Mexico. Chance Garton traces his own route from the film Zeitgeist through atheism and back again. Language as Atomic Technology A long stretch of the conversation treats words as physical forces. Santos argues that youngsters, ministers, pastors, monsters and ancestors all carry star inside them, that torus is an anagram of star, and that etymology is really atomology, the study of atomic words. Adam, madam and atom give every word three genders. Chance raises nomen as the no man hidden inside a legal name, and the two agree that speaking builds torsion fields, that the word made flesh describes cymatics and sonoluminescence rather than a virgin birth, and that conversation itself conditions the listener's body. Chrism, Charisma and Sexual Continence Santos describes the Christ story as biology: chrism oil produced in the claustrum, the santa claustrum, descending the spine to the sacrum and being raised again through practice, which is how a person becomes christened rather than ignorant. He reads seminaries as semen aries, calls lost chrism lost charisma, and says the same principle of internal orgasm applies to women. Chance connects it to the porn industry, to food too nutrient depleted to replenish what is spent, and asks whether nocturnal emissions can ever come under conscious control. Lion, Lamb, and the Mandela Effect Asked whether scripture once read lion and wolf rather than lion and lamb, Santos answers that both pairings are genuine and both ancient, universal motifs that have always travelled together, since where there is the lamb there is always the wolf. He then reads them anatomically: the lamb as the right hemisphere of the cerebrum with the wolf beside it, Aries as the cerebrum and Leo as the lion, so the verse is really describing two hemispheres brought into harmony and the mind reconciled with the heart. The claim that history itself was rewritten mistakes an old astrological theme for a changed text. Tropical Versus Sidereal and a Slowed Sun Asked to weigh the two astrological systems, Santos frames both as parts of one torus field, with tropical tracking its fixed energy and sidereal tracking precession. He insists tropical is the more penetrating system because the equinoxes never move and because he can read a person's sign from their face, noting that he and Chance are both Aries with Leo rising. Drawing on Immanuel Velikovsky's Worlds in Collision and Ages in Chaos, he claims the sun was slowed roughly 2,750 years ago when Venus entered the system and cultures worldwide added five days.
extra.royal-stars: Why Dylan says history is encoded allegory Four royal stars and the order of the beasts Saint Luke, the bull and Aldebaran Saint Mark, the lion and Regulus Venice, Venus and Mary, star of the sea The Strength card and Gnostic misdirection Saint John, the eagle and Antares Saint Matthew, the angel and Fomalhaut The riddle of the Sphinx and Oedipus Hermes as Lord Eight and the divine name Shiva, Brahma and Vishnu as three seasons Hades, Poseidon, Zeus and Noah's three sons Revelation as the great unveiling When philosophy loses touch with reality Decoding the white, red and black horses The pale horse, winter and Persephone The optic thalamus and the law of attraction The caduceus, the spine and the serpents Why Moses is shown with horns The nine Muses and the Nile flood If you understand the truth that is encoded in all that stuff that's being passed off as actual, well, then it goes back to being truth. Dylan Saccoccio The world is not a prison. This is not Satan's playground. You're giving evil so much power by believing all of this is a fallen world and mankind is fallen. Chance Garton Numbers are systems of identifying another layer of language or symbolism when actual pictures and words fail. Dylan Saccoccio The whole point of all this is that reality is salvation. Reality itself is the only way that we can exist. We have to exist in reality. We can't exist in ideas only. Dylan Saccoccio Four Evangelists as the Royal Stars Dylan Saccoccio argues that the four evangelists are the four royal stars of the fixed signs: Luke with the bull is Aldebaran in Taurus, Mark with the lion is Regulus in Leo, John with the eagle is Antares in Scorpio, and Matthew with the angel is Fomalhaut, the star in the southern fish's mouth beneath Aquarius. He reads Ezekiel 1:10 and Revelation 4:7 as listing the beasts out of seasonal order, points to the Wheel of Fortune card's four corners, and notes that the two equinox stars glow red while the two solstice stars shine white. Venus, Mary and the Sea Moving from Saint Mark to Venice, Dylan hears Venus in the city's name and traces her to Aphrodite, the foam-sprung goddess, and to Rhode, the sea wife of Helios. In his reading, Mary comes from mare, the Latin sea, so hymns like Ave Maris Stella hail a star of the sea, and he connects Rhodian sea law to modern maritime admiralty law. Their slides of Saint Mark's Basilica show its golden lion, which Dylan reads as a monument to Regulus, the summer king star. The Sphinx, Hermes and Lord Eight Dylan treats the Sphinx as a key: the body of a bull, the paws of a lion, the wings of an eagle and the head of a man give the same four fixed signs, which he takes as evidence that the Egyptian symbolism is younger than claimed. He links Oedipus becoming king at Thebes to solving that riddle, calls Hermes Lord Eight through Hermopolis, and adds Yod He Vav He to 26, reducing to eight. The analemma's figure eight joins the pattern, and Dylan says numbers are a further layer of language rather than fortune telling. Four Horsemen as the Four Seasons Reading Revelation 6 aloud, Chance and Dylan walk through each seal as one season in Dylan's interpretation. The lamb is Aries opening spring, and the white rider with a bow and crown is Sagittarius beside Corona Australis. The red rider with a great sword is the scorching summer sun, which Dylan links to King Herod beheading John the Baptist. The black rider holding balances is Libra and the autumn harvest, where a failed reaping means famine, and the pale rider followed by Hades is winter, which Dylan connects to Persephone, Virgo and the star Spica. Reality Over Mysteria Chance describes the old symbolism as a sky clock, where seeing a red star once told people what time of year it was. He warns against mysteria, which he describes as ideas about ideas cut off from nature, and recommends Michael Tsarion's Disciples of the Mysterium. He rejects the idea of a fallen world, and Dylan answers that evil is a choice rather than something people are born with. Dylan calls the popular law of attraction a new age perversion, the caduceus is read as a picture of the spine and nervous system, and Chance sums the strand up as reality is salvation.
extra.miownize-michael-martin-talking-music: Chance introduces Michael Martin of MioWnize Life on a family farm with little internet The meaning behind the MioWnize name Music as sculpture and the value of silence Dancefestopia plans and Paul joins the stream Why caring for yourself fuels your art Cherokee history and the Trail of Tears Listening to First Impressions by MioWnize Kids, phones and why seeing faces matters Chance on an ozone infused olive oil balm Michael describes and plays his newest track Hearing his music like diving underwater Even aptitude, or the myth of talent, is more of a function of how much you care than something innately within you. Chance Garton When I intend for others to hear my music, I want them to see through my own eyes. Michael Martin (MioWnize) Just having my studio with a window facing a bluff down to the Cuivre River, and I can just see eagles fly over out of this window. Michael Martin (MioWnize) We have a creative ebb, and then a sort of recession of our energy more into an introspective, inward state, and we're naturally supposed to have that. Chance Garton In my head you can come up with the most elaborate stuff, but actually getting it out, especially when you're sitting in a session, is almost impossible. Michael Martin (MioWnize) I feel like you play the digital world the way that a virtuoso guitar player does. A lot of the coolest music that I enjoy is so crazy simple to me that I couldn't even think of myself making it. Michael Martin (MioWnize) Maybe you just need to open up a suite, like a bed and breakfast. Let someone rent out a room in your house, and then you also take them over to the studio and help them record a track. It'll be like music bed and breakfast. Chance Garton I feel people kind of get into this conditioned perception of what they manifest their reality to be. Michael Martin (MioWnize) Talent as a function of caring Chance opens with the idea that shaped InnerVerse from the start: the gap between people and their heroes is time and effort, and what gets called talent is really a measure of how much you care. He adds a second layer he learned along the way, that your capacity to care about your passions tracks how well you care for yourself. Later he puts that to Michael directly, and Michael says that since leaving Springfield, unplugging from the internet and focusing on the farm, his music and his hopes for a career in music have started to take shape. Off the grid on a Missouri family farm Michael now lives on his fiancée's family farm near Troy in Lincoln County, where he gets decent hotspot data for about a week a month, uploads everything to SoundCloud in that window, then disappears into Ableton. His old studio was a closet facing a neighbor's house; now his window looks over a bluff down to the Cuivre River, with eagles flying past. He has taken up foraging chicken of the woods and lion's mane, and Chance links this rhythm to what he describes as natural monthly creative ebbs and inward phases that a Monday to Friday schedule ignores. Dense but intelligible electronic music Michael describes rooting a track in one groove or chord pattern and fleshing out every fractal direction it can go within two to four minutes, sometimes stacking around 150 channels and then cleaning up the mud so each sound gets its own space. The conversation borrows a sculpture metaphor, where less material ends up saying more. Chance says Michael plays the digital world like a virtuoso guitarist, with a soulful humanness he finds rare in cookie cutter electronic music, while Michael insists there is no shame in simplicity, since much of the music he loves is crazy simple. New tracks, trumpet and the Undone EP After some live troubleshooting, the stream plays two MioWnize tracks from SoundCloud. First Impressions is headed for an EP called Undone, which Michael says includes some of his own processed singing, and he reveals the trumpet on it is really him, picking back up the instrument he played in middle and high school. The second track starts chill before twisting into something spacey and in your face. Michael also talks about a new studio job where he is about to record a metal band, a hoped for set at Dancefestopia, and a farm retreat idea Chance dubs a music bed and breakfast. Screens, faces and a disconnected culture Paul, a listener who joins the stream from Lexington, Kentucky, brings observations from years of grocery work: supply chains he expects to strain further, and a growing share of young children who ignore Trader Joe's stickers because they are hunched over phones. The group talks about why seeing human faces matters and how masks turn regular customers into strangers. Michael argues that people slip into a conditioned perception of the reality they manifest, a loop that is hard to break, and says outlets like Chance's show can help pull people out to see for themselves.
extra.david-weiss: Welcome and Questioning Where We Live David Weiss Joins: It's the Lie That Matters The Sophia Smallstorm Conversion: From Skeptic to Researcher Spinning at 1,000 Miles an Hour and Feeling Nothing Why the Lie: Disempowerment and the Godless Void Narrative David's Flat Earth Model: The Antarctic Basin The Antarctic Treaty and the 60 Degree South Line Admiral Byrd and the Iron Republic Stories The Flat Earth Clock App Demonstrated Live How David Explains Seasons on a Flat Earth Experiments to Try: The Nikon P900 Superzoom David's Sped Up Drone Sunset Video Are Pictures of Earth From Space Real? Where to Find David: The App and DITRH Wrapping Hour One and the Bitcoin Challenge Chance on Censorship, Parler and Alternative History Why the Lie and Where Our Globe Story Began Norb's World, Cosmic Egg, and Orb Theory Recapping Hour Two: NASA, the Moon and the Stars Share the Show and Detach From the System No Ads, One Affiliate, and Other Ways to Help Send Me Music and the Drum Spider Play Out If you can repeatedly catch someone in a lie, at what point do you just assume they're always lying? Chance Garton You don't just jump to flat Earth. You realize the spinning globe helio-nonsensical model is complete and total nonsense, and then you have to figure out what it is from there. David Weiss I'm going to say some crazy things today, and I'm going to say some things that make sense, and you're going to notice all the crazy things are trying to explain the heliocentric model. David Weiss It's just time that we can trust our senses more and don't take things for granted just because that's the story we've been told about something. Chance Garton If you go to Antarctica, the land is 200 feet over your head. We live in the Antarctic Basin. We're surrounded by Antarctica. David Weiss I'm just pointing towards some doors here for everyone to look at. Don't believe anything I say. Go verify it yourself. David Weiss If nature is all of reality in existence, then how can something be supernatural? How can it be beyond nature? Chance Garton The stars keep track of the seasons and the years. So the sky is a perfect clock. David Weiss Trusting the Evidence of Your Senses The conversation keeps asking why there is always some magical reason our senses must be lying. An oil rig photo shared on screen, referred to as the black swan, is offered as proof that the sea stays visible where globe curvature math predicts a 59 foot wall of water, and the refraction explanation is dismissed for lifting only the water, never the platform. Weiss offers a seasonal test too, comparing the sun's heat at a summer sunrise with a winter noon, which he says shows the sun is simply farther away. Chance urges listeners to trust their senses over the story they were told. From Skeptic to Convert in Two Weeks Weiss recalls a call with researcher Sophia Smallstorm, who told him the Earth might be flat just after he had spent half an hour banning people from his social media for suggesting it. He set out to disprove it and says he came out two weeks later convinced the spinning globe was nonsense. His first arguments are about motion: we are told we spin at 1,000 miles an hour and orbit at 66,000, he says, yet feel nothing, lakes lie like mirrors, and the three body problem that he says breaks computer models never seems to disturb the sky. Chance, who arrived through syncretism, calls himself Earth-shape agnostic. Antarctica and Talk of Lands Beyond Weiss explains his model with a puddle that grows into a pond and then a lake, until the oceans become one basin whose shoreline, Antarctica, is simply land higher than the water. He points to the Antarctic Treaty, a line at 60 degrees south past which he says nobody may explore independently, and a treaty he says cannot be questioned until 2041. Chance raises Admiral Byrd's reported land past the ice, which in his syncretic view could be the next ring out, and pictures the North Pole as the spinal cord of a living realm, while Weiss adds the Iron Republic story from magazine articles he says have vanished. Reading the Sky Like a Clock Sharing his Flat Earth clock app, Weiss describes a sky in which the sun circles every 24 hours and laps the moon about every 28 days, while the stars lap the sun once a year, so the sun keeps the days, the moon the months and the stars the seasons. He treats the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn as rings the sun moves between, explaining winter as the sun sitting farther off to the side, like a plane at the same height twenty miles away. Chance says he will use the clock to work out the time for guests in other countries. Horizons, Superzooms and Sunset Tests Asked for experiments listeners can run themselves, Weiss says our optics have outgrown the lie: a Nikon P900 superzoom can bring back a boat that seemed to sink over the horizon. He explains the effect through perspective, with the ground appearing to rise toward eye level until distant clouds merge with the horizon, and Chance compares it to the vanishing point in art. Weiss then shows a sped up drone video in which the sun never drops below the horizon but fades into the thickness of the air, and argues that a sunset is really the sun passing beyond distant clouds or land.
extra.clint-richardson-red-pill-sunday-school: Clint's Warning About Lab Grown Viruses Welcome and What Is Truth Why We Must Speak the Same Language Looking Up God and Jehovah The Rock Paper Scissors Metaphor Clint on the Original Matrix Script Are You Still You in Transhumanism Clint's Take on Church and State Freedom as Self Responsibility Equal Punishment, Money and Jail Time Could a Contract Exist Without Time The Meaning of Life Is Life Wrapping Up the Final Show of 2020 Creation is something that's always happening. Creation didn't just happen. It is a continuous, beautiful thing that keeps going and going and going. Clint Richardson When we stop asking what is truth and actually answer that question by defining truth as reality itself, we no longer need to seek truth. Chance Garton Freedom is one and only one thing, self-responsibility. Included in that has to be self-sustainability, obviously. Clint Richardson Without time, there is no legal system. There is no power. There is no debt. There is nothing. Clint Richardson The real time, our spiritual currency, is what we pay attention to and how we change based on what we're taking in, what we're choosing to continue doing. Chance Garton What's the meaning of life? That's a question I've heard quite a bit. And honestly, if you think about it, the answer is, again, self-evident. The meaning of life is life. Clint Richardson Don't allow persons to have power. Persons are not real. Well, what is a corporation? It's an artificial person. Clint Richardson The higher you climb the spiritual mountain, the further into the dark valleys and the shadow of death you'll be able to peer. Chance Garton God as a Verb, Truth as Reality Chance opens by proposing that once truth is defined as reality itself, nobody needs to go seeking it, because what exists is the truth. Clint builds on that through grammar. He argues the legal system runs on nouns, names and titles, which are empty forms, while verbs and adjectives stay closer to the truth. He notes that "the truth will set you free" is a Bible verse most people quote without knowing it, reads God in the old sense of a magistrate or anyone holding power over you, and says Webster's 1828 treats Jehovah as a verb, so creation is something always happening rather than a past event. Rock, Paper, Scissors as an Order of Needs Clint offers rock, paper and scissors as a ranking of human priorities. The rock is need, the foundation and the truth. The scissors are ease, a tool like a plow, and also the intellect, which cuts and categorizes. The paper is want and desire, a thin covering like a noun, and in a materialist world he says it has covered the rock. Chance notes the paper is two dimensional against a three dimensional rock and casts the scissors as the reason that can separate fiction from reality. Clint answers that the same tool can lead to sin, a word he links to synthetic and to words carrying the prefix dis. Simulators, Copies and the Replaced Axe Clint says the original script of The Matrix made it a voluntary virtual reality people chose and then lost the will to leave. Clint argues that in the old dictionaries simulation means hypocrisy, knowing the moral law and acting against it, while a simulacrum is a copy without an original. Chance recalls an example from Clint's own show, an axe whose head and then handle are both replaced. Clint carries it into transhumanism, asking whether a person rebuilt from new parts is the same, and says change is part of life and worth embracing. In his outro Chance points to Cyberpunk 2077 as that transhuman future. Why Freedom Means Self-Responsibility Clint describes church and state as a mutual pardon, the priest class forgiving the politicians and the politicians forgiving the priests, and cites maxims of law holding that the king can break no law. Chance says this is why he is not chasing researchers who promise ways to game the legal system. Clint argues most slaves would not have chosen freedom because the plantation felt safe, and reads offers of hope, safety and security as the sign of coming tyranny. Freedom, in his telling, is self-responsibility, including self-sustainability, which he doubts anyone manages alone. He adds that insurance still recognizes acts of God, and that legal freedom really means franchise. Time as the Currency of the Legal System Clint argues that legal equality means everyone is equally punishable, so a poor man pays for a crime with jail time while the rich and corporations pay fines, because time is money and money is time. He asks whether a contract or a mortgage could bind anyone without a due date, suggests a good job is one you would keep doing without pay, and calls time one of the four corners of the fiction. Chance adds that debt-based money works like musical chairs. In his outro he explains Clint's cartoon metaphor: a life logged as timestamped transactions, frame by frame, looks alive to an algorithm.
extra.benny-wills: Benny Wills Not Benny Willis Reading the Peacock Poem From Acting Dream to Truth Comedy Defining the Grand Conspiracy Masks, Smiles and Lost Humanity Word Magic and Legalese Great Reset Schooling and Digital IDs Why Benny Says the Future Is Unwritten Redefining Success as Friends and Love Parrhesia and Fearless Free Speech Benny Performs His Poem About They Chance on reading the Bible poetically Great Conjunction Meets the Great Reset Solstice Gematria and the Number 322 Group Podcast Invite and Sign Off Bringing humor to the situation, it's not just something that will maybe hold someone's attention better, but it actually is a healing mechanism. Benny Wills We're co-conspirators every time that we are willfully ignorant of participating in things that are harming us. Chance Garton Even someone who claims to be an introvert or they like being alone, they still crave some kind of friendship, some kind of companionship, because that's what we are born needing. Benny Wills Success is really much more simple. Success is having good friends and people who care about you and love in your life. Benny Wills From Hollywood Dreams to Truth Comedy Benny grew up in Hollywood with two actor parents and chased the acting dream from childhood into his late twenties or early thirties, along the way noticing inconsistencies in official stories, questioning authority, and reaching people through comedy in ways that conversation and link sharing could not. He later tried poetry at a conference without telling anybody and now performs at truth-based conferences. He says most people in Hollywood have no idea what they are participating in, which Chance ties to the compartmentalization every mafia runs on, and Benny says it took him a long time to see that real success is simple: friends, love and family. Who Is Really Doing the Conspiring? Asked to define the grand conspiracy, Benny describes forces that want people distracted, unhealthy, dependent and divided, working through toxicity on every level, and he urges detoxifying physically, spiritually and emotionally. Chance turns the word around: a conspiracy is people acting in unison, so anyone willfully ignorant of what is harming them becomes a co-conspirator, and he casts levity as the opposite of that weight. Benny closes the first hour with his poem They, written for the curveball question of who they are, which runs through a long list of suspects before answering with we, us, and you and me. Hope in a Year of Distance Benny's positive story of 2020 is his newborn son, whose arrival in the middle of the pandemic he came to see as exactly the right time. Watching a newborn who shows only discomfort or contentment convinced him people are born needing one another, which is why he calls social distancing so destructive. Chance recalls a child hiding from a masked grandmother he did not recognize, and Benny, a self-described apocaloptimist, argues that every push of an agenda also liberates people, that the future is unwritten, and that homesteading is his answer. Labels, Buzzwords and Word Magic Benny's comedy channel Joy Camp was listed as far right in a late November analysis of YouTube echo chambers, which he says shows the label is not rooted in any truth, while joking that he is honored to make the cut. Chance argues society labels something and that makes it so, noting that a movement of people sharing information gets branded an echo chamber. Benny says news-trained audiences react like Pavlov's dogs to buzzwords, calling it programming through language, and Chance, whose podcast keeps bringing him back to word magic, singles out legalese, which he frames as an unchanging priestly language beside a vulgar tongue that keeps shifting. Parrhesia and the Art of Planting Seeds Benny spent six months building Parrhesia, a course named for a word he says means free speech, aimed at conquering the fear of speaking, finding a creative voice, and no longer being the conspiracy theorist who fire hoses people with information. You open a door and let someone walk through, he says, and the victory is when they reach the idea on their own and give you no credit. Chance likens it to scattering seeds on fertile ground instead of glaring at one in rocky soil, and Benny adds that most people resist conspiracy because they cannot accept that level of deception.
extra.derek-tikkuri-gematrinator-second-wave: Welcome Back to the Gematria Rabbit Hole How the Gematria Ciphers Work Number Codes Inside the Bible The Eddie Haskell Name Synchronicity How Decoding Can Turn Lives Around The Mandela Effect Trips Them Up What Makes the Great Conjunction Rare Checking Their Second Wave Predictions Kary Mullis and the PCR Test Elvis and His 1956 Polio Vaccine Shot Derek Reads Bill Gates by the Numbers The Decade of Vaccines Wraps Up Where to Find Derek and Closing Thoughts Thanks for Making It to the End Normally, I don't look at numbers first and have an idea in mind. I just look at what the numbers are, and the pattern emerges. Derek Tikkuri When you're playing with numbers, the cosmic giggle will reach out and poke you and wink at you. Chance Garton Some people who come into this information realize that, wow, there's been something very bright that's been hidden from me. What other kind of brightness is out there? Derek Tikkuri If someone can break out of the fully materialistic worldview because they encountered Gematria, that's going to lead them places you could never predict. Chance Garton I think these numeric synchronicities that we're seeing are not just man-made. Derek Tikkuri This stuff, when we talk about gematria, it is knowledge. It's exploring yourself, it's exploring the world around you, and finding a deeper meaning in things, I think, ultimately. Derek Tikkuri Have trust and faith that the right things are going to happen because nature doesn't make permanent mistakes. Chance Garton You can choose to be as dumb as you want right now, or you can choose to be as smart as you want right now. There's been no time like this in history. Derek Tikkuri Ciphers, Bible Codes and a Digital Ouija Board Derek walks through the ciphers on his calculator: ordinal, where A is 1 and Z is 26; reverse, which counts Z as 1 back to A; reduction, which adds digits so J becomes 1; and English extended, which he likens to Hebrew and Greek charts. He argues their ranges overlap so little that matches between random names and phrases are harder to force than people think, then reads the crucifixion age of 33, Judas and Jesus through Jewish gematria. Finding his own name matching the word gematria, he says, felt like building a digital Ouija board, and Chance frames it as divination alongside his I Ching readings. The Eddie Haskell Name Riddle Derek shares a decode that began with a plain hunch: when an actor named Eddie Hassell died on November 1, 2020, the first name that came to mind was Eddie Haskell of Leave It to Beaver, whose actor Ken Osmond had died that May. He counts 167 days between the two deaths, echoing Hassell's July 16 birthday, and 168 counting the end date, matching Edward Clark Haskell in ordinal. He says the character debuted November 1, 1957, exactly 63 years earlier, and Leave It to Beaver sums to 63 in reduction. His point, he says, is that people make the logical connection first and the numbers then run surprisingly deep. Natural Synchronicity or Engineered Riddle Derek argues the numbers cannot all be man-made, pointing to people who die in their 80s and 90s with striking alignments and asking who kept them alive all that time, and he theorizes that anyone constructing a lie would build it on reality's own numerical code to convince the subconscious. Chance suggests that gematria only works on man-made material like calendar dates and words, and wonders whether artificial, adversarial entities help line that material up, citing the Mandela effect. Closing the episode, he calls organic versus artificial a toss-up, while crediting Derek's examples from his own life with showing organic significance. A Great Conjunction on the Solstice Derek explains the Great Conjunction, when Jupiter and Saturn pass each other roughly every 20 years, and ties past ones to political upheaval: an early '80s triple conjunction as Reagan took office, and the Bush and Gore dispute in 2000. He calls the December 21, 2020 conjunction the first on a solstice in recorded history, seven days after a total solar eclipse, a phrase he sums to 202. He says that eclipse fell 1,212 days from each great American eclipse and on the first day of the 1,212th lunation since 1923. Chance reads Jupiter and Saturn as expansion and contraction, the mix of elation and nostalgic sadness his 2020 brought. Second Wave Decodes From Mullis to Gates Revisiting their earlier call that a second wave would be pushed through the winter, Derek argues deaths are being reclassified and decodes Kary Mullis, inventor of the PCR test, matching his name to polymerase chain reaction and placing his 2019 death 217 days before the pandemic declaration. Chance relays his understanding of Mullis's objection to using a quantitative test this way. Derek then reads Elvis Presley's 1956 polio shot on The Ed Sullivan Show through a run of 42s and through 228, the ordinal of William Henry Gates III, and sees the number of the beast in the Gates Foundation, the World Health Organization and Fauci's institute.
extra.tom-barnett-global-biodynamics: Meet Tom Barnett of Global Biodynamics Start by Getting to Know Your Breath Rethinking Our Relationship With Time Perfectionism as an Avoidance Mechanism CEOs, Celebrities and the Same Struggles What Biodynamic Farming Actually Is Applying Astrology to Your Energy Levels A Month of Charting Your Energy Tom's Case Against Training Every Day Working In Versus Working Out A Starter Practice Called the Lung Jing, the Creative Life Force Celibacy, Porn Culture and Finding Balance Closing Thoughts and Synchronicity Waking Up and Owning Responsibility for Yourself There's an old expression, actually, that if somebody doesn't have time to meditate for 20 minutes a day, then they should meditate for an hour a day. Tom Barnett Even just closing your eyes, spending that time, it's like putting in gaps in the song of your life. Chance Garton A lot of people go along like they're just this passenger, and they're at the whim and they're at the mercy of the elements or society. But we're not. Tom Barnett You're never alone. Alone and all one are the same thing because we all are all one. Chance Garton Everyone's always the same. It doesn't matter if they've got some royal role or if they're a CEO or if they're a celebrity or if they're a mom down the road. Tom Barnett The deepest part of waking up is coming to terms with your own responsibility for yourself, but also the knowledge that you have the power to be responsible for yourself. Chance Garton The moon has a big effect, don't get me wrong, but too many people blame extraneous circumstances because you don't control the moon, but you do control what you do with your life. Tom Barnett That force of creativity that only knows how to create and can only create, we put a dam on it with our thoughts, thinking, judging, and criticizing. Tom Barnett Start With Where Your Breath Is Asked where someone with no starting point should begin, Tom says the breath, and offers a question for any moment of overwhelm: where am I right now, and where's my breath? He says that finding it and feeling it lower and lower brings anxiety, anger and fear down a long way. He splits rest into passive rest, like watching TV, and active rest such as meditation, tai chi and qigong, and argues that screens are not restful because light carries coded information that bypasses our rationale. He also cites an old expression: anyone without twenty minutes a day to meditate should meditate for an hour. The Busyness We Create for Ourselves Chance describes weeks crunched together like music that never respects the pause between notes, and says closing your eyes puts gaps back into the song of your life. Tom argues that we create our own busyness, often from a sense of unworthiness, and that people driven from a place of unrest never find fulfillment in attainment, whether that means world championships or a billion dollars. Chance admits he once deleted every um and pause from two-hour episodes, which he calls procrastination masquerading as perfectionism. Tom adds that the royalty, CEOs and celebrities he has coached carry the same issues and fears as a mom down the road. Biodynamics and the Body's Own Cycles Tom says he came to biodynamics through Paul Chek, one of whose influences was Rudolf Steiner. He describes it as organic farming taken a level further, harmonizing an ecosystem with moon phases, seasons and some astrology, and calls it the cream of the crop for growing food, though he ranks wild food higher still. Chance ties it to the old Farmers' Almanac and to folk knowledge handed over to corporations. Tom times his own heavy training and sexual activity to the sky clock, arguing that men also have libido, energy and emotional cycles tied to the moon, which each person must feel before charting. Working In to Balance Working Out Tom recommends charting a month hour by hour, noting sleep, food, work and training, then lining it up against a lunar calendar, but insists on ruling out tangible causes first: staying up until 2am explains a tired day better than Saturn. He argues that strength gains come only with rest and that the body puts every kind of stress into one basket. His answer, learned from Paul Chek, is working in: tai chi, qigong or a starter he calls the lung, syncing breath with movement to cultivate energy rather than spend it. Chance's closing names it his highlight. Sexual Energy as a Creative Force Chance raises jing from Chinese medicine, and Tom starts from creativity itself: the force that made us only knows how to create, he says, until childhood scolding about coloring outside the lines teaches the mind to judge, damming that flow and, in his view, building constriction into the body. He calls sexual energy our fundamental creative energy, argues that porn bastardizes something natural and takes connection away, and says celibacy is fine for spiritual reasons as long as you are not running from something. His suggestion is to draw that energy up and express it through a poem, a song or something built by hand.
extra.sonia-barrett-business-of-disease: A Health Conversation With Sonia Barrett The Marketing of Breast Cancer How the Business of Disease Film Happened When Pink Was for Boys Why Everyone Asks Who Your Doctor Is Your Body Is Its Own Territory When Doctors Were Paid to Keep You Well Barrett on Disease as a Body Signal Hiking Without a Cellphone How Symbols Market Disease and Fear Barrett on Not Owning Your Illness Where to Find Sonia's Work Outro and Final Thoughts Chance on Stress and Feeling Good in Your Body The cure is in the body, not in the business. Sonia Barrett In my understanding of mind, body, spirit, it's kind of a hierarchy where spirit guides the mind, and mind guides the body. But if you take spirit out of your entire equation, you become two-thirds. Chance Garton You're uniquely tied to your body, so it is absolutely yours to govern. Sonia Barrett We're not anything that's a noun. We're nothing static. We are an expression in motion in the present moment. Chance Garton Having your cellphone, it completely disconnects you from truly being bonded with the healing powers of nature. Sonia Barrett Feeling good is its own reward. I just wish that we hadn't all been conditioned to think that stuff that's bad for us feels good, and that stuff that's good for us feels bad. Chance Garton Nature is the original artist in what is being created and continues to be recreated. We are a work of art. Sonia Barrett Reality is just much more incredible and expansive than what we've been sold. Sonia Barrett Pink Ribbons and the Language of Symbols Barrett traces The Business of Disease to an October around 2010, when she kept being asked to donate at the store and felt she was watching a marketing of breast cancer, more promotion than cause. She argues that symbols are our first language, likening the pink ribbon to the brown of a delivery truck or a car badge that carries a whole concept, and recalls pink on everything down to toilet paper. She offers her account that pink was once for boys as an example of how quietly beliefs get switched. Chance calls the familiar red spiky ball image an artist's rendering that stirs fear in some people. Who Governs Your Own Body Barrett argues that people are conditioned to believe someone else knows what is best for them, which is why it seems strange to say you have no doctor, and why categories like career, church and provider decide who we value. She calls the body its own country and territory, uniquely yours to govern, and says the system is built to make people doubt they can. For her, information moves you away from fear rather than into it, and she says she never uses fear to sell anything. Chance hears in the word evaluate a taking and eating of someone's energy, and says we are verbs rather than nouns. Illness as a Signal, Not an Identity Chance recalls a time when some families paid a doctor a subscription fee for monthly checkups and owed nothing when someone fell sick, and calls today's reversal a value flip. Barrett argues that allopathic medicine fragments the body and that dis-ease is the body looking for ease, an extreme signal sent after subtler ones were ignored. She contends that emotions can matter even more than food, and urges listeners not to take ownership of an illness as who they are, but to look at themselves honestly, without shame, and give themselves new instructions. Chance adds his view that pain is a signal, and that ignoring it makes it louder. Nature Without a Safety Net Barrett hikes every day without a phone, arguing that the device breeds a false sense of security and cuts people off from tuning in to where they are. Strip away every building, she says, and the human race would carry on, because nature provides what is needed and, in her view, the body is designed to fix itself under the right conditions. She hears home alarm commercials and insurance ads as fear programming. Chance agrees there is no safety net in nature and argues that technology is art, which only serves us when it follows nature instead of exploiting it. Barrett replies that nature is the original artist. Feeling at Home in Your Body In his closing reflections, Chance returns to what he calls the first hour's thread, unmanaged stress, and says it matters to get real with yourself about how you feel in your own skin, like a pack-a-day smoker who cannot know how bad it feels until they quit. He argues that much of the world's trouble comes from people not feeling good in their bodies, a short step from body hate, which he links to religions that call the world a prison. He says we were conditioned, from the family table to cartoons, to think what is bad for us feels good, but that you can align with nature's healthier aspects.
extra.dylan-saccoccio-spirit-whirled: Introducing Dylan Saccoccio and Spirit Whirled Clown World and the Presidential Freak Show Art as Ritual and Service to God Flattery Is the Psychic Vampire's First Weapon Media Control and the Independent Artist The Lost Boys Vampire Allegory Debt-Based Currency as Musical Chairs Satan as Adversary and Astrological Opposition Nine as the Number of Satan Tenets of Satanism: Self-Preservation and Moral Relativism Social Darwinism and Might Is Right Mind Control as the Removal of Spirit Outro and Reflections on the Conversation A lot of times people need to just shut their TV off and get off social media and go outside, and that's the real news. Dylan Saccoccio We put the boot on our own throat with our belief and our love of government and the legal system as our God. Chance Garton What you do with your gifts that God gave you is your gift back to God. Dylan Saccoccio What mind control really is, is not really actually the controlling of the mind, it's the removal of spirit. Chance Garton I can't look at myself in the mirror if I have to compromise who I am to get what I want. Dylan Saccoccio Real privacy has nothing to do with being secluded and able to act in an actual isolated vacuum. No matter what, you know what you did. Chance Garton Freedom is always going to be the solution to everything. It doesn't matter what the problem is. Dylan Saccoccio Reading is one of those things where it's like it gives you the recipe and your imagination does the work. Dylan Saccoccio A Puppet Show in Clown World The conversation opens in the week of the 2020 election, with Chance describing a celebrating shopper in the hummus aisle and a line of honking Stop the Steal cars on his drive home, and marveling at grown adults so invested in a puppet show. Dylan calls it the presidential freak show and argues the razor-thin margins keep half the country convinced the result is illegitimate whoever wins. He cites Trump's cabinet, including Wilbur Ross and Steve Mnuchin, as his evidence that the government always wins, predicts a digital universal basic income built to push spending over saving, and says the real news is outside, away from the TV. Art as Service and Its Price Dylan traces ritual to the Latin ritus, service to God, and argues that whatever you do with your God-given gifts is your gift back, whether you paint, practice medicine or build in stone. He walks through the ten thousand hours and the sacrifices an entertainer makes to reach the top, which he says is why so many go along when an offer arrives that would cost them everything they worked for. Recognition, he warns, is one of the tools these circles use, and he calls much of it kind of insincere. He credits a strong family, led by powerful women, for his refusal to trade integrity for a career. Flattery and the Energy Vampire Chance answers with a party story in which a new acquaintance flattered him, then cut across him mid-thought with a pro-state speech and announced that the vibe felt better, leaving him drained; he reads flattery as the psychic vampire's first weapon. He also questions the ten thousand hours idea, asking whether those hours are practiced the right way and suggesting they can amount to indoctrination. Dylan turns to The Lost Boys, where Michael drinks to fit in, as an allegory for newcomers drawn into powerful crowds. The conversation then widens vampirism to the earth itself, and Chance describes debt-based currency as a game of musical chairs. Satan in the Night Sky Asked what Satanism really is, Dylan starts with the Hebrew root meaning adversary and argues it is an astronomical term for the sign opposite the sun. He reads Herod beheading John the Baptist as Leo against Aquarius, and Paul and Saul as Pollux against Sagittarius, suggesting scripture passed star allegories off as history. The modern tradition, he says, treats Satan as the ego, which is why Anton LaVey named nine its number, a point Dylan demonstrates with a live calculation. He then lays out three of the four major tenets, self-preservation, moral relativism and social Darwinism, and points listeners to Mark Passio for more. Spirit, Imagination and Honor Chance frames mind control as the removal of spirit, leaving two thirds of a man, and sets the adverse against the universe: the artificial put before nature. Dylan ties the word Magi to imagination through an older Akkadian word and calls imagination the key to what makes us different. He explains that the title of his fantasy series plays on honor, and warns that solipsism is a trap handed to useful idiots. Chance replies that real privacy is not isolation, since you always know what you did, and his closing outro urges listeners to see themselves as a verb rather than a noun and to put nature before fiction.
extra.matt-landman-west-coast-fires: Welcoming Back Matt Landman Steering the Ship Toward the Fires How Matt Tests Official Narratives Questioning the 11,000 Lightning Strikes Why Landman Says Arson, Not Climate Why Matt Doubts Viral DEW Claims Matt's Weaponized Trees Hypothesis Matt's Case That Almeda Was Planned Rubble, Cleanup Costs and 2,200 Homes What Real Science Actually Means The PTFE Teflon Mask Claim GMO Lessons and Showing Your Face Wrapping Up a Heavy Duty Show I feel and preach that truth is a frequency, and once you start to elevate to that frequency and really hold on to that vibration, all these other truths become self-evident. Matt Landman Maybe there's karmic repercussions for those of us who grab onto a story like directed energy weapons and spread it and cause fear and panic without ourselves finding out, is that really 100% true? Chance Garton When things go really, really viral, I start to ask questions. Matt Landman Who's going to really see the truth? It's the people that have nothing to lose. Matt Landman What nature does is the only truth that exists, because it was already doing what it does before we arrived, and it will continue doing what it does with or without us. Chance Garton You don't need a carpenter, you can do it. Maybe you need to learn, but learning is doing, and that's how you teach the kids and all this stuff. Don't give all your powers away. Matt Landman Be careful what you put your belief in, because that means you love it. Chance Garton Activists got loud, they brought GMO to the forefront, and people did their part. And everyone can play their part just by showing their beautiful face. Matt Landman An Activist Who Wears Many Hats Matt describes how five to seven years of activism made him the chemtrail guy and the maker of Frankenskies, a documentary tracing the history of weather modification from the 1920s, then a self-taught student of meteorology, nutrition, herbs and EMF, which led to a clothing line built with silver and to speaking at city halls that have since moved to Zoom. Chance answers that paths which seem to pull in opposite directions eventually tie together. Matt later cites Edward Bernays and a school system that says pick one profession, arguing that growing your own food and learning by doing keep your powers in your own hands. Matt's Theory of the Almeda Fire Matt asks whether the 11,000 lightning strikes California took in about two days, which he calls a world record, were natural, then turns to the Almeda fire in Talent and Phoenix, Oregon, where he says 2,200 families lost their homes. He contends that arson fires on a day of what he calls engineered winds were a distraction while energy was pulled along a line of three cell towers, through trees he believes hold decades of sprayed aluminum and through homes fitted with one smart meter model. He cites towers untouched amid rubble, melted cars beside barely charred trees, no emergency alert, and losses he puts at 90% low income. Testing a Story Before Spreading It Matt lays out how he tests an official story: first ask whether it insults your soul, then dig in, as he did with fluoridated water, and weigh the official version against the alternatives. He grows suspicious when something goes viral, recalling how a story of cloaked drones firing lasers spread everywhere during the Santa Rosa fires, which he suspects was allowed to spread to hide the truth inside a little bit of truth. Chance wonders whether spreading an unverified, frightening story carries its own karmic cost, and Matt answers that intentions count, admitting he once taught a distinction between contrails and chemtrails he has since abandoned. Nature Before Art Chance draws a line between the natural sciences, where a hypothesis stands or falls on what nature self-evidently does, and what he calls artifice: doing things that would never happen in nature in order to benefit from the results. He recommends Clint Richardson's documentary on the story behind COVID-19, which he says shows officials debating gain of function research, and argues the remedy is to put nature before art so that art follows natural law. In his solo outro he lists declassified cases he says show such experiments are the rule, naming the Willowbrook hepatitis studies on disabled children, Operation Big Buzz and Operation Sea Spray. Why Showing Your Face Matters Matt argues that the common blue masks contain PTFE, which he describes as synthetic fluoride and the same material as Teflon, and says even surgeons do not think such masks should be worn for long. Chance notices more people shopping bare faced just as nearby towns add mandates, a pattern he reads as pushing a rule again and again until it sticks. Matt compares the moment to organic food, which reached grocery shelves because shoppers voted with their dollars, and says anyone can play their part by showing their face, while a story of a small child who hid from a masked grandmother lands the point.
extra.emily-ridout-psychic-energy-vampires: Welcome Back and Ideas as Energy Introducing Returning Guest Emily Ridout America's Pluto Return and Energy Vampires Emily on 1776, Astrology and the Founding Fathers Vampire Folklore From Ancient Babylon How a Vampire Bite Spreads Reading From Joe Slate's Psychic Vampires What Energy Drain Feels Like When You Vampirize Yourself A Ritual to Cut Energetic Tethers Burning Samskaras Through Practice Outro: Where Chance Has Been A Technique for Psychic Defense I've often said that ideas are energy, and whether good or bad, the thoughts we believe most strongly can have the biggest effect on how we feel. Chance Garton The image of the vampire is so potent because they can actually pierce your energetic field and take, and in doing so, either kill you or turn you into a vampire. Emily Ridout The real important thing to recognize, and I'll reiterate it over and over again for the rest of my life to people, is that spiritual energy is your attention span. Chance Garton When I think about vampires, like the energy vampires, I just think you can't bleed something dry that's infinite. Emily Ridout If you live backwards, you're evil. So you're living backwards when you're seeking attention, because what you should be seeking is to pay attention. Chance Garton Once we learn to not drain ourselves, we'll probably learn not to either allow ourselves to be drained or to drain others in turn because we'll feel whole. Emily Ridout Imagination is not fake, guys. It's actually a sensory apparatus and a creative capacity. Chance Garton Stand in the truth and have a deep commitment to acknowledging truth, no matter how hard it is to see. You don't have to like it. Emily Ridout America's Pluto Return and Group Vampirism Emily frames 2020 through America's Pluto return, a transit no human lifespan is long enough to see, since Pluto rules the subconscious and the unconscious shadow, personal and collective. She expects what the cheery histories leave out, from wars and slavery to forced sterilization in the 1920s, to surface as the return goes exact in 2022, and stresses that its nature is surprise: we do not yet know what is really going on. Chance widens vampirism to institutions, arguing the federal government acts as a group parasite echoing the taxation without representation story, and hopes the result is a revolution in consciousness rather than a bloody one. How Vampire Folklore Maps Energy Theft Emily traces the vampire back at least to Mesopotamia and the Babylonian precursors of the Hebrew Lilith folklore, a demonic woman who drinks the blood of children, and forward to Twilight. For two thousand years, she says, life energy was understood as blood, hence the laws about bloodlines, consuming blood and slaughter; now the question is what we may take of another person's energy and attention. The bite leaves three choices, defeating the vampire, being destroyed, or becoming one, and she ties the last to how harm gets passed on. Chance adds the older tales of nightly visits that weaken a victim until they must feed on others. Joe Slate's Research on Psychic Vampires Chance reads from Psychic Vampires by Joe Slate, a research book built on case studies, which sorts vampires into twelve types. He singles out the narcissistic vampire, with its grandiose self-importance, fragile self-esteem and lack of empathy, and admits it described his own younger behavior. Slate's list of effects on repeated victims runs from chronic fatigue and poor concentration to sleep disturbances and irritability, and Chance adds that the book finds many of the same symptoms in the vampire. Its answer, as Chance relays it, is teaching both the drained and the drainer to connect to a cosmic source Emily says cannot be bled dry. Habit, Multitasking and Draining Yourself Emily argues nothing is bad in itself, but letting social media, the news or email dictate your life out of habit hands them the time and attention that could feed what you care about, and if cosmic energy sounds too crazy, plug into nature. Chance admits gaming on his phone while working and finding his work full of mistakes, since nobody has more than 100 percent of their attention to split. That leads to what Slate calls parasitic vampirism, draining yourself. Emily describes a multi-elemental self whose mind wants busyness and body wants comfort, and suggests five or ten minutes of meditation to pull it back into unity. Boundaries, Samskaras and a Five-Step Defense Emily calls sharing energy essential; one-way taking is what throws things off balance, and you never truly have to give anyone anything, even when boundaries carry earth plane consequences. In yoga, she explains, practice burns the samskaras, the latent reactive tendencies, and she urges listeners to stand in the truth rather than believe the Pluto return's lie that the world is simply awful. Chance warns against vampirizing yourself over a lapsed routine, and in the outro he walks through a five-step technique he reads aloud: a body scan, focusing on the solar plexus, self-infusion, cosmic infusion through upturned palms, and a hand clasp that cues the whole practice.
extra.john-coleman-apocatastasis: Chance welcomes John Coleman back Recapping John Taylor Gatto's famous 1991 speech Gatto on listlessness, busyness and lost agency Fake time versus real spiritual time John's five kinds of wealth beyond money Social wealth and knowing your local history Why insiders rarely challenge the system What healthy pedagogy looks like Why trust matters between teachers and families The missing rites of passage into adulthood Ivan Illich and Deschooling Society What the Apocatastasis institute is building Sometimes people think private schools or homeschoolers get off the hook, but it's actually the exact same DNA model that comes from the industrial system, and it produces the same people. John Coleman It's supposed to feel good to be you and to be in your body, and you're not supposed to really need to achieve anything to feel good, because just being you is goodness itself. Chance Garton Knowing the poetry of this particular part of the country, the architecture, the food: these things are like their own species. We've been denuded of these things, and deliberately so. John Coleman Your time is the real currency. Spiritual currency is attention, and energy flows where attention is directed in your life. Chance Garton In terms of the perpetuation of knowledge, systemic knowledge, deep learning, I would suggest that it doesn't begin with student-centered learning. We hear that a lot, but I would say with scholar-centered learning. John Coleman It's not really just up to this one group called the government or to the teachers to be concerned with how people are being raised. It's actually everyone's concern. Chance Garton If you go into one of these alternative schools or even one of the mainstream schools, you shouldn't be there if you don't trust the people. John Coleman Speaking of graduation, we need to make that graduation from just consuming the critique to actually acting on it in real life. John Coleman Gatto and the factory model of schooling John recaps John Taylor Gatto, a New York teacher of the year who gave a 1991 speech, left the classroom and spent his later years writing and lecturing against what he saw as a factory model of education. John places Gatto in a longer line of critics running from Maria Montessori and Rudolf Steiner to Ivan Illich and John Holt, and traces early homeschooling to a mix of sixties counterculture and evangelical Protestantism. His own twist is that private schools and homeschooling curricula share the same industrial DNA as public schools, so the critique should not stop at public education. Listlessness, busyness and lost agency Both men describe a schooling built on busyness and obedience for their own sake, which John says leaves former students unable to take agency, the habit of self-direction. John notes that the word course comes from the Latin for a racetrack, a circle that goes nowhere. Chance recalls reaching his early twenties with no working internal compass, cycling between work, class and video games that felt like more stimulus and reward. He contrasts that man-made clock of repeating cycles with what he calls real time, the passage marked by your own spiritual development. Five kinds of wealth beyond money John grounds his teaching in an expanded idea of wealth: spiritual, cultural, social, personal and commercial, with commerce kept in its place. Social wealth, he says, means knowing why a street is called Smith Lane, the families, poetry, architecture and food of a place, things he argues people have been deliberately stripped of. Chance answers that health is wealth and that real wealth is a garden, clean water and skills, while fiat money, in his view, is built on debt and buys products that end up as trash. He calls time the true currency, since energy flows where attention goes. John's case for a healthier pedagogy Asked what healthy pedagogy looks like, John argues deep learning starts with scholar-centered rather than student-centered learning, since teachers cannot give what they do not have. He questions how early formal schooling should begin, citing Thomas Hine's history of the American teenager for the view that compulsory high school also served the labor market. He asks for long-term bonds between scholars, students and subject matter, saying real intellectual growth often shows only after two or three years, and he calls trust the foundation. Chance adds his concern about separating young children from their parents so early. From critique to action and further reading John says the research community falls flat when it only consumes critiques instead of building something, and urges listeners to graduate into action in real life. He recommends Ivan Illich's Deschooling Society, which he says compares modern schooling to the automobile's effect on cities and imagined something like a chat room decades early, along with Horace Mann's writings, Anna Kamenetz and a fresh reading of John Dewey. Chance argues that nobody learns except autodidactically and that rites of passage are missing. John closes on Apocatastasis, a Greek word meaning restoration, and his work to preserve the classroom.

Frank Castle Despite the limitations you have as a human being, you're actually still omnificent. There's no way of arguing that away or tricking yourself into believing that's not true. Chance Garton Why Source Wants You Creating Frank frames his own story as a hero's journey, the kind where you get hurt, hit rock bottom and work your way up. After an injury, he says, he went looking for what could really help him and found ayahuasca, which he credits with pulling him back. He describes going to sit inside Source to argue his case, only to be asked a single question: why are you not creating? As he tells it, you are Source and yourself at once, that is the gift, and you can do anything Source can do and are supposed to do more. He came back, he says, ready to start his mission. Big You Moving Into the Body Frank pictures the self as a Russian nesting doll stacked through twelve densities, an octave that runs from the elements and the ants of the lowest levels up to a higher self that is now walking into the body. He compares it to steering a character in The Sims, clumsy on a Commodore 64 and smooth on a PS5, and says the calm inner voice that steers you away from a crowd looking for trouble is big you. Making room means clearing old programming and dropping self-judgment, since nobody is judging you but you, and what shines out afterwards is more big you in you. Letting the Hater Roll Off Chance takes Frank's Spider-Man lesson about not getting mad at J. Jonah Jameson and makes it his own: when a woman in a grocery line chewed him out for going without a mask, the old welling-up of emotion never came, and her anger rolled off like water on duck feathers. He argues that calm, rational honesty defuses tension better than anything, and that fear works by convincing you to control things with artifice instead. Frank adds that the emotion itself is fuel: catch the surge with a breath, and whatever you say next carries all that power in a friendly tone that leaves the other person short-circuited. Walking Out of the Industry Ritual Frank's name comes from the hip hop group he was in, not from the Punisher, and has stuck for twenty-five years, and music is where he says the darker rituals first showed themselves. He recalls Wu-Tang Killa Beez pulling him aside on tour, where he opened as the only fire sign among some forty groups, to tell him demons and rituals are real. Signed to Def Jam, he says he watched people chant by candlelight over the master copy of a song on an altar, objected, and saw his group fired at sixteen weeks with their contract torn up. Walking away, he says, led straight to Disney bookings. Health, Imagination and Inner Space Chance describes his turning point: fresh out of college with no ambition, he had been getting healthier when his first deep psychedelic experience let the person he was always meant to be walk in. Health, he argues, is the clearest path to feeling yourself as Source, because the body is the tree the seed of your divine spark grows into, and Frank offers his clogged fluoride filter as a picture of what we collect. Chance calls imagination the primary form of thinking, insists in the outro that we remain omnificent despite human limits, and recommends the game Control for its idea that real entities come from inner space.
extra.paul-lenda-shift: Welcome to the One Within All Why Paul Left America Behind Escaping to Laos Before Borders Closed When Your Cats Are Your Guides Ways to Connect With Your Guides Fractal Time and Changing the Past Journaling as the Omniscient Narrator The Power of Perpetual Summer Chance on Personal Charge and Synchronicity The Halo Chakra as Spiritual Armor True Versus False Synchronicities Reality Alchemy and Evolving Mandala Outro Reflections and Gratitude It's always good to remind ourselves that we're embedded inside a unified field of conscious energy that is essentially limitless. Chance Garton Your higher self isn't somewhere higher than you. It's not spatially like that. It's already within you. Paul Lenda There's no safety guaranteed in reality, but challenges are always a direct result of what is necessary, and the obstacles are the course, as you might say. Not just your money, but your spiritual money is attention. That's your spiritual currency. Paul Lenda Chasing Perpetual Summer to Laos Paul describes leaving the United States after Washington State, which he expected to feel like home, stopped feeling right. He says he questioned his higher self through regression hypnotherapy, the I Ching and meditation, and the answer was to live in perpetual summer for at least a year so his energy field could stay expanded instead of contracting through winter as it had in Vermont. After about seven months in Thailand, where a Buddhist rather than Christian culture shaped daily life, he says he and his partner were the last two people granted visas into Laos. He also recounts being told his cats were his guides. Meeting Your Guides in Meditation Asked how to connect with guides, Paul starts with getting into a receptive mode past the noise of distracting thoughts, using a square breath of four counts each, the 4-7-8 breath, breathing mantras, or ambient tracks from the Insight Timer app. Longer sits bring an alpha state of pure awareness where, he says, the messages arrive. He describes close to a baker's dozen guides, including towering blue and black beings with gold accents and a crystalline figure in a meditation circle around the planet. Both men urge testing unfamiliar beings, and Chance suggests simply asking fearlessly whether they are of the highest and greatest good. Time Fractals and Reframing the Past Paul says the higher self is not somewhere above us but already within, stretched through dimensions in the same space, and he prefers the term time fractal to timeline because past, present and future happen at once and shape each other. He describes healing the past of his lineage and setting blueprints for the future. Chance frames changing the past as reframing your view of an event, and offers a simple method: journal a hard memory from the view of an omniscient narrator who loves the main character unconditionally. He calls imagination the core operating system of thought, and Paul extends the same approach to inner child work. Tuning Forks, Toning and the Energy Centers Chance shares his work with tuning forks and toning with his own voice, and his sense that sound and electromagnetism are two sides of one phenomenon, like thunder and lightning. Paul recommends Sacred Sounds by Ted Andrews, whose author suggests a pitch pipe for tuning the seven energy centers, and The Emotion Code by Dr. Bradley Nelson. Chance then raises the idea of two hidden notes beyond the familiar seven, tying it to nine as the number of the self. Paul answers from his own visions of a toroidal energy body, describing one energy center above the head and another below it, like infrared and ultraviolet. Charge, Synchronicity and Spiritual Armor Chance argues that personal charge shapes how much synchronicity and manifesting show up, calling the knowledge that health is wealth the real life hack. He describes the halo chakra as a kind of spiritual armor, like a coach high in the bleachers calling plays. Paul adds that synchronicities come in many forms beyond numbers and that synthetic ones exist too, so one that leaves a situation still feeling wrong may not be authentic. Chance casts trickster entities as split off parts of the psyche, and closes on attention as spiritual currency.
extra.eileen-day-mckusick-biofield-tuning: In the Beginning Was the Word Eileen's Path to Tuning Forks Electric Body, Electric Health Your Inner Light as an Electrical System The Body as a Self-Tuning Instrument What Eileen Calls a Low Battery Was the Ether Erased From Education Syntropy, the Missing Force of Creation Every Cosmology Requires One Miracle The Electric Sky Changed Her Story Enter the Sonic Slider Is the Schumann Resonance Rising Chance's Recap and Closing Thoughts The difference between human language and the frequency of nature is in the difference between a sunset and a painting of a sunset. Chance Garton The amazing thing about the human body is that it's a self-tuning instrument. Eileen McKusick We've all been taught to attack ourselves with our own minds instead of using our minds powerfully and creatively and using our words powerfully and creatively. Eileen McKusick No matter what you think about the origins of the cosmos, basically you have to accept at least one miracle regardless of your belief system. Chance Garton The ether, I believe, was taken out of our cosmological story, and our education, was made to disappear in the same way that Tesla was made to disappear. Eileen McKusick A tree falls over in the forest and turns back into dirt, but new trees sprout up. And that's the nature of life, is entropy giving rise to syntropy. Eileen McKusick The whole thing with any type of energy healing is, to a degree, it's going to have to be something you make your own. Chance Garton I moved from a cosmological story of darkness and blackness and disconnection and meaningless into a cosmology of light and connection, and that was what I was looking for. Eileen McKusick The Body's Hidden Electrical System Eileen describes her next book, Electric Body, Electric Health, as a response to a culture trained to see the body chemically and mechanically. She starts from what most people already accept, the heart's pulse on an EKG, brainwaves on an EEG, bones she calls piezoelectric, and argues these are parts of one electrical system she treats as the biofield, a toroidal bubble in which she believes memories are stored magnetically. In her model the electrical body is the blueprint and the physical body the building, so she uses a tuning fork like sonar to find noise in the signal, trusting what she calls a self-tuning instrument to correct itself. Healing as Making the Self Whole Eileen holds that our essential being is light and that light is fundamentally indivisible, so splitting ourselves into head versus heart is, in her words, compartmentalizing with words a division that does not exist. She describes a pattern she calls a low battery, where people have given more than they received, and says inner division feeds dramas of attack and defense. Healing, she notes, means to make whole: the stuck bits of self she locates in the field behave like frozen light, and when they return to circulation she says people look as if a three-way bulb got turned up a click. Four Ideas She Says School Left Out Eileen argues that secular education erased the ether and plasma, two connective elements that could be mistaken for religious ideas, swapping a luminiferous medium for an empty vacuum and asking students to accept that light travels through nothing. She links that omission to Tesla vanishing from school lessons and cites Einstein's later remark that space without an ether is unthinkable. She adds two more: syntropy, the life-assembling force she refused to call negative entropy, and levity, the counterpart to gravity she says you can feel sitting beside a Caribbean steel drum band. Missing all four, she contends, is why people feel disconnected and deflated. Trading a Dark Cosmology for Light Chance argues that every origin story demands at least one miracle, whether a Big Bang or let there be light, and calls scientism the dominant religion of today, whose picture of space leaves each of us a speck on a speck in an empty void. Eileen recalls that hundreds of self-help books and workshops never delivered what they promised, and The Electric Sky by Donald Scott was the book that stopped her reading self-help altogether. A cosmology of black holes and randomness, she says, had been a depressing backdrop in her own mind, and moving to one of light and connection gave her new tools for old problems. Getting Back Into Flow Chance treats the flow state as a gauge of where someone sits energetically, recalling that after his first biofield tuning sessions on willing test subjects he caught himself making up a rhyming rap while driving with no music on. Eileen answers that electric health is flow and describes inflammation as a restriction in flow, a traffic jam with too much voltage in the wires. She built the Sonic Slider for self-care on the twelfth harmonic of the Schumann resonance, 93.96 hertz, after finding the eleventh too heavy and the thirteenth too hyper, and citing Rollin McCraty of HeartMath, she says the resonance itself is not rising.
