Dylan Saccoccio Truth Known by What It Is Not Chance opens with the idea that truth, like freedom, is understood negatively: you could never list everything it is, only delete what it is not, the way natural law leaves countless rights and only a few wrongs. Dylan answers that the truth simply is, whatever our perceptions of it, and traces his framing to the Hermetic tradition of Hermes, Thoth and Mercury and to Mark Passio's natural law podcasts, arguing that wrong behavior programs slavery while right behavior programs freedom. Matt reads a Spirit Whirled passage on polarity, in which every paradox is unified once truth is treated as absolute. Symbolic Literacy as Psychic Self-Defense Chance argues that pairing Mark Passio's teaching on manipulation with the symbolic literacy in Dylan's work gives a listener a black belt in psychic self-defense, like putting on the truth glasses from They Live. Dylan says ancient allegory encoded survival knowledge in sun and Saturn imagery, and that recognizing it makes a person unhexable; he reads the name corona as crown symbolism running back to Kronos, the cube of the Kaaba and Solomon's seal. Matt holds up a San Francisco Chronicle front page and, in his reading, finds a long spell, a demon and the pandemic packed into one headline seen by millions. Matt's Traveling Truth Box Library Matt describes turning a neighborhood book box idea into a traveling library of truth-oriented media, mailed from person to person across the United States, and walks through its contents: Spirit Whirled, Behold a Pale Horse, 1984 and Animal Farm, his FrankenSkies DVD, Dark City, They Live, Brave New World, Edward Bernays's Propaganda, Manufacturing Consent and Arthur Firstenberg's The Invisible Rainbow. Dylan shares mixed feelings about Behold a Pale Horse, physical copies are championed as insurance against a censored digital future, and Chance detours into This Person Does Not Exist and AI-cloned voices as a digital echo of They Live. Anarchy, Rights and the Legal Name Dylan says the word anarchy has been so poisoned that it is easier to talk about voluntarism, and asks who would seriously argue that actions should not be voluntary. The group recasts anarchy as life without rulers rather than without rules, and Clint Richardson's work is cited to contrast natural use, like a bird's claim to its nest, with property as a legal fiction. Matt reads Superman as an allegory of shedding the lowercase legal name Clark Kent, while Dylan, whose surname he says means a pocket or sack in Italian, explains he never changed his name because the work matters more than the personality. Self-Reliance as the Price of Freedom After Dylan urges storable food, warm clothing and preparation for a hard winter, Chance argues that being ready to take full responsibility for your own survival is what real sovereignty means, and the highest form of positivity. He points to Derrick Broze's freedom cells and barter networks and says inner mastery creates outer freedom from masters, while the homeless village in They Live is held up as a picture of natural cooperation. Dylan closes by recommending silver and stored food against what he sees as a coming centralized digital system, and Matt celebrates simple ancestral knowledge: potatoes grow from potatoes, coriander grows cilantro.

A slave can never, ever speak your language, or he becomes your equal. Clint Richardson Freedom Recast as Franchise Clint opens by refusing the label of free man, calling himself a fellow slave who has worked out the system of law that governs everyone who takes part in it. He argues that in legal language freedom is defined as franchise, comparing a citizen to a McDonald's outlet run under a parent corporation, and describes the United States as a municipal corporation separate from the fifty states. The more free people believe they are, he says, the more they trust voting and democracy. Chance returns to this in his closing, asking how government can license people to do what none of them has the right to do in nature. Birth Certificate, Person and Mask Clint traces what he calls the voluntary slavery of modern citizenship back to the birth certificate. In his reading, delivery means abandonment, so parents surrender their property rights in the child, who becomes a ward of the state with the United States as domicile. He says over 140 countries share an international Social Security system that keeps everyone in contract. The footprint stamped onto the certificate and the word identity, heard as id entity, come up as symbols of the same trade. The result, Clint argues, is a person, which he says simply means status, and he notes that persona is Latin for mask. A Law Book Behind the Religion Clint says he once despised the Bible until he found references to it in legal texts, and he now argues it is a book of law rather than a religion, with religion built around it. He asks why the Bible has been treated as common law in Pennsylvania and England, recommends the 1828 Webster's dictionary for its scriptural citations, and contends that church and courtroom keep people from the language. He describes the first rule of slavery as never teaching a slave your language, which he ties to legal terms of art, meaning anything not of nature. Chance frames all this beforehand, asking literalists and atheists alike to stay open. Money, Mammon and Living in Fiction Identity, Clint argues, means sameness, and every name, address and number offered to prove it ties a person to something that does not exist in nature. He calls money fiction with no intrinsic value, and reads mammon as pricing a tree, livestock or a man as a commodity instead of valuing it as a self-evident part of existence, which is why no one can have two gods. Chance adds that dictionary breaks into diction and Ares, the god of war, casting commerce as a state of war, and Clint recalls a line that a civil war is a war over words. Jehovah Restored as a Verb Chance sets this up in his opening, asking listeners to hear God as nature and the forces of the cosmos rather than anything supernatural. Clint then says the name Jehovah appeared in scripture more than 6,000 times before later Bibles swapped it for lord, king and God. He argues god is a generic title for any magistrate or status that gives orders, and says older court records addressed judges as gods. Reading the 1828 Webster's entry, which says the name denotes permanent being, to be fixed, to stand or to abide, he concludes Jehovah is a verb: existence itself, everything self-evident and not created by man.
extra.matt-presti: Intro and Welcoming Back Matt Presti Moving 64 Tons of Walter Russell's Art Russell's Art as Proof of His Message Which of 80,000 Daily Thoughts Will You Birth Exploring the Nature of the Self Natural Hierarchies and Invented Authority Balance as the Key to Creativity Learning to Hear the Still Small Voice Blake and Imagination as the Foundation Shadow Work and the Body Creativity in the Age of Accessible Arts Balancing the Triangle of Life Episode Outro and Closing Reflections The creator is you to the degree that you're aware of it. Matt Presti Bringing Walter Russell's Art Back on Display Matt, president of the University of Science and Philosophy, recounts moving what he estimates at 64 tons of the Russells' art, sculpture and personal effects in September 2018: roughly 11 semis' worth, unloaded over nine days with zero breakage, then a full year to ready the building in Waynesboro, Virginia. He says the old Swannanoa Palace headquarters showed perhaps 60 percent of Walter Russell's art and the new museum about 98 percent, though he reckons the collection is only 2 percent of everything Russell made. He adds that Russell pointed to that prolific output, made with a fourth-grade education, as proof his spiritual message worked. Birthing a Thought Into a Body Chance frames the conversation with a Russell passage on the genius who thinks inwardly, visions an idea, then gives it physical form. Matt picks up the thread: of 60 to 80,000 thoughts a day, which one will you hold and actually birth? He urges holding an idea, writing it down, gathering resources and, above all, waiting, calling patience the virtue a fast food culture has lost. Borrowing from the Russells, he describes the universe as a perfect mirror that takes a step toward your goal for every step you take, and offers the museum as proof, a thought he held for 11 years before it stood finished. Ego, Inward Thinking and Becoming Whole Matt reads ego as externally generated outlook, how you imagine others see you, and sets it against the inward thinking direction that every great artist and poet shares. He calls materialistic externalism one of the most profound illnesses taught today, names the self as the most priceless possession anyone can have, and describes the journey of life as integrating the shadows of the mind until you are whole. Chance calls that the true mystical path, the kingdom of heaven within. Matt adds the alchemist Fulcanelli's line that the vital transmutation is of the experimenter himself, and Russell's answer to a wealthy doctor: he listened to his still small voice. Blake, Imagination and Creative Power Chance, drawing on William Blake, argues that imagination is not a mode of thinking but the foundation all thinking grows from, a spiritual mode of perception, not fantasy: an idea that can be given a body was real before it was built. Matt reads the Russells' line that humanity's imagination, and so its creative power, has not yet awakened, and recalls hunting the devil under his basement stairs with a childhood BB gun and finding nothing there. With a mixing board that once cost $2,000 now about 80 dollars, he sees the arts opened to anyone, and calls himself a prosumer who chooses what he takes in. Balance Through the Seasons of a Life Matt says Russell taught the law of balance even in business ethics lectures, which Russell called the Sermon on the Mount in disguise, and sketches a life arc: pleasure in the 20s, vocation in the 30s, honing skills in the 40s, wisdom in the 50s. Chance maps it onto Saturn, whose returns near 30 and 60 test whether a person has learned discipline and balance. Matt's triangle of life sets the physical and mental at the base, with spirituality born from their balance, and he cites Bruce Lee: balance is the ultimate power. In his closing reflections Chance ties a healthy, balanced body to biophilia, the love of life.

John recalls Gurdjieff's challenge to notice yourself opening a door and calls ritual a geometric ordering of daily life, and both men push back on a spirituality that dismisses the material world as illusion, which John says Steiner would class as Luciferian. He recounts Keely's claim to have divided matter into at least 27 sub-levels governed by three streams from celestial bodies, and argues the popular Tesla quote about three, six and nine has never been found, pointing to Keely's harmonics instead. Chance adds the Gnostic meme to that list, rejecting the body as a meat puppet trapped by archons and arguing that we are already in the ascended state, here to make nature a little more perfect through art. Walter Russell's Still Center John opens with Walter Russell, one of several visionaries, with Tesla and Steiner, whom he credits with an inner sight modern science lacks. He recounts Russell's 39 day illumination, whose hundreds of pages became The Divine Iliad, and quotes Russell's line that genius is self-bestowed and mediocrity self-inflicted. Russell's model sets an unmoving spiritual universe behind a physical universe that exists only through polarity, like the still fulcrum of a seesaw. Our senses, John says, only detect motion, so decentration rather than concentration opens the mind to that stillness. Chance applies it to thought, asking who tells you to do something and who is the I that does it. Cubes, Vortexes and a Musical Periodic Table Russell's physics, as John lays it out, runs on two kinds of vortex motion: centripetal compression toward suns and stable elements like carbon, and centrifugal expansion that we call radiation. His periodic tables are spirals built on musical octaves, with the inert gases, which Russell called the Akashic records, on the equilibrium line. In his model every system sits in a cube whose faces, planes of zero curvature, reverse the motion like mirrors, so that, in Russell's words, waves of light do not travel but reproduce each other from wave field to wave field. John describes Russell's optical dynamo generator, which he says heated its core without an electrical drive. Steiner, Ahriman and Moral Technology Turning to Rudolf Steiner, John sets anthroposophy against the theosophy it grew out of and describes Steiner's two forces, Lucifer and Ahriman, the second driving materialism and mechanization. He reads Steiner as warning that transhumanism could cut mankind off from the etheric body, while insisting we meet technology head on with moral, etheric technology rather than flee to the woods. He walks through Steiner's ethers, cites Lili Kolisko's decades of crystallization experiments timed to celestial events, and describes biodynamic farming. His big lesson is that information comes from the stars, and he argues that people are themselves the ultimate radionics machine, with every device a set of training wheels.
extra.becca-tarnas-perilous-realm: Becca Tarnas returns to explore the perilous realm Why chance is never an accident in Tolkien Defining fairy stories through Tolkien's own essay Iceland's hidden folk and respect for the land From myth to legend to fairy story Philology and the spell of the adjective Owen Barfield on language and evolving consciousness Entering fairy with the heart of a child Gandalf versus Saruman on humility and power Recovery, escape and fairy as our own world Living through the middle of our own story Chance on Gnosticism and whether the world is fallen We as human beings imagine ourselves to be separate from the natural world. That is not something that an elf or a fairy would ever conceive of. They are of the natural world. Becca Tarnas If we are in our modern age seeing wind and breath and spirit as being different, doesn't that allow for humanity, or even influence humanity, to see the earth as a nonliving and non-spiritual entity? Chance Garton Grammar itself is a word that comes from glamour, which is a reference to the kind of enchanted quality that language has. Becca Tarnas If you've tried to use evil as a means that are justified because you think that's for good ends, then you've already been taken over by evil. Evil's already won. Chance Garton To be an adult is to protect that part of ourselves, so we have to be strong in our adult selves to really be able to show up for that inner child. Becca Tarnas Middle-earth is our earth, not some other planet. It's not some out there, it's right here. You just have to be enchanted to see it. That is what the recovery is. Becca Tarnas The real meaning of personal responsibility and sovereignty is to treat your body and mind like a little child that you're raising with love and care instead of as a meat robot. Chance Garton Logic is important, rationality is important, reason is so important. What is necessary is to balance them with imagination, with emotion, with embodiment, not to just flip the hierarchy. Becca Tarnas Why Tolkien Called Fairies Natural Chance reads from Tolkien's essay On Fairy Stories, where man rather than the fairy is called supernatural, and Becca Tarnas hears a not-so-hidden ecological ethic in it: humans imagine themselves separate from nature, while elves are of the natural world. She points to Iceland, where by her account about 5% of people firmly believe in the hidden folk, 5% firmly deny them and the rest leave room, so roads curve around rocks said to be elf homes. She traces a path from myth to legend to fairy story to fantasy novel, and argues that the imagination itself is a natural feature of the cosmos. Language as a Kind of Spell Chance reads Tolkien's rebuttal of Max Müller's view of mythology as a disease of language, and his praise of the adjective as the most potent spell in faerie. Becca explains that Tolkien was a philologist, a lover of the word, who saw words as carrying their meaning rather than as arbitrary labels, and she links spell to spelling and grammar to glamour. Drawing on Owen Barfield's Poetic Diction and Saving the Appearances, she describes how the Latin spiritus once meant spirit, wind and breath at once. Chance asks whether splitting those meanings made it easier to treat the earth as lifeless. Childlike Wonder and the Inner Child Chance brings up Tolkien's line that whoever would enter the kingdom of fairy should have the heart of a little child, and asks what is happening to the inner child in the collective psyche. Becca separates childlike from childish, borrowing the beginner's mind of Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, and argues that many adults have lost their wonder without ever being initiated into adulthood. For her, a true adult protects that inner child as an everyday practice. Chance names the failure adultism and offers the adept as its opposite, pointing to Gandalf, Aragorn, and Frodo, who saves the Shire but not for himself. Gandalf, Saruman and the Limits of Reason Becca contrasts Gandalf with Saruman, head of the White Council, who would never sit down with hobbits over ale and pipe weed. She ties humility to humus, the soil, and to being human, and sees that closeness to the earth as the reason Gandalf alone among the Istari succeeds, while Saruman eyes the Shire as country to industrialize and sell off. Chance argues that Saruman's slide began with fear dressed up as logic: once you use evil as a means to good ends, evil has already won. Becca adds that reason matters but needs balancing with imagination, emotion and embodiment, citing Gregory Bateson. Recovery, Escape and Re-Enchantment Becca takes up Tolkien's defense of fantasy against the charge of escapism: the escape of the prisoner is not the flight of the deserter, and the world beyond the prison walls is still real. In his essay, she notes, the land of fairy is our world, holding sun, moon, sea and mortal humans when they are enchanted, and she says Tolkien is clear that Middle-earth is our earth. She frames recovery as reclaiming a birthright of enchantment while keeping what the modern split has won, such as individual rights, and sees the early pandemic as a pivotal moment. Chance worries fear could revive old divisions like xenophobia.
extra.david-whitehead-truth-warrior: Chance sets up the hero's journey David's new Lord of the Rings series Chance meets Gandalf as a spirit guide Carl Jung's archetypes inside the Fellowship Moral victory, free choice and the Ring Boromir, Frodo and the lure of power Integrating the shadow instead of repressing fear Cults and the search for an external savior Chance's theory that creativity means decisiveness David on freedom versus liberty David's view of China, communism and the West Chance's closing thoughts on heroism The way we're taught to view the world is that the world is something happening to us. David Whitehead The real battle with evil is our own inner struggle to do the small good things that we can do in the face of overwhelming opposition. Freedom is something that is the ground of your being. David Whitehead Love is the force that expands and allows us to see the infinite potential in things. Chance Garton I didn't call my show Truth Warrior because I'm sitting there saying I've got the truth, listen to me. I'm not trying to start a cult. David Whitehead Lord of the Rings as Guiding Myth David Whitehead explains why he launched a four-part Truth Warrior series with Laura Lee on The Lord of the Rings as the guiding myth of our time. Reading from her synopsis, he says the tale matters not because it is new but because it draws on a body of ancient knowledge obscured through distortion and deception, and he describes rewatching the trilogy during lockdown to find strength. In his view Tolkien gathered myths and legends from many traditions, with echoes of the Bhagavad Gita, into a story rooted in the Western magical tradition. Chance adds that he has read, heard and watched the saga repeatedly over the past year. The Archetypes Live Inside Us Drawing on Carl Jung, David lists the persona, shadow, anima or animus and self alongside the wise old man, the hero and the trickster, and suggests that the Fellowship, Sauron and Saruman are all figures within each reader, echoing Joseph Campbell's line that the heavens and hells live inside us. Chance describes meeting Gandalf as a spirit guide during a meditative exercise, and offers his view that ignored archetypes return in tyrannical outer form to tear down the ego. David argues that a priest class literalized myth, and reads the saying that the kingdom of heaven is within you as a call to inner relationship rather than worship. Evil, Fear and the Ring of Power Chance recalls David's line from the Laura Lee series that a moral victory requires choice, choice requires freedom, and freedom is exactly what the Ring of Power takes away. David points to Boromir, who wants to wield the Ring for good, as a picture of well-meaning people persuaded that the ends justify the means, and to Frodo's innocence as the quality that lets him bear it. He argues that evil must be admitted to exist, that meaning well is not enough, and that lingering fear and evil are closely tied. His remedy is to study fear and integrate the shadow through art, martial arts or calligraphy rather than repress it. Creativity and the Next Step Chance shares a pet theory that creative people are decisive: faced with a blank canvas or page, the artist takes the first step and trusts the next one to become clear. He links the artist's flow state to the synchronicity of the hero's journey, where the Fellowship never sees the whole road but takes the next step through Caradhras, Moria and Lothlorien, and he suggests that facing today's troubles is likewise one step at a time on the way to Mount Doom. David calls this a source of hope, recalling how often the story hangs on a thread, and says a voice of doubt accompanies every creative step. Freedom Versus Liberty in David's View David sums up what he believes is worth preserving in Western civilization as freedom, which he separates from liberty. Liberty, he says, is something a government grants, while freedom is the ground of your being and rests on individual sovereignty, free but not free to take another's freedom. He credits individual genius, quoting Walter Russell, with the West's achievements, and contrasts the histories of China and the West, arguing that communism turned Chinese civilization from its course, though he voices deep respect for its martial arts. Chance suggests communism may act like an egregore in the collective psyche, and that what people call God is, at root, freedom.
extra.michael-wann-inception-etheric-pathways: Decolonizing the imagination and meeting Michael Wann Lockstep media and the lockdown narrative Neural pathways in us, etheric pathways in the world Flow arts, rock climbing and rising skill levels Inception and the multi-tiered dream reality Minds of Men and the cybernetics movement Michael's hundred year plan since the first computer Controlled awakenings and the dream within a dream Trivium before quadrivium: reason, then imagination Etheric pathways and Michael's river research Chance on Sheldrake and morphic fields Chance on rivers, ley lines and etheric influence Just as hypnosis can establish neural pathways in the brain, what we call magic can establish etheric pathways in the world. Michael Wann The more people that were doing something and becoming skilled at it, the more quickly someone that was new to it could jump in and get to a high level at it. Michael Wann Neural pathways inside, etheric pathways outside Chance reads Michael's formula aloud: just as hypnosis can establish neural pathways in the brain, what we call magic can establish etheric pathways in the world. Michael describes neural pathways as entrained routes linking a thought to a behaviour, laid by experience, repetition and strong emotion and set off again by anything symbolically similar, recalling touching his face in the mirror whenever he rehearsed a line he did not believe. Applying as above so below, he maps rivers onto the body's veins and arteries and argues that what he calls the planet's oldest river, the Susquehanna, anchors the first expressions of computing, globalism and wired electricity. Skill that spreads through the collective Chance says he first sensed a link between personal patterns and a collective field at music festivals, watching the average level of hula hoopers rise each year as more people practised, and he points to climbers who now free climb in hours big walls that first took weeks. He pictures skills as tunnels others have already dug. Michael calls flow arts, festivals and climbing the most human things imaginable, set against war as the most unhuman, and argues for a split where 20 percent competition brings out our best. In his outro Chance adds Rupert Sheldrake's morphic fields and a rat maze experiment he remembers hearing about. Inception as a map of the dream Michael rewatched Inception and reads it as a model of an engineered reality: a machine hosts the shared dream, its maze is designed by a psychology student rather than a coder, lucid dreamers work the mark, and when the subconscious senses something is wrong a second dream waits behind the first. He links this to Gnostic ideas of an archonic false reality, to Truthstream Media's Minds of Men on the cybernetics movement, and to the internet as the ultimate machine. Chance adds his idea of controlled awakenings, citing the Protestant Reformation and the QAnon phenomenon as moments where people thought they woke up but were steered into a new worldview. Michael's hundred year plan theory Michael describes what he calls a hundred year plan that began with the first computer, arguing that anyone born since 1945 has been hooked on the culture and technology of their earliest years. He ties the present moment to Jupiter and Saturn moving into Aquarius with Pluto to follow, and says the pressure now is to get people to commit to an inverted, anti-human expression of the Age of Aquarius, which he calls Robosapien rather than human. Because force would incur karma, he argues this dream runs on loopholes, and Chance asks whether a mass inception is steering the manifesting power of millions of imaginations toward a chosen outcome. Navigating the dream as a human Michael's approach to navigating the dream starts with separating human nature from second nature, which he describes as a learned neural pathway, and then tracing anything made back to its origins to ask whether it is in harmony with being human. Computers are his main example: he values being able to talk with Chance across distance but argues the industry rests on a foundation of decay, from rare metal extraction to slave labour. He says the trivium's rational mind must come before the quadrivium's imagination, and that waking up means getting back into the body through dancing, yoga, climbing and flow arts.
extra.laurel-airica-linguistic-ascension: Chance welcomes Laurel Airica back to InnerVerse Kakistocracy and a word that defines the times The secret spells hidden in the English language Sacred path words like earth and heart Entering the god zone by doing what you love Chance on computer code as the new colonizer Two kinds of I in the alphabet Laurel recites her poem about the two I's Murmuration and the human impulse to unite Homer, oral tradition and the memory castle Green language, energy and the name Solomon Chance on reading fiction to sharpen language We are creating the world right now in the image and likeness of the least aspects of ourselves, our least enlightened selves. The culture encourages the beast instead of the best in us all. Laurel Airica The special thing I'm here to tell is that our words create the spell, and that our problems are compounded because English is confounded. Laurel Airica You can even say that the way that English colonized the world at a certain point, when the British Empire was spreading, was also the way that computer code has now colonized the world. Chance Garton One of the obvious sacred path words is the fact that the word earth is the same as the word heart; it's just where you put the letter H. Laurel Airica Since the feeling of my being all depends on how I'm seeing, it's perception, not perfection, that is ultimately freeing. Laurel Airica Trying to attain perfection is impossible, but expanding your perception actually shows you the perfection that's already there. Laurel Airica See if you can get closer to creating as much as you consume, in whatever way feels like your way to do that. Chance Garton English as Spell and Software Laurel Airica argues that English is laced with secret spells, the subject of her most popular video, and that its sounds hide second meanings, as in her pun on the mettle, metal, meddle and medal of mind. She says the British Empire receded but left English behind to colonize consciousness everywhere, and her Word Magic vision statement calls our forked tongue English the leading software of the Western mind, badly in need of retuning and upgrading. In her view its hidden biases work like computer viruses, echoing an antiquated vision of reality that she says the church promulgated as mind control. Sacred Path Words and Double Hearing Alongside the spells, Laurel describes what she calls sacred path words, where innate human wisdom bubbles up: earth and heart differ only by where the H sits, a seven year old she asked guessed the earth is the heart of our solar system, and the heart holds an ear she calls our third ear. Her double hearing turns Chance's word bard into barring the bards so truth cannot be spoken. Chance runs with it, tying bard to lawyers being barred, judges in black robes and Saturn, which he says some ancient cultures called Bar, then turns to rating culture, which Laurel hears as berating. Computer Code as the New Colonizer Chance carries Laurel's point about English into the digital age, arguing that just as English colonized the world while the British Empire spread, computer code has now colonized it, a language most of us cannot even translate for ourselves. He points to the surveillance and AI future he sees coming from companies like Google and Facebook and from intelligence agencies, and to how quickly we accept the top search result as the answer. He describes China's social credit system as the ultimate language prison, a web of words spun around your name that limits where you can go, much like online restaurant ratings. The Little i and the Capital I Laurel reads the alphabet as a code we barely understand, and invites animators to bring her poem on the letter S to life. She starts with the two I's: the lowercase i, its dot floating apart from its line, is for her the mind separated from the body, the small ego that feels diminished and grows irate, while the capital I touches the sky and connects it to earth. Her poem from Word Magic, recited here, ends on perception, not perfection, being what is ultimately freeing, a line Chance reads as saying that widening perception shows the perfection already there. A Global Experiment in the Word Laurel proposes using the lockdown as a global experiment in how powerful the word is, and backs it with quotes she has gathered: Confucius on correcting the language first, Orwell tying political chaos to the decay of language, and Octavio Paz on corruption turning language gangrenous. Her literary lotto invites listeners to download new words and phrases that lift consciousness, with the best ones printed on shirts and mugs to profit the prophet. She pictures humanity joining in a murmuration like starlings, and she and Chance agree that doing what you love, which she calls entering the god zone, raises a contagious vibration.

Chance lays out three ways to read regression material: a linear chain of lives, one shared consciousness that has lived every life, or the unconscious inventing a symbolic answer when a therapist prompts it. Shelley says each has some validity. She personally believes in reincarnation but treats regression as a process, asks open-ended questions to avoid leading, and cares less whether a memory is a real life, an archetype or something seen on the Discovery Channel than whether it brings healing to the present. She says historical verification has not been part of her practice, while Chance points to reported cases of children in India recalling previous families. The RELIEF method and the future self Shelley coined the acronym RELIEF for the process she has used with clients for about twenty years. She compares it to pulling a weed by the root instead of mowing it: find the source event, cut the cords to unwanted influences, often with a guide such as Archangel Michael, then lift the memory with light and frequency. The last step takes the client into a happier future, the one place she says she deliberately leads. Chance likens this to setting an anchor that later choices are drawn toward, a link he ties to Dean Radin's work, and the book gives readers scripts to record and replay. Pain, silence and staying grounded Asked why negative emotions have to be felt, Shelley says pain may not be strictly necessary, but people tend to do the work only once discomfort turns into pain they cannot ignore. She describes ten days of silence at a Vipassana retreat south of Dallas, where sitting still with discomfort echoed what she says Buddhists teach, that thoughts are forms carrying karma from past lives. Chance recalls a stranger handing him black tourmaline and walking him through grounding, and Shelley, who says many people are empaths, leads listeners through a brown grounding light sent down through the feet into the core of the earth. Karma, patterns and chosen challenges Shelley says some people wear their karma openly while others hide it, and that clients usually find several past lives where they repeated the same pattern, which she believes can end once it is recognised. She suggests lives spent in survival mode left little room for that reflection, and floats the idea, controversial by her own account, that souls sign up for some hardships before birth, which she uses as a tool for empowerment rather than victimhood. Chance takes a middle view, and in his outro warns that belief in chosen suffering must never become an excuse for mistreating other people. Imagination as a source of real answers Shelley calls imagination critical to regression and to life, asking readers of Meet Your Karma to record her scripts, play them back and trust the first random thought that floats up, much as they would a dream image; she says the client supplies every answer from the higher self. Chance, calling himself a philosophical idealist, argues that all thinking and perception are forms of imagination, and in his outro says visualization improves with practice. He then describes recording Shelley's exercises for his own self-guided regression, meeting a guide in the form of Gandalf and glimpsing what felt like a life in medieval France.

Chance Garton Fear, trauma and the chance to wake up Matt Landman opens with a line he has long used: if you can wake up to chemtrails, or now to the coronavirus, you can wake up to anything. Chance describes the trauma of the situation as a kindling that can go one of two ways, and argues that every new trauma reawakens old ones, possibly even ancestral memory. Matt likens the daily drip of new rules and headlines to a movie theater of suspended disbelief that holds people in fight, flight or freeze, Chance argues that some people become addicted to fear, and Matt urges listeners to reach out to their neighbors. Chance's doubts about testing and case counts Chance questions whether the coronavirus has ever been purified and isolated, and says the PCR test amplifies genetic material until a subjective cutoff decides who counts as positive. He walks through the World Health Organization's early suspect case criteria, argues that China's February 16 switch to stricter definitions, not quarantine, is what brought its numbers down, and cites David Crowe's paper and the Diamond Princess cruise ship as reasons to doubt how infectious it is. Matt reads a Los Angeles Times estimate of a 0.9 to 3.4 percent fatality rate aloud and argues that mass testing means the curve will not flatten. Is the crisis cover for a bigger agenda? Matt asks who benefits, pointing to the 5G and Beyond Act, which he says was signed just as California locked down, a wave of CEO departures he links to Bill Gates, and the Event 201 pandemic exercise held the previous fall. Chance adds the Federal Reserve changing its capital reserve rules, the EARN IT Act he says would end online encryption, and a sweeping gun bill, HR 5717. Matt points to New Zealand's stage four lockdown and China's social credit system, and Trump's order for General Motors to build ventilators, with bailouts likely to follow, is framed as a drift toward fascism. Disinformation, QAnon and the truth movement Matt, who lobbies his own mayor about 5G, calls the theory that 5G is the virus bait that makes activists sound ungrounded, borrowing a friend's image of a turd in the punch bowl. Chance compares the infighting to 9/11 truthers arguing over thermite and directed energy. He calls the QAnon message of trusting the plan a comfort culture that outsources truth, and Matt, describing co-opted activists he met in the chemtrail scene, says following a faceless source like Q or Anonymous is self-destructive. Matt also says fear-based posts go viral while much of what he posts stalls, proof to him that virality is no longer organic. Real hope versus hopium Matt believes humanity is on a timeline toward ascension that is being hijacked, and says you can either take authority as the truth or truth as the authority. Chance answers that love allows infinity to grow rather than controlling it, that evil can only invert, and passes on Gordon White's advice that the old world is not coming back, so create your own reality, pointing to the April 4 Jupiter and Pluto conjunction as a window to do it. Matt suggests planting gardens, reading ingredient labels and helping neighbors, and Chance closes by contrasting real hope with the hopium of waiting to be rescued.

Learning Forms Without Fooling Yourself Asked what a practice actually looks like, C-Free suggests starting with a classical set such as the Eight Brocades, learning from video, then paying a teacher to check that what you have is the real thing. He warns that energy work carries a danger of simply imagining it, so he urges students to feel movement in the body rather than only visualize it. Chance counters that imagery can give the body a language for sensation, and C-Free agrees, calling a working visualization an inference or VR interface. Both describe the forms as self-teaching, correcting themselves through daily repetition. Song, Breath and the Skill of Letting Go C-Free introduces song, the Taoist idea of relaxing, releasing and letting go, and insists it is physical rather than abstract. He walks listeners through a single breath that sends a wave of relaxation from the skull to the toes, so the muscles feel as if they hang from the bones. In his account, each inhale brings a small arousal and awareness back into the body while each exhale releases it, so a practitioner inhales joy and exhales detachment. Chance connects this to wu wei, describing a point in his practice when the breath itself moved his hands around a ball of energy. Becoming a Spiritual Scientist When Chance describes defocusing his gaze in a mirror and seeing a faint outline shift as he pushed his energy body sideways, C-Free turns the story into a method he calls spiritual science: observe, record and hold off on conclusions. He says clairvoyance is idiosyncratic in a way bodily sensation is not, which he uses to explain why teachers assign different colors to the chakras and why near-death accounts share common events yet vary by person. He also cautions against pushing energy outside the body, and suggests writing experiences down and interpreting them like a dream. Chi, the Subconscious and Psychic Perception C-Free, who teaches Qi Gong and is training as a hypnotherapist, says a major realization for him was connecting Chi with the subconscious mind, treating both as built-in patterns, one named by an Eastern source and one by a Western source. He calls auras a kind of spiritual biofeedback, giving the example of an acupuncturist who might see colors matching the five elements. Citing remote viewer Lyn Buchanan's idea of a seventh sense and the research of Dean Radin, he argues telepathy is real and places perception on a spectrum from confabulation to direct knowing.
extra.becca-tarnas-imaginal-realm: Archetypes, myth and the stories that shape us How Becca Tarnas first found Tolkien Sacred numbers and the One Ring Atlantis, Númenor and Tolkien's Great Wave dream Sun and moon in Tolkien's painting of Faerie Tolkien's creation myth and parallels with Jung How Melkor's shame turned him to darkness Coleridge, imagination and Tolkien's sub-creation What makes a story truly enchanting Creating art as an act of surrender Why nobody in the story fights Sauron Chance's theory of reincarnation in Middle-earth The imagination is actually something that gives us access to a real place, the imaginal realm, that is not physical, it is not simply abstract, it is most definitely not made up. Becca Tarnas Like all universal principles in our cosmos, the truth seems to be founded on paradox. Chance Garton A fantasy for Tolkien isn't something that's made up. It's something that has organically emerged through one and actually been discovered, and then shaped and honed by the artist. Becca Tarnas The reason we feel that longing at the edge of the sea, and that calling for the sea, is because we're remembering creation when we hear it. Becca Tarnas The only thing that makes the shadow or the darkness frightening or threatening is that we don't know what it is. Chance Garton Nothing in Tolkien's accidental. He has revised and edited and so carefully shaped the material coming through him. Becca Tarnas It's not up to us to slay the dragon or defeat the Dark Lord. It's up to us to maintain the small acts of goodness and kindness and decency that we're capable of doing. Chance Garton The enchantment lies in what is inherently beyond us. We as creators are actually along for the journey as much as everyone else in the story. Becca Tarnas Sacred Numbers and the One Ring Chance opens on the numbers packed into the first chapter of The Fellowship of the Ring, Bilbo's eleventy-first birthday and Frodo's coming of age at 33, and Becca argues nothing in Tolkien is accidental. Drawing on the Pythagorean lineage of Western archetypal astrology, she treats number as qualitative, tracing the three, seven, nine and one of the ring poem into the seven stars, seven stones, white tree and nine ships of Númenor. She reads the One Ring as a perverse inversion of sacred unity that tries to homogenize difference, while Chance contrasts it with the hero who individuates into a true one. Atlantis and Tolkien's Great Wave Dream Becca recounts the recurring dream Tolkien described from around age seven, a great wave drowning the land, which he later called his Atlantis haunting. She follows it through The Lost Road, the time travel story he began after a pact with C.S. Lewis, and The Notion Club Papers, where she says a storm foretold for 1987 was later matched by Christopher Tolkien to England's great storm that year. The dream finally settled into the drowning of Númenor behind Aragorn's lineage and Faramir's dream, and Chance takes the episode as a sign, in his view, that imagination can glimpse past and future. Jung, Tolkien and Their Two Red Books Becca's dissertation traces parallels between Carl Jung's Red Book, begun in 1913, and the legendarium Tolkien started in the same years, framed in his fiction as the Red Book of Westmarch, even though the two men never met. She points out that Jung wrote his Seven Sermons to the Dead in 1916, three years before Tolkien's first cosmogony. For her, synchronicities between the two that she says outside influence cannot explain opened the idea that imagination gives access to a real imaginal realm, neither physical nor made up but participatory, an idea she hears in Sufism, Neoplatonism and Gnosticism. Melkor's Discord and the Roots of Evil Becca retells the Ainulindalë, where Ilúvatar gives the Ainur a theme to adorn in song, Melkor weaves in his own discordant theme, and a third, sorrowful theme folds that discord into the whole before the music becomes a vision of the world. In the myth, water still carries that first music, which is why, she suggests, the sea calls to us. She reads Melkor's secret shame and anger as the seed of Morgoth and Sauron, while Chance frames the secret fire as awareness itself and argues evil only twists what already exists, a scavenger rather than a source. Imagination as Discovery, Not Invention Working from Coleridge's Biographia Literaria, Becca separates the primary imagination, the divine creativity behind all perception, from the secondary imagination of the human artist and from mere fancy. Tolkien's essay On Fairy-Stories reframes this as sub-creation: images arise, art shapes them, and fantasy adds strangeness and wonder. She describes Tolkien less as a god of Middle-earth than a witness and translator, a devout Catholic who felt creative work carried creation forward. Chance adds that Ilúvatar simply sings what he sees, and Becca closes on art as surrender, gestated like a child rather than controlled, with enchantment lying beyond the creator.
